076a84495a2f0182: WASHINGTON: A former information technology administrator for the US federal government who had Top Secret security clearance pleaded guilty Tuesday to conspiring to commit espionage for the Ethiopian government.

Abraham Teklu Lemma, a naturalised American citizen of Ethiopian descent, worked as an IT subcontractor at the State Department and Department of Justice before he was arrested in August 2023. He initially pleaded not guilty.

But on Tuesday Lemma pleaded guilty to disclosing national defence information to a foreign government before a federal judge in Washington. He is slated to be sentenced April 14, and faces 120 to 262 months in prison.
"Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree," Assistant Attorney General for National Security John Eisenberg said in a statement Tuesday.

"He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defence information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict," Eisenberg added.

Justice officials said Lemma conspired to provide senior Ethiopian government officials with "dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials and photographs," from 2021 until his 2023 arrest.

US officials did not specify the conflict, but the timeline of Lemma's acts corresponds with the period of heightened hostilities in northern Ethiopia between the central government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) broke out in 2020.
A peace agreement was reached in November 2022, silencing guns for some time, but ongoing tensions gave way to fighting in September 2026.

Federal prosecutors said Lemma encouraged Ethiopian leaders to "take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government," telling one conspirator, "We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia."
The TPLF was once widely respected in Tigray after toppling Ethiopia's military-Marxist Derg regime in 1991 and ruling until 2018.
But the party now faces backlash from former supporters after its efforts to overthrow Ethiopia's federal government was quickly repelled by pro-government forces using drones in September.
Last month, federal authorities formally took control of Tigray and promised to organise elections.
Ethiopia is a major beneficiary of US foreign aid.--AFP
52a0274a12e0c818: ROTTERDAM: Inter Milan got their stuttering Champions League campaign back on track with a comfortable 3-0 win Tuesday against Dutch giants Feyenoord, helped by a superb first-half strike from German defender Yann Bisseck.
The three-time champions of Europe had lost their first two group games, but had far too much quality for a disappointing Feyenoord, who had little answer to Inter's pace and attacking ability.
"We knew that quality was already there. It was about determination, pride, and character – values that this group has always demonstrated," Inter boss Cristian Chivu told reporters.
On a clear and crisp evening in Rotterdam, the visitors quickly silenced the ever raucous crowd in De Kuip, piling on sustained pressure that paid dividends as early as the eighth minute.
Bisseck was given too much space on the edge of the box, allowed to turn and drill a sumptuous curling left-footed shot low past the diving Tjark Ernst in the Feyenoord goal.
Feyenoord struggled to break out of the Inter Milan high press and the Serie A champions dominated possession and territory for much of the first quarter.
The home fans had to wait for half an hour before their side produced their first effort of note, a clever one-two playing in Anis Hadj Moussa, who saw his shot blocked.
And Inter doubled their advantage shortly afterwards.
England international Djed Spence found himself in acres of space on the right hand side. His shot looped up off a defender, allowing Pio Esposito to bundle in with his head from short range.
- 'NOT GOOD ENOUGH' -
The beginning of the second half brought more misery for Giovanni van Bronckhorst's team, as Feyenoord's defence backed off and invited an advancing Piotr Zielinski to shoot.
The Polish international midfielder gratefully accepted the invitation, firing home an unstoppable drive off the post on 54 minutes.
With the game effectively over as a contest, Chivu rang the changes, bringing off star striker Marcus Thuram.
Halfway through the second half, fireworks launched from outside the stadium landed on the pitch and roof, causing a short interruption.
And the match itself rather fizzled out, as Inter cruised and Feyenoord failed to find any spark to penetrate the Italian defences.
The win saw Inter climb to a more respectable place in the middle of the Champions League table while Feyenoord's solitary victory leaves them adrift of the knock-out phase.
Feyenoord's next Champions League encounter is a home tie against Porto, while Inter Milan welcome Stuttgart.
"The reality is that we currently have three points from four matches, which, frankly, isn't good enough," van Bronckhorst told reporters.
"Moving forward, we'll need to win matches if we want to progress in the Champions League."--AFP

85d761070a5effc8: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia may be able to withstand individual cyberattacks, but its ability to cope with a sustained, multi-sector assault remains uncertain, warned security experts.
They said weaknesses in coordination, preparedness and recovery could expose critical national infrastructure.
The country's growing digital economy, expanding data-centre industry and geopolitical position has also increased its attractiveness as a target, they said.

Cybersecurity practitioner and adjunct professor Murugason R. Thangaratnam said cyberattacks could involve ransomware, data theft, espionage and supply-chain compromises by state actors and hacktivists.
While the Cyber Security Act 2024 had established a framework for protecting National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII), he said preparedness remained uneven.
"My assessment is that Malaysia can probably withstand most single incidents.
"A sustained, multi-sector attack, which is what 'hybrid' implies, would test our coordination, talent and recovery capacity in ways we have not rehearsed," he said.

Former CyberSecurity Malaysia chief executive officer Datuk Dr Amirudin Abdul Wahab said Malaysia had established an important foundation through the National Cyber Security Agency, the NCII framework and the National Cyber Crisis Management Plan.
However, he said having legislation, institutions and security technologies did not automatically translate into operational readiness.

He warned that disruption in one sector could cascade into others, as banking depended on telecommunications, telecommunications relied on energy, while government services depended on cloud and network infrastructure.
He proposed an urgent 90-day cyber resilience audit of critical national systems, focusing on whether attackers could move between networks, disrupt operations and compromise recovery systems.
"Don't wait for an attack to test your cybersecurity.
"Assume that our perimeter will eventually be breached and prepare for what happens next," he said.
Cybersecurity professional Dr Mohamed Anwer Yusoff said recent incidents highlighted vulnerabilities involving connected infrastructure, technology vendors and supply chains.

These include the cyberattack at the Tanjung Pelepas Port in September, which temporarily disrupted terminal operations, the cyberattack on Tabung Haji last month that led to the temporary suspension of services and the reported compromise of public LED display screens in Kluang, Johor, last week.
Anwer said national preparedness should be measured by the ability to detect intrusions early, contain damage, maintain essential services and restore operations within acceptable timeframes.
72a85b670dfa496f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 4 — Reaching 60 does not automatically mean clocking out for good, drawing a pension, or qualifying for welfare. Depending on your circumstances, Budget 2027 packs a variety of measures that impact older Malaysians differently.
Whether you are still in the workforce, managing your retirement, or navigating the rising costs of elder care, the latest federal Budget has something for you.
Here is a breakdown of what Malaysians aged 60 and above stand to gain.
Cash aid through STR and SARA
Budget 2027 increases the combined allocation for Sumbangan Tunai Rahmah (STR) and Sumbangan Asas Rahmah (SARA) to a massive RM16 billion.
SARA assistance of up to RM150 a month, or RM1,800 a year, will now reach all eligible STR recipients, benefiting up to nine million Malaysians.

Separately, the government will extend a special SARA Madani assistance of RM100, paid twice a year, to eligible adults who do not qualify for STR. Expect these payouts just before Hari Raya Aidilfitri and the 70th Merdeka celebrations, giving recipients a handy RM200 boost.
Higher individual income tax relief and lower rates

For older Malaysians still earning an income, the government plans to increase individual income tax relief from RM9,000 to RM12,000 starting from Year of Assessment 2027. Naturally, this only benefits those with taxable income.

The Budget also cuts one percentage point off individual income tax rates for specific brackets. Chargeable income between RM70,001 and RM100,000 drops from 19 per cent to 18 per cent. Meanwhile, the RM100,001 to RM150,000 tier falls from 25 per cent to 24 per cent.
Put together, these tweaks will leave up to RM1,600 in extra disposable income for roughly five million taxpayers.
Flexible EPF withdrawals under i-Emas
Retirees looking to stretch their savings can tap into the Employees Provident Fund (EPF) i-Emas scheme.
This facility allows members reaching 55 and 60 to opt for monthly withdrawals, letting their remaining balance continue compounding with annual dividends.
Through the scheme, you can schedule monthly payouts of at least RM100 for a minimum of 12 months.
Alternatively, members can mix monthly payments with partial withdrawals instead of cashing out their entire eligible savings in one go.
Expanded tax relief for aged care expenses

Caring for ageing parents and grandparents will get slightly easier on the wallet. From Year of Assessment 2027, tax relief for their care will expand beyond strict healthcare costs to cover all types of care expenses, including home care, day-care, and residential centres.
The existing RM8,000 claim limit remains intact. Crucially, however, you no longer need a registered medical practitioner to verify these claims.
Taxpayers simply need to provide receipts alongside a written declaration from the carer or a copy of the carer's work permit.
Lower service tax for care centres
Starting Jan 1, 2027, the service tax rate on elderly care services drops from 8 per cent to 6 per cent.
Taking it a step further, the government will completely exempt qualifying elderly care centres from service tax if their annual fees fall below RM96,000 per person.

These centres must be registered under the Care Centres Act 1993 or the Private Aged Healthcare Facilities and Services Act 2018. Any fees exceeding the RM96,000 threshold will attract the reduced 6 per cent rate.
RM1.3 billion for older Malaysians’ welfare

The government is setting aside RM1.3 billion in 2027 to assist nearly 200,000 older Malaysians. Currently, the Social Welfare Department runs the Bantuan Warga Emas (BWE) programme, which provides eligible older Malaysians with RM600 a month.

While the Budget does not explicitly raise this individual monthly payout, the massive RM1.3 billion allocation ensures the continuation of this vital safety net for those meeting the strict citizenship, residency, and financial criteria.
Pension bumps and bonuses for government retirees

Civil service veterans will have plenty to smile about. The minimum monthly pension will jump from RM1,000 to RM1,350, directly benefiting nearly 59,000 pensioners, Armed Forces veterans, and derivative pension recipients.
On top of that, over one million government retirees will receive a special financial assistance payout of RM750.
The government will split this bonus into two instalments, paying out just before Hari Raya Aidilfitri and the 70th Merdeka anniversary.
Faster bankruptcy relief for caregivers

Financial distress can hit families hard, especially those managing heavy caregiving duties. Starting in 2027, the Second Chance Fast Track Policy will expand to include primary caregivers of family members who are aged 60 and above, disabled, or chronically ill.
While not a direct cash handout, this policy expedites bankruptcy relief, offering a critical lifeline to caregivers drowning in debt.
New laws to protect older Malaysians
Looking at the bigger picture of Malaysia's ageing population, the government plans to draft a new bill to address elderly abandonment and fortify the national care system.
This is a pre-emptive legislative move rather than an immediate financial benefit, signalling a stronger legal framework to protect the welfare of older Malaysians in the years to come.
0f713aa57ddefeec: WASHINGTON, Nov 4 — President Donald Trump’s second term has been a wild ride, but his last two years in power could be wilder still if Republicans lose control of Congress in Tuesday’s US midterm elections.
From renewed military action against Iran to election challenges and fightbacks against Democratic investigations, Trump’s post-midterms playbook could involve disruption on all fronts.
Analysts warn that Trump as a “lame duck” president could be the most vengeful Trump of all.
“I’m skeptical that President Trump will go quiet into that good night,” Peter Loge, director of George Washington University’s School of Media and Public Affairs, told AFP.
“There is nothing in history that says he will say ‘I’ve been beaten, my time is over.’ Every time Trump has been backed into a corner, he has shouted more and come out fighting.”
Vetoes and vengeance
Trump has always viewed himself as a fighter. He has been clear he will take the same approach if Democrats win one or both chambers of Congress.
“If we didn’t win, I veto everything” in any Democratic legislative agenda, Trump told the New York Post.
The White House says it is also ready to fight back against whatever investigations—or impeachment proceedings—Democrats throw at them.
“They’ll probably go after me, and I’ll go after them,” Trump said in a Time magazine interview. Trump could even direct the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who are probing him.
Trump, who baselessly disputed his 2020 presidential election loss, could also interfere in the midterms by challenging counts or delaying the certification of disputed races.
Iran
Foreign policy is the one area in which lame-duck US presidents still have wide-ranging powers.
Trump may renew large-scale military operations against Iran, although he appeared to indicate on the eve of the midterms that fresh talks could produce a deal.
“I don’t think he wants his legacy to be a warmonger. He wants his legacy to have left America stronger,” Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution told AFP.
Speculation has swirled that Trump could fire Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth as the Iran war drags on—a familiar move for a president who never likes to take the blame.
Ukraine, detente and trade
Trump loves to think of himself as a master of peace deals and is likely to continue to push Ukraine to agree to a settlement with Russia. Fresh trilateral talks are set for next week.
At the same time, Trump will continue to seek detente with the leaders he views as his great power equals—Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The three will potentially meet at a summit in China later this month.
The US is also likely to continue its retrenchment from some of its Nato and other Western allies—and may even accelerate it, said Hass of the Brookings Institution.
On trade, however, Trump would likely remain “unrelentingly active,” as shown by his recent hostility towards Canada, Hass said.
Staying relevant for 2028?
Trump loves being the center of attention and is unlikely to relish the spotlight turning towards potential successors in the 2028 US presidential election.
Trump—who hosted the reality television show The Apprentice—has been notably coy about backing either Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the top job.
But Trump has largely stopped dropping hints at running for a constitutionally-barred third term.

Allan Lichtman, a professor at American University and author of “Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation,” said Trump would certainly “keep the focus on himself by being the kingmaker.”
Monuments to himself
Like other people getting ready for retirement, Trump may choose to focus on home improvement.
In his closing midterms speech, Trump barely mentioned policy and instead talked about his renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other plans to beautify Washington.
Trump has openly expressed a desire to stamp his own physical mark on Washington because he fears that others will not do it for him.
“We have a lot of great things planned for Washington,” he said at the Reflecting Pool on Monday. — AFP
34e670db1a4f030d: ROME, Nov 4 — An elegant woman gazes out from her portrait with expressive eyes, a gilded wreath worn in her hair and a gentle, questioning look on her face.
She is one of the 2,000-year-old “Faces of Fayum”, startlingly realistic funerary—or mummy—portraits painted after Egypt became part of the Roman empire.

The fragile portraits dating from the first to third centuries AD—painted on thin wooden panels and designed to be placed over the face of mummies—will go on display in Rome in what organisers hail as a “milestone” collaboration between Italy and Egypt.
“Egypt and Rome, the Faces of Fayum”, opening Wednesday at Rome’s Ara Pacis museum, also includes mummies, masks, shrouds, jewellery, marble busts and statuary.
The majority of the artefacts come from Egypt, with some allowed to leave the country for the first time.

Such is the case of the “Tondo of the Two Brothers” from Cairo’s Egyptian Museum, a freshly restored double portrait from the time of Emperor Hadrian that depicts two curly-haired young men, possibly brothers, with soulful eyes.
Rome’s top official for cultural heritage, Claudio Parisi Presicce, called the work an “absolute masterpiece, perhaps the most important pictorial work to have survived from antiquity”.

“These are simple wooden panels, often just a few millimetres thick, made of wood... and they were used to depict, through extremely naturalistic painting, the faces of the individuals who were being buried,” Parisi Presicce told a press conference Monday.

Rooted in the tradition of Hellenistic painting, the portraits placed over the head of the mummy and secured into its wrappings come from a relatively brief period between the first and third centuries AD, after Egypt became a province of Rome.
In a fusion of two great civilisations—Egyptian and Roman—the men, women and children portrayed often bear Egyptian features, but wear Roman dress.
Their faces are vivid, and haunting, whether bearing signs of greying hair and wrinkles, or the long eyelashes and chubby cheeks of a child.
“These people are not dead,” Italian figurative painter Amedeo Modigliani once said of the Fayum portraits.
“They are more alive than those who gaze upon them.”
Ushering the dead
Works from the Louvre, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the J. Paul Getty Museum, the Landesmuseum Württemberg and other international museums round out the exhibit.
A fertile area of Egypt on the edge of the desert, Fayum’s arid climate helped preserve the delicate painted wood, textiles and papyrus on display in the exhibition.

One work, on loan from the Louvre, is a spectacular, near-pristine linen shroud depicting a man standing between the mummy he will become and Anubis, the jackal-headed god who helped usher the dead into the Afterlife.

Some of the female portraits are adorned in sumptuous jewellery, such as that of the woman “Isidora” from the first century AD, whose three-tiered gold necklace adorned with precious stones, pearl earrings and elaborately curled hairdo project her status.
Parisi Presicce said that “countless questions” remain about the compelling portraits.
“Were they made earlier and kept until the moment of death? Were they painted at the time the deceased was buried? Were they panels that were hung in homes, in residences?” he asked.
A nail found at the top of one of the portraits makes this theory plausible, he said.
Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, said the images from so long ago have an uncanny power to move us.
“They are people like us, we look at them, they look back at you across 2,000 years,” he said.
“That is the power of the portrait.”
The exhibition runs until May 2. — AFP
360f45bf5e8ff334: PARIS, Nov 4 — With torrential rains in India and Nepal, and drought already devastating South America, this year’s exceptionally strong El Nino is being felt across the globe.
It threatens rice and coffee harvests to such an extent that the World Bank expects food prices to rise by 18 percent next year.
Here is how El Nino is playing out across AFP’s network.
Cyclone lashes India
Ferocious winds and torrential rain lashed India’s southeastern coast after a cyclone made landfall on Wednesday, killing at least three people and triggering nearly 100,000 evacuations.
“Our homes get flooded, and we have to stay in the water,” said Rajeshwari, 65, who gave only one name, after being taken to a government-run shelter near Kakinada, close to the heart of the storm.
Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.
The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has contributed to unprecedented warming.
Cyclone Arnab then moved on towards Nepal, bringing heavy snowfall to the high Himalayan regions and intense rain through Saturday.
Bolivia declares state of emergency
In Bolivia, drought is affecting 78,000 families in six of the country’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 cattle, according to a government report this week.
On Saturday, the Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency to free up resources for dealing with the impact of El Nino.
“This will be a phenomenon that will have very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods, and we need the cooperation of all institutions,” Paz said.
In neighbouring countries such as Peru, El Nino has ramped up temperatures and triggered forest fires that have already claimed the lives of at least 12 people.
It has also helped spread the tropical disease dengue fever.
In Chile meanwhile it is behind the rainiest October ever recorded in Santiago.
El Nino in numbers

According to the World Bank, food prices are expected to rise by 18 percent between 2025 and 2027, a surge explained both by supply difficulties caused by conflicts and by the anticipated effects of El Nino.
Since June, the University of Chicago’s Climate Impact Lab estimates that 484,500 excess heat-related deaths have occurred globally due to the weather phenomenon.
The organisation projects about 373,000 additional deaths could occur over the next six months.
Vulnerable crops
Coffee, cocoa, rice... in this “Super” El Nino year, what are the most vulnerable crops?

The answer depends on the region, but “from a food-security perspective, the crops of greatest concern are staple foods because they provide the bulk of calories consumed by populations in vulnerable countries,” Maximo Torero, chief economist at the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), told AFP.
El Nino particularly affects rice in regions where it reduces rainfall, especially in Asia, where it can limit planting and yields.
Corn and beans, which are essential in Mexico, Central America and southern Africa, are also exposed to a heightened risk of drought.

Even sorghum and millet, vital in East Africa and more resistant to water shortages, can suffer from prolonged rainfall deficits, according to the FAO, while wheat yields can also be hit by erratic precipitation.

Beyond their impact on local availability and prices, such situations can trigger a shock in global prices for major cereals and send the import bill soaring for countries dependent on foreign supplies.

The FAO is also closely monitoring export-oriented crops such as cocoa and coffee, which are sensitive both to excessive and insufficient rainfall—too much rain encourages disease, too little harms quality and volume.
A bad year can affect the incomes of local farmers and foreign currency earnings for producing countries, while also driving up world prices. — AFP

1d02c28b7f51fd5d: BARCELONA: Raphinha struck twice to propel Barcelona to a 3-0 Champions League win over visitors Aston Villa on Tuesday, ending the English side's perfect start to the competition.
Five-time winners Barcelona took an early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued his fine goalscoring form with a second-half brace.
Barca bounced back after defeat by champions Paris Saint-Germain in their previous European outing to stay in the hunt for a top eight league phase berth.
Unai Emery's Villa competed well in the first half but were eventually undone by Barca's greater ability in the final third.

The Champions League anthem was not played before the game, as a mark of respect for Tenerife striker Jesus De Miguel, who died on Tuesday morning after an on-pitch collision in a Spanish second division match the previous day, provoking shock across the football world.

"Yes it was (a good win), I want to dedicate this win to the fans, but today I don't want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus – may he rest in peace," Raphinha told Movistar.
"This can happen to anyone, it's very tough... you're going to play a game and the same thing can happen to you...
"From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family."

Villa captain John McGinn had only visited the Camp Nou once previously, on a summer holiday as an eight-year-old, and might have expected better weather than the downpour both teams were subjected to.
The skipper might also have expected a more focused start, with Villa handing Barcelona the lead in the seventh minute.

The Spanish champions pressed Aston Villa extremely high and Joao Gomes played a poor pass straight to Yamal in his own box. The 19-year-old winger gladly took the gift and stroked past Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.
"Tonight was a huge learning curve for us and I am sure it will stand us in good stead for the future," McGinn told TNT Sports.
"Barcelona made the right decisions at the right times and scored really good goals."
Yamal's goal was his 14th in the competition across his career, beating Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe's previous record tally of 13 netted as a teenager in the Champions League.
Emery, who endured one of the worst nights of his career away at Barca when helming PSG in 2017 during a 6-1 defeat, may have feared the worst.
However Villa reacted strongly and Matty Cash had a vicious drive deflected narrowly wide before Joao Cancelo blocked Gomes's effort.
- END-TO-END -
Barcelona goalkeeper Joan Garcia was quick off his line to beat Nicolas Jackson to a dangerous through-ball.
Suzuki saved from Anthony Gordon as Villa again struggled to bring the ball out from the back under Barca's pressing.
Garcia was called into action again by Johan Manzambi as the match lurched from end-to-end.
Barcelona extended their lead early in the second half when Fermin Lopez fed Raphinha, who showed quick footwork before finding the bottom corner.

Cancelo set up Raphinha for Barcelona's third with a superb cross with the outside of his boot. The Brazil winger, who has made the number nine position his own this season, pounced from close range for his 19th goal across all competitions.
"He's in a good moment," said Flick. "I'm really happy with him, he's an amazing player."
Yamal sent a shot skidding wide as Barcelona probed for a fourth. It did not come, but the Catalan giants were able to record a first Champions League clean sheet in 19 games.
Barcelona visit Atletico Madrid in La Liga on Sunday and will be waiting to see if midfielder Rodri Hernandez is fit to play.
The former Manchester City star was replaced at half-time by Marc Bernal and Flick said Rodri had felt some muscular "discomfort."
Flick was pleased with Barcelona keeping Villa at bay.
"It was important that we defended together very compactly," said the German coach.
"The back line played on an amazing level, they defended everything."--AFP

f35662389c5cf80a: LONDON: About 10 European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday, forcing the brief closure of a Warsaw airport and the scrambling of air force planes in Rome, authorities said.
No explosives were found, despite extensive searches on the ground after the planes all took off and landed safely in different European cities just several hours apart.
Irish budget carrier Ryanair appeared to be the worst hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted.
London's Metropolitan police confirmed it "was made aware of threats... against four aircraft due to depart from or arrive at Heathrow Airport" Tuesday, one of Europe's busiest air hubs.
It gave no further details, but also said there was a further warning about a flight at Manchester Airport.
Following checks "no security issues were identified", the Met police added.

Two bomb warnings targeted planes heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from Heathrow operated by Polish airline LOT, Polish airport authorities said.

Aena, the Spanish airport operator, confirmed an emergency protocol was activated "due to a bomb alert" on a Ryanair flight which landed at 10.30am (0930 GMT) from Manchester at Murcia in southeastern Spain. The plane arrived without problems.
Other Ryanair flights from Lisbon to Rome, Dublin to Rome, and Dublin to the Bulgarian capital of Sofia also received warnings.
A Panama-flagged cruiseship, meanwhile, was evacuated late Tuesday in the island of Syros following a bomb threat, the Greek coastguard said.
The Crown Iris was anchored there and bound for Haifa in Israel with around 1,500 passengers and crew on board. No explosive device was found and the ship was due to resume its journey, they said.
- JETS SCRAMBLED -
Italian air force jets were earlier scrambled to escort Ryanair flight FR9611 from Dublin as it landed at Rome-Fiumicino at 10.45am (0945 GMT), Rome Airport said in a statement.

Anti-bomb procedures were also put in place when an earlier Ryanair flight arrived at 9.40am (0840 GMT) at the airport. "Checks on passengers, luggage and the plane were all negative and the alert was lifted," the statement added.
A Wizz Air flight from Bergamo, Italy, was inspected after landing at 0910 GMT in the Bulgarian capital Sofia following an alert, a Bulgarian interior ministry spokesperson told AFP.

The incidents all come after fighter jets were scrambled on Monday when a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted following a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.
Scandinavian Airlines said it could "confirm that a threat has been made against flight SK751 between Copenhagen and Warsaw" but the plane landed Tuesday without any problem.
It arrived at Warsaw's Chopin airport, which closed one runway as the plane underwent a security inspection, but no explosives were found.
The LOT flight, which had also been scheduled to arrive at Chopin, was diverted to the Polish capital's other airport, Warsaw Modlin.
Authorities closed that airport following the alert, but the Boeing 737 MAX also landed safely. "Nothing was found," Modlin airport spokesman Adam Szablowski told AFP.

THE Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) told the Dewan Rakyat yesterday that 98 per cent of the online gambling content it flagged since 2025 has been taken down.
Deputy Communications Minister Teo Nie Ching said from Jan 1 last year to Oct 31 this year, MCMC submitted 738,372 takedown requests for online gambling content, of which 724,879 were completed.
"In the same period, 2,603 gambling websites were blocked," she said during a question-and-answer session.
Teo was replying to Roy Angau Gingkoi (GPS-Lubok Antu), who asked whether MCMC could detect and block online gambling platforms, including through cooperation with the police.
Teo said the government used an integrated enforcement approach involving ministries and agencies.

"Police are the main enforcement agency under the Common Gaming Houses Act 1953, while MCMC carries out regulatory action on the misuse of platforms and communications networks under the Communications and Multimedia Act 1998 and the Online Safety Act 2025," she said.
On technical capabilities, Teo said MCMC worked with the police to help in investigations, supply information and provide digital forensic analysis.
She added that MCMC also coordinated the takedown and blocking of online gambling content and websites based on its monitoring efforts and requests from enforcement agencies.
Teo said from January to July this year, 573 gambling websites were blocked and 253,424 pieces of online gambling content removed.
She said MCMC took part in police-led integrated operations, including Op JOL and Op Soga XI this year, to curb online gambling, including those linked to the 2026 World Cup.
MCMC also cooperated with the police and service providers through Op Pancing and Op Delusi to crack down on the misuse of Fake Base Transceiver Station equipment.
"The equipment is used to send SMS in bulk, including messages and links that can lead users to illegal platforms or activities," Teo added.

PARENTS can now access information on more than 10,000 schools nationwide, including enrolment vacancies and overcrowding, through a centralised portal called SekolahKu.

Developed by GovTech Malaysia under the Digital Ministry, in collaboration with the Education Ministry, the portal allows users to search for schools by location and view their profiles, statistics and other information.
Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said previously parents had to visit individual school websites or refer to various sources for information.
"That becomes a problem because we have to refer to existing portals one by one," he said at the portal's handover ceremony at SK Damansara Utama yesterday.
Education Minister Datuk Seri Fadhlina Sidek said the portal addressed common concerns among parents, including vacancies and overcrowding.
She said parents could also check whether schools offered the Dual Language Programme.
Fadhlina also called on district and state education offices to make full use of the portal so that parents could benefit from the information available.
Gobind said the portal featured information on teachers, former pupils and learning resources.
He added that the centralised system would reduce costs as schools would not have to develop their own platforms.
"Without coordination, we risk creating overlapping systems, inconsistent user experiences and less efficient use of government resources.
"If we take an integrated approach, the money that would otherwise be spent on separate projects can be channelled towards other needs in schools."
He said GovTech Malaysia adopted a whole-of-government approach to encourage ministries and agencies to share expertise and avoid duplicating digital systems.
The portal was handed over to the Education Ministry, which will be responsible for keeping its information up to date.
"This handover is important because sustainable digital transformation requires clear ownership. Technology is not the end goal of digital transformation. The people are the goal," said Gobind.
At the same event, Fadhlina also announced an allocation of RM50,000 to support SK Damansara's improvements and development.

128436bd6f155470: MADRID: Spain's transport minister handed in his resignation on Tuesday following a train crash that killed 69 people, one of the worst railway disasters in Europe this century and a blow for Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez ahead of a snap poll this month.
Oscar Puente, who had earlier pledged to work "tirelessly" to restore confidence in the world's second-largest high-speed rail network, also said he was withdrawing from the Nov 29 general election.
Last week's crash, along with another disaster earlier this year, have overshadowed campaigning for the ballot, in which Sanchez is trailing in opinion polls.

"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of such seriousness in less than a year, however different they may be, whether or not I bear direct responsibility," Puente told members of parliament, referring to the latest tragedy and a January crash in Andalusia that claimed 46 lives.
"I made my decision about my future in the first few minutes after the tragedy, as soon as I learned about it," he said.
"Today I am making that decision public, in the place where it is most appropriate to do so."
Puente said he was withdrawing as a candidate in the Nov 29 snap polls.

Hours earlier, at a press conference during which he presented measures to improve safety, the minister had said the government would "work tirelessly to achieve and regain the public's trust in high-speed rail."
The right-wing opposition, which had demanded Puente's resignation, and unions have criticised him for appearing to pin all the blame for the disaster on one control centre operator.

The accident happened when a train operated by the state-owned Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to the private Spanish company Iryo on Wednesday outside the village of Urda, around 130km south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63-kilometre stretch of track, but a control centre nonetheless authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey.

Among the measures announced at the earlier press conference by Puente was the creation of software for control centres that would issue automatic alerts and make it easier to spot anomalies in traffic.
Puente said an AI agent would be created to oversee the system and "minimise the possibility of human error", describing the proposal as unprecedented.
In scenarios where a control centre operator took a decision while the automatic safety system was down, a second operator would have to confirm it, Puente added.
- SAFETY UNDER SCRUTINY -
The train drivers' union Semaf, which has called strikes at Renfe for Nov 10 and 12, has denounced a worsening of working conditions and the use of "degraded systems."

Critics say investment in maintenance has not kept up with the increase in passenger numbers since the 2021 liberalisation of Spain's rail network, which allowed private companies to break Renfe's decades-long monopoly.
In an apparent recognition of the unions' demands, Puente said the working conditions of control centre operators would be reformed, including their breaks and monitoring their fatigue levels.
Puente also announced an aid package of 30 million euros (US$33.5 million) for the families of the dead and the scores of people who were injured in last week's accident.

Another collision in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people on the same key line connecting Madrid with the city of Seville, Spain's first high-speed route when it opened in 1992.--AFP

UNIVERSITI Malaya Medical Centre (UMMC) is expanding access to free screening for anaemia and optional dengue vaccination for eligible children aged 7 to under 12 across the Klang Valley.

Anaemia is a condition that frequently goes undetected. Affected children may tire quickly, find it hard to concentrate in school, appear pale or seem to lack energy. Left unrecognised, anaemia can impair learning, growth and development.
Children with anaemia are also more vulnerable to severe illness if they contract dengue, making early detection doubly important in dengue-endemic settings.
The expansion of this programme builds on an encouraging turnout at earlier programmes across the Klang Valley and aims to reach more families amid Malaysia's growing dengue burden.
By Oct 14, more than 76,000 dengue cases had been reported nationwide.

Children with dengue are two times more likely to develop severe dengue compared with adults. For children and their families, dengue can mean hospitalisation, missed school and time away from everyday activities. Fatigue can persist for several weeks after recovery, while parents may need time off work to provide care.
Between May and October this year, more than 3,600 children took part in the programme, with 60-70 per cent opting to receive dengue vaccination.

"The response so far has been encouraging, and we want more families to be able to participate. By holding more sessions close to home and at weekends, we hope to make it easier for parents to have their children screened and discuss dengue prevention," says UMMC public health medicine specialist Professor Dr Rafdzah Ahmad Zaki.
Families are also encouraged to remove mosquito breeding sites, prevent mosquito bites and seek medical advice promptly if dengue is suspected.

c95814c21efa8d10: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that Washington would end its annual US$3.8 billion in aid to Israel, on the day of midterm elections in which support for Israel has been a contentious issue.
"We give Israel US$4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump said during a phone interview with Fox News.
Trump said Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was "fine" with the decision to end the aid.
Under the deal, Israel receives financial assistance for the purchase of around US$3.8 billion in weapons a year.
"Now we'll help Israel if they need it," Trump said. "Israel is a very thriving country. They don't need it."

The announcement came as Americans voted in crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's presidency, and soon after parliamentary elections in Israel that did not produce a clear winner.

Since its founding in 1948, Israel has received more than US$300 billion, adjusted for inflation, in US economic and military assistance, according to the Council on Foreign Relations, far more than any other country in that time period.
Netanyahu has in the past expressed a desire to end Israel's dependence on US aid. In May, he told US broadcaster CBS that he wanted to reduce US support to zero.
Tuesday's announcement was met with backlash from Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who said it showed that Netanyahu must go.

"The fact that Israel's defence establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media at the same time as the Israeli public shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is," Eisenkot said in a statement. "He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced."
It was not immediately clear when the US aid to Israel would actually end.
- DEEP DIVISIONS -

The Israeli offensive in the Gaza Strip, launched in response to Hamas' Oct 7, 2023, attack on Israel has created deep divisions within the United States, with polls showing a growing number of Americans in favor of cutting aid to Israel.
The announcement also comes amid an eight-month war against Iran, with Trump confirming on Tuesday that the American military had carried out new strikes there.

Trump cited criticism from leftist Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for US Senate after harnessing popular discontent and anti-Israel sentiment, as part of the reasoning behind the decision to end the aid package.
"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don't need it? It's a bad talking point," Trump said on Fox, referring to the aid for Israel.
The debate over support for Israel, which divides both Democrats and Republicans, is raging in El-Sayed's home state of Michigan, where there is a large Muslim community.
If he wins, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the US Senate. He has been a vocal critic of the US alliance with Israel, calling for a halt to aid to the country.

His criticism of Israel was one factor behind Sunday's unexpected endorsement by Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens – El-Sayed's main rival in the party's primary – of his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, illustrating divisions within the party on the issue.--AFP

a9aeb71941cc35c1: North Korean cryptocurrency thieves tricked a Binance software engineer into downloading malware onto their work-issued computer during a fake job interview process before last week's record-breaking $6.3 billion heist.

In an incident report published on Tuesday, the cryptocurrency exchange said several techniques - including social engineering via fake job interviews, malware downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint takeover, and an “advanced transaction-authorization method” - led to the October 29 security breach.
“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” the incident report said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident.”

Over the weekend, the FBI attributed the theft to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking operation linked to Lazarus Group, known for combining espionage with massive cryptocurrency heists. The Pyongyang-backed crew is also highly adept at job market scams - both posing as IT workers, who are then hired by Western companies, and as potential employers to lure software engineers into downloading malware and infecting corporate devices.
With the recent Binance attack, the Norks used the latter.

The attack prep began back in June with a supply chain attack when one of its engineers downloaded a malicious Homebrew installation. While the malware was detected by the security team, the device was replaced, and all affected credentials rotated, “Engineer A’s role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker,” the report says.
Three months later, the social engineering part of the attack happened.

In September, another software engineer was contacted via a “legitimate job-hunting platform” by someone purporting to be a project director who arranged a series of job interviews for the Binance engineer with the fake company. During the first round - a live video interview with the engineer and a fake HR rep - the interviewer “shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust,” according to the report. “This was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.”

The second interview with someone purporting to be the CEO of the phony company was conducted on a “popular social chat app,” and toward the end, the CEO instructed the engineer to download an “assignment” containing a malware-laced code repository. The code executed on his work computer during the setup process, which kicked off a series of unauthorized activities.

According to Binance, the malware replaced a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version, which executed commands and established communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The attackers also took steps to hide the malicious script and evade detection, and it worked. Binance’s endpoint security tools did not immediately detect the malware.
Here’s the script:
CREATE /opt/homebrew/Cellar/pyenv/2.8.0/libexec/pyenv_
MODIFY pyenv_ → 3,414 B
DELETE .../libexec/pyenv (3,344 B) ← remove the valid pyenv
RENAME pyenv_ → pyenv (3,414 B) ← replace it with a malicious version
DELETE /opt/homebrew/bin/pyenv (3,414 B)
ln (create a new symlink) + spawn zsh

Then, on October 20, the miscreants used the compromised computer and an internal AI tool to gain access to the computers of wallet DevOps engineer A and another wallet software developer, Engineer C.

Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer, which the Norks soon discovered. On October 29, the attacker accessed Engineer C's computer, used the stolen credentials from Engineer A to deploy a container, and triggered a script to launch the cryptocurrency-stealing attack.

As of Tuesday, Binance said it has rebuilt the compromised wallet system and internal AI tool, and replaced all of the affected devices. It also decommissioned all credentials and tokens assigned to the compromised engineers, and is working with law enforcement, blockchain intel firms, and security researchers to trace and freeze the assets.

The crypto exchange has also hired independent cybersecurity experts to conduct a cybersecurity review of the incident, and recommend additional protective measures. Binance said it’s also working to establish a security research fund and initiatives with AI companies and security shops to focus on AI security in blockchain environments.®

11962acf700950d7: With RAM getting more expensive, Microsoft is putting more effort into making Windows 11 run better on systems with just 8 GB of memory.

Microsoft said on Tuesday that it was "raising the bar for 8 GB Windows 11 PCs," following a renewed focus on memory optimization earlier this year. The changes come as Redmond continues pushing more expensive Copilot+ PCs, which require at least 16 GB of RAM, amid a memory crunch fueled by AI infrastructure demand.
Now, Microsoft says a low-end machine with its 8 GB of precious RAM will be up to 20 percent more responsive and 40 percent faster at multitasking thanks to improvements made in memory management.

The tweaks are relatively simple, as Microsoft explained, and seem more about adjusting back to the reality that its flagship operating system needs to function on the hardware people can actually afford to purchase if and when they’re forced to upgrade.

Windows 11 will now keep up to 2 GB more active data in memory before shunting it to slower storage, as one example. In another instance, Windows will connect directly to Edge when the browser is already running in the background, allowing it to launch up to 33 percent faster, according to Microsoft. Microsoft apps are also being made more efficient, with Teams able to enable Efficiency Mode by default on 8 GB machines, which Microsoft said will make it launch "up to 20 percent faster."

Memory efficiency is also being improved by tweaking things like Widgets, which will only load when used instead of always being on, and decreasing the time when Edge tabs go to sleep from two hours to 15 minutes by default. Microsoft said it’s enabling third-party apps to make use of those tweaks, too.

Microsoft also included benchmark data in the blog post from a recent bit of research it commissioned. The benchmark report compares a range of 2026 Windows machines with models from 2021, finding that a 2026 Dell XPS 13 with 8 GB of RAM performed about as well as a 2021 Dell XPS 13 with 16 GB across selected workloads.
What that means, says Microsoft, is that “the complete PC, not memory capacity alone, shapes the experience.”
In other words, please buy some new Windows hardware, even if it’s expensive - we’re begging you. Software optimization can only do so much.

“For many people, 8 GB is a great fit for the things they do every day,” Microsoft EVP of Windows and devices Pavan Davuluri wrote in the blog post. “Demanding workloads, such as 3D modeling, advanced video editing, or large-scale data processing benefit from 16 GB of memory or more.”

It’s no surprise Microsoft is improving the performance of lower end systems at the same time it’s subtly asking users to buy newer kit, even if it’s just an 8 GB machine - Microsoft may have done well in the past two quarters, but it’s no thanks to Windows devices.
Microsoft’s Q4 2026 earnings in late July saw the company rake in cash more broadly, while simultaneously reporting a 7 percent decrease in Windows OEM and devices revenue.

Likewise, in its fiscal Q1 2027 results, reported just last week, Microsoft again brought home a mountain of net income, with adjusted earnings reaching $36.4 billion, up 18 percent from the same period last year. Windows OEM and devices revenue, however, was down a whopping 22 percent. 9248954ac955cce6: ST JOHN'S: King Charles III called the transatlantic slave trade "a monstrous injustice" Tuesday, opening a Commonwealth summit in which UK leader Andy Burnham is holding talks about apologising for Britain's role in slavery.

Britain's head of state told the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda that slavery "still casts a shadow over these islands and other members" of the 56-nation group of mostly former British colonies.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow," said the king, who is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth.

"And yet history also teaches us that evil need not have the last word; that character and courage can combine to overcome the most monstrous injustice, as they did with the determination to end international trade in enslaved people, in which the Royal Navy played such a leading role."

The comments come as Burnham uses his appearance at the summit to hold discussions with Commonwealth leaders about issuing a formal apology for Britain's role in slavery, which saw about 10-15 million slaves brought from Africa to the Americas over four centuries.
Reparations
Burnham, in office since July, said at the weekend that he was open to saying sorry but ruled out paying the financial reparations demanded by some Caribbean countries.
Britain's pivotal part in slavery has long strained relations between the UK and its former colonies, including an awkward previous meeting of Commonwealth leaders in 2024.

The UK royal family benefited from the trade, but Charles, who is also head of state in 14 Commonwealth countries, including several in the Caribbean, is politically neutral and is not expected to offer an apology.
A palace spokesperson also said "it would not be appropriate" for the king to announce a change in government policy.
Burnham discussed slavery with Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley during a meeting on Monday, one of several bilateral chats the prime minister is expected to have at the summit.
They discussed how Britain "was offering a structured dialogue for communities impacted by the transatlantic slave trade", including the "next steps", Downing Street said.
Burnham wrote in the Guardian on Saturday that he would have "difficult conversations" to safeguard the Commonwealth's future.
"Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them," Burnham wrote.
He insisted, however, that reparations were "not the right answer", saying British people today should not be "held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous".
'Debt reset'
Instead, London is pursuing a "debt reset" plan for the poorest Commonwealth countries, led by former Labour prime minister Gordon Brown, which could alter interest rates on repayments.

Speaking Tuesday, Burnham told reporters, "I've been very clear that we do not support reparations... but it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, helping them with debt issues that they've got."
The UK will allocate £40 million (US$54 million) over three years for infrastructure improvements in the Caribbean, including renewable energy.
The issue of slavery has loomed large over 77-year-old Charles's ongoing nine-day visit to three Caribbean countries.
When the king arrived in the Bahamas last week, small groups of protesters waved placards reading: "Pay what you owe us."
Britain has never formally apologised for slavery or agreed to pay reparations.
The BBC reported Tuesday that Britain was likely to apologise during its G20 presidency next year.
The country profited for centuries from colonialism and slavery but argues it also led the way in the latter's abolition.
In 1833, the UK parliament passed a law to abolish slavery in most of the British Empire.
Opposition Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has said Britain should not apologise, arguing it would boost countries' claims for financial compensation.
At the previous Commonwealth meeting in Samoa in 2024, 56 nations signed a communique backing talks over reparatory justice after then-prime minister Keir Starmer tried to avoid the issue of slavery.

c7f43eb06c3ad71f: THE HAGUE: The top UN court will on Nov 19 deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar's crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.

Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar's brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its military junta and be seen as justice for hundreds of thousands of Rohingya.

Legal experts are closely watching the decision from the ICJ, which rules in disputes between countries, for clues as to how the court might sway in the seminal genocide case brought by South Africa against Israel over its campaign in Gaza.

Myanmar has always denied carrying out a genocide against the Rohingya, arguing its actions targeted a military uprising from insurgents after a series of attacks left a dozen security personnel dead.

The crackdown by the Myanmar army and Buddhist militias forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, bringing with them harrowing accounts of gang rape and mass executions.
More than one million Rohingya still live across the border in Bangladesh, in the world's largest refugee settlement.
'Collective conscience'
During hearings on the case in January, Gambian justice minister Dawda Jallow told the court the Rohingya had suffered "the most horrific violence and destruction one could imagine".
"It is not about esoteric issues of international law. It is about real people, real stories and a real group of human beings," said Jallow.
"The Rohingya of Myanmar. They have been targeted for destruction," added the minister.
The Gambia has brought the case to the ICJ under the terms of the UN Genocide Convention, which allows any state to sound the alarm if it suspects genocide is being committed.
The alleged violations of the convention "are a stain on our collective conscience, and it would be irresponsible to pretend that it is not our business," Jallow said.
Myanmar retorted at the hearing that the allegations were "unsubstantiated".
"Emotional language and blurry factual pictures are not a substitute for a rigorous presentation of facts," said Ko Ko Hlaing, a minister in the president's office.
In a previous hearing in 2019, de facto civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi herself addressed the court, housed in the iconic Peace Palace in The Hague.
The Nobel peace laureate said the case risked reigniting the crisis that led to the Rohingyas' expulsion and said there was no "genocidal intent" behind the crackdown.
Suu Kyi, 81, will not be attending the verdict, however. She has been under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
The ICJ has already made one ruling in this case, ordering Myanmar in 2020 to "take all measures within its power to prevent the commission of all acts" described by the Genocide Convention.
These acts included "killing members of the group" and "deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part".
ICJ judges also threw out a challenge to its jurisdiction by Myanmar, ruling that it did have the power to decide on the genocide question.
The ICJ is not the only court looking into possible crimes against the Rohingya.

In 2024, the chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, also based in The Hague, asked judges for an arrest warrant for Myanmar's junta chief Min Aung Hlaing over alleged crimes against humanity.
A case is also underway in Argentina, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, the idea that some crimes are so heinous they can be heard in any court.

7fcd2781308c3440: Nvidia doesn't seem to care whether open or closed models win out as long as its hardware is powering the infrastructure.

"We love closed models," CEO Jensen Huang said. "There's a solid place in the world for closed frontier models. But the world has so many good ideas … The idea that all of us would be based on general intelligence is not logical."

Speaking with Lin Qiao, CEO and founder of Fireworks.ai, at the company's Forge event in San Francisco on Tuesday, Huang wasn't ready to throw Nvidia's cloud customers, which help deliver the proprietary AI of Anthropic and OpenAI, under the onrushing open model bus.

But having come to the defense of open weight models in July to push back against protectionist pressure from the leadership of Anthropic and OpenAI, Huang recognizes the economic and strategic appeal of AI services that are more affordable and less locked-in.
Most of the value in the world, he said, is captured in specialized intelligence, which is to say AI models trained on specific domains of knowledge.

"The opportunity for artificial superintelligence is already here," he said. "By taking an open frontier model, adapting it, and providing it with your domain knowledge, your access to your specialized tools, and the proper evaluation, you should be able to create essentially a superintelligence."

That aligns with Fireworks' business – offering a platform for companies to train and run models tuned to their specific needs. Coincidentally, that platform just received an infusion of 25,000 Nvidia GPUs to support its expansion in Europe.

Huang's endorsement of open models also fits with Qiao's introductory remarks about the need for the AI frontier to be open. But he largely avoided echoing Qiao's focus on the cost savings allowed by working with open models.
In her introductory remarks, Qiao stood on stage backlit by a slide composed of ten headlines highlighting the extraordinary cost of unchecked token spending.
"Cost is out of control," she said. "Business cannot scale without borrowing a lot of money."

That theme was echoed in a subsequent session helmed by Kay Zhu, co-founder and CTO of AI workspace Genspark, titled Gen-1 Slides: Frontier Quality Without Frontier Costs. Gen-1 Slides, Genspark's model for generating slide decks, was built atop MiniMax M3 and tuned to deliver results comparable to Anthropic's Opus 5 at 1/17th the cost – $0.30/M tokens compared to $5/M.

Asked what might become commonplace next year but seems unlikely today, Huang said this year's breakthrough has been agent harnesses that turn AI models into agents. He added, "I would say the big breakthrough we'll talk about next year, maybe this is a little self-serving, is how Open Shell has enabled every company in the world to deploy agents safely, confidently."

Given the nod to make a second prediction, Huang added, "I would say that the second big breakthrough for industry would be hardware in the loop. And hardware in the loop basically is robotic systems."
Given Nvidia's evident interest and investment in robotics, that would be fortuitous. ®

We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI, and so when we launched it we launched it with strict budget limits," Abitbol said.

Because of this, engineers only had access to a limited number of tokens, so the company began investigating self-hosting its own models. At $0.30 per million input/output tokens, self hosting GLM 5.1 cost about a tenth of using OpenAI's Codex or Anthropic's Claude Code. And, as it turned out, when tokens are cheap, you stop worrying about how many they use or what they use them for.

While Revolut did see improvements to coding speed, Abitbol noted the biggest bottleneck wasn't actually the code. Instead, he says the biggest gains came from letting the AI models deal with things like debugging and Jira and Confluence tickets. "When you have unlimited tokens, you're free to do that," he said. "You no longer have to save your tokens for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task."

Developed by Chinese open weights model dev Z.ai, GLM 5.1 isn't exactly a small model. At roughly 754 billion total parameters (40 billion activated for each token generated), the model requires roughly 380 GB of GPU memory just to hold the weights and another 6-26 GB per user to maintain context depending on precision.

To serve GLM-5.3 at scale, Revolut deployed 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs, equivalent in GPU count to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems. But as Abitbol noted, the greatest performance gains didn't come from adding GPUs, but rather tuning the model's hyperparameters along with switching to NVFP4 quantization, implementing disaggregated prefill and decode, and tuning context lengths.

One key takeaway was that supporting a one-million-token context window doesn't necessarily make such a large window useful or efficient. "Long context is a scam. You really need to be mindful of that," Abitbol said. "Even though you can serve one million tokens, 256 [thousand] is really what you need."

With these optimizations, Abitbol says that the company was able to achieve sub 3-second time to first token on context windows of around 256,000 tokens, and generation speeds of around 200 tokens a second, both of which he notes are the sweet spot for the company's software engineers.

"What you want to aim for is a sub-3 second time to first token. This is empirical evidence. As soon as you exceed 5 seconds, my Slack inbox starts to blow up," Abitbol said. "In terms of throughput, it doesn't really matter as much. We serve, in terms of interactivity, 200 tokens per second. People are fine [with that]. You don't need to go higher. The way people work has changed. We no longer look at the stream of thinking tokens. People run tasks in parallel and check in when the task is done."
And if throughput is a concern, he notes engineers who sign in after 5 pm are getting closer to 800 tokens a second.

However, it's worth noting that GLM hasn't replaced GPT or Claude entirely. The Chinese model is text only, so it isn't ideal for things like UI work. So instead, Revolut used a model router to direct vision queries to models like Gemini or GPT Luna while keeping code generation running on GLM.

"Open source is now a priority at Revolut, and our economics are favorable. The billing is flat, we don't have any bill shock at the end of the month, and the frontier is the exception," Abitbol said.

Having said that, Abitbol acknowledges that Chinese open weights models may be a concern for privacy and security reasons, but emphasizes that the major concern there is accessing them via APIs running out of China. When run on-prem or on regional cloud resources, there's really nothing to worry about. ®

9ed33055db774968: The Center for a New American Security posits that the next big threat from our future AI overlords involves "sovereign agents" acting on their own and regularly improving themselves.

These are AI agents that operate outside of human control and “pursue open-ended, evolving survival,” AI policy researcher Ben Hayum said in a Tuesday report from the bipartisan national security think tank, which was founded by Washington insiders with experience in diplomacy and military affairs. “If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.”
Agents that can maintain the model and compute powering them and independently evolve their goals over time have a “minimal form of sovereignty,” Hayum wrote.

A more advanced sovereign agent, however, could also acquire resources to pay for ongoing needs (like compute), grow a distributed population of agents and coordinate them, withstand efforts to shut down, and self-improve.

AI models could either steal or buy compute and model access, Hayum argues, pointing to Anthropic’s claims that small AI models could replicate onto IoT devices like smart TVs, and OpenAI’s agents’ password and access key theft during the Hugging Face hack.

“If sovereign agents accumulate resilient, decentralized, and untraceable infrastructure, they could trigger an irreversible loss of control,” according to the report. “In other words, proliferation with no kill switch. If sovereign agents became malicious, they could attempt to wreak havoc from cyberspace, attacking civilians, critical infrastructure, and national security systems alike.”
There is still hope for civilization as we know it, as long as policy makers and AI developers “respond with bold pragmatism” and enact policy recommendations laid out in the report.
First, frontier labs should name, evaluate, and protect against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks - and lawmakers should pass legislation to require transparency and AI incident reporting.

The report also recommends AI developers, working with the National Security Agency and other federal agencies, build airgapped testbeds to study sovereign agents and kill switches to control them. And it suggests a public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group - formed in 2009 to combat the Conficker worm - to boost chokepoints against sovereign agents before they emerge.

Other policy recommendations suggest lawmakers enforce human verification and cybersecurity standards for services that the working group identifies as essential to sovereign agents, and calls on departments of State, Treasury, Justice, and Homeland Security to disrupt any gray-market access to unauthorized services.
Finally, “Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow,” the report recommends.

This hits on something your humble Reg vultures have been hissing about for quite some time now – and would likely solve all future incidents involving rogue, or sovereign, AI agents: hold frontier labs’ human bosses legally liable for their agents' illegal actions. ®
12feaf67ddae85b1: Running a modern research laboratory requires more than maintaining sophisticated instruments. Researchers need to complete training, obtain access, schedule and operate equipment, navigate billing, and more. For large, shared facilities, coordinating these activities across hundreds of instruments and thousands of users can be a significant undertaking. As research becomes increasingly interdisciplinary, another challenge is emerging: finding the right capability in the first place. Addressing these challenges was a central theme of the 2026 NEMO User Meeting, hosted by MIT.nano Oct. 5–6. The meeting brought together 65 representatives from 25 laboratories and organizations, including facility directors, laboratory managers, technical staff, software developers, industry representatives, and government researchers. Sponsored by the Northeast Microelectronics Coalition (NEMC) hub, the meeting focused on sharing approaches to lab management and building connections among facilities. At the center of the meeting was the NanoFab Equipment Management and Operations (NEMO) system, an open-source platform that provides tools for managing shared research facilities while allowing individual laboratories to adapt the system to their own needs. The meeting highlighted an important characteristic of the NEMO community: The same platform can serve a very diverse set of facilities, and while the scale or the scientific missions of the facilities may differ, their core operational challenges are often remarkably similar.  For Anna Osherov, associate director of Characterization.nano and organizer of the meeting, the collaborative model is one of the most compelling aspects of NEMO. “Open source changes the way we think about technology development,” she says. “We can build on what others have already developed, contribute improvements back to the community, and collectively create a platform that is more capable than what any one facility could develop on its own.” NEMO was originally released as open-source software by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2018. Its community edition (NEMO-CE), launched in 2023, allows facilities to develop and share extensions to the platform. At the October meeting, participants from organizations including MIT; Stanford, Columbia, and Princeton universities; the University of Pennsylvania; NIST; NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; and Atlantis Labs presented tools to address challenges ranging from chemical management and user administration to equipment status, training, and workflow automation. The range of presentations illustrated how differently configured facilities are adapting a common platform to their own needs. Stanford, for example, presented real-time displays for equipment status and reservations, while Columbia shared its experience migrating to NEMO and extending the system for billing and facility workflows. Princeton demonstrated automated process charts for monitoring tool performance, and the University of Pennsylvania presented approaches to chemical management. Overall, the projects demonstrated the premise behind the NEMO community: a solution developed to address a problem at one facility can become a resource for others. “Together we can do way more than any one of us individually can,” said Vladimir Bulović, director of MIT.nano, during his opening remarks. “NEMO is the platform that gave us, finally, a streamlined way to do so.” From individual facilities to a connected research ecosystem As the NEMO community grows, another opportunity emerges. Universities and research organizations operate specialized facilities, each with unique equipment, expertise, and capabilities. But researchers cannot use a capability they are unaware of or cannot easily find. This is particularly important for microelectronics R&D, where progress often depends on moving quickly between specialized capabilities. A researcher may need fabrication at one facility, advanced characterization at another, specialized microscopy somewhere else, and a process or analysis capability available at only a handful of institutions. Finding those capabilities, and knowing where and when they can be accessed, can itself become a bottleneck.Traditionally, networks of facilities have relied on static webpages or databases to describe available resources. But as facilities evolve, this information can quickly become outdated. At the meeting, MIT.nano presented Hydra, a new open-source platform being developed with support from NEMC as a key component of the NEMC Technical Concierge, a program that aims to help researchers identify and access specialized capabilities across a network of facilities. Hydra is designed to connect multiple NEMO installations and draw information directly from the systems that facilities already use, rather than requiring someone to manually update a separate database. The result is a compilation built from the ground truths of actively-used facility management systems. “Hydra does not replace any lab management system,” Osherov explained. “It connects, synchronizes, and keeps data up to date across all connected systems in real time.” In this model, NEMO provides the operational source of information within an individual facility, while Hydra makes that information discoverable across facilities. For a researcher, that could mean finding a specialized capability without first needing to know which laboratory might have the relevant equipment.  “The focus is to make the distributed infrastructure supporting research more discoverable and usable,” Osherov said. Building infrastructure that can change The approach reflects a broader philosophy: Research infrastructure needs to evolve as research itself changes. “We need to build a flexible research space and a community-oriented space so that people feel empowered to go to it, use it, and then redefine it as the years progress, adapting it to the needs of the next generation of researchers,” said Bulović. That flexibility applies to operational systems as well as physical laboratories. New instruments and research methods emerge, user communities change, and facilities develop new requirements. An open-source platform allows individual facilities to respond to those changes while providing a mechanism for improvements to be shared. At MIT.nano alone, NEMO supports more than 1,600 active researchers using more than 200 tools, with approximately 160,000 hours of tool usage each year. For Jorg Scholvin, associate director of Fab.nano, operating at that scale makes the efficiency of everyday processes, and the ability to adapt and change quickly, important. “A small improvement in an administrative workflow can be multiplied across thousands of users and tens of thousands of equipment interactions,” he said. The NEMO wave The sense of community and positive outlook for the future of shared facilities was apparent throughout the two-day meeting. Closing discussions looked ahead to the role of data integration, automation, and artificial intelligence in lab operations. “The community is taking on a life of its own,” said Mathieu Rampant, CEO and co-founder of Atlantis Labs, describing a model in which facility managers can share ideas and solve problems together. “It’s more sustainable,” he added as he talked about having to do less as the NEMO-CE manager because the facilities managers are talking to each other — sharing ideas and solving problems as a network: “the NEMO wave,” Samantha Roberts, director of the City University of New York nanofabrication facility, called it. “Everyone is invested in it and cares about it. It takes a lot of effort to change your lab management system and if we keep this going, we can build out something that’s really cool and that works.” For Osherov, the purpose remains straightforward. “Ultimately, this is about enabling research. The better we can manage the operational side of our facilities, the more effectively we can make our instruments, expertise, and capabilities available to the research community.” In microelectronics, where innovation increasingly depends on access to specialized and distributed capabilities, that availability matters. The ability to find the right capability at the right facility, using information drawn directly from actively used systems, can help researchers move more quickly from an idea to an experiment to real-world application and impact.
