9b8e76b45c503938: The GSMA wants governments and regulators to work more closely with mobile operators to help protect networks against growing risks from extreme weather.

As the global body representing the mobile network industry, the GSMA claims that severe storms and floods already cost operators $1.7 billion annually to repair damage to cell radio sites, and it believes that figure could nearly double to more than $3 billion a year by 2050, under the climate conditions expected then.

The GSMA sets out its findings in a six-part research series, Futureproofing Connectivity: Climate Risk and Resilience in Telecommunications, alongside a separate document outlining its Policy Principles for Mobile Network Resilience.

The report identifies weather-related risks that can affect telecoms networks, along with the associated restoration costs. Towers, masts, and rooftop sites are particularly exposed to wind and storms or lightning, for example, while ground-level equipment at mobile sites can be inundated in flooding incidents.
High temperatures can cause radio equipment to overheat, while heavy rain can degrade wireless signal strength, and infrastructure in coastal locations may be exposed to storm surges.

However, the report fingers the electricity supply as the biggest vulnerability. If that gets knocked out, the network could go offline once any backup power is exhausted, which may take anywhere from a few hours to considerably longer, depending on the site.

Under current climate conditions, the cost of damage to cell sites is estimated at $1 billion associated with severe storms, while river and coastal floods account for $577 million and $124 million, respectively.
Based on projected mid-century climate conditions, the GSMA expects costs due to severe storms to rise significantly to about $2.37 billion, accounting for three-quarters of all damage.
The report asserts that cell network resilience requires a whole ecosystem approach, pointing out that if severe weather impacts power networks, then that also affects the telecoms infrastructure.

The GSMA says that network firms have traditionally managed the operational risks that may affect network availability, but claims they face barriers in conducting full assessments of those associated with climate change.

Some of these barriers are internal, such as lack of shared information between departments. Other barriers are in the different regulatory reporting frameworks, with infrastructure rules tending to focus on service continuity, while climate disclosure frameworks focus on governance, financial exposure, and reporting for investors and other stakeholders.
The report lists separate recommendations for network firms and for policymakers and regulators.

Operators are advised to embed resilience by design, using modeled projections for severe weather and future risk scenarios. They are also told to plan and test resilience across the wider ecosystem, engaging with others such as public authorities.

When it comes to policymakers and regulators, the report asks for resilience frameworks to be developed through consultation with the operators. It also advises coordination among mobile operators, electricity and fuel providers, and emergency services to help maintain vital communications during major disruptions.

And as if that isn't enough to chew over, the separate policy document sets out five principles for governments and regulators. These include avoiding prescriptive regulations and instead promoting outcome-based policies, encouraging dialog and consultation between governments, regulators, and operators, and developing resilience as a cross-sector responsibility.
“Mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure,” says GSMA Foundation president and chief regulatory officer John Giusti.
“Whether responding to extreme weather, power failures or other major disruptions, people, businesses and emergency services depend heavily on mobile networks,” he added.

“Severe weather is already costing the industry billions of dollars, and those costs are set to rise substantially. Building resilience will require a coordinated effort amongst operators, governments and the wider ecosystem.” ®

d47fc09b56067629: Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories have developed a method to make asteroid deflection modeling faster and more detailed. Their simulations also demonstrated just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate efforts to deflect a threatening space rock.

Sandia researchers, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, were looking for a way to better model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid can change its trajectory, as explained in a recently published research paper.

“Before, the calculations were so time-consuming, one could not do very many of them,” Moore told The Register. “So it was very difficult to explore different scenarios, different asteroids, or different mission concepts.”
The complexity of those calculations forced earlier researchers to make compromises, often modeling asteroids as spheres or simplifying the physics involved.
Perfectly spherical asteroids are rare, and their irregular shapes present an additional challenge for those keeping an eye on the skies to avert a potential asteroid apocalypse.

To overcome the computational problem and enable better modeling of irregular asteroid shapes, Moore and his team combined two high-fidelity simulation codes already in use at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates the behavior of low-density gases.
As Moore explained to us in an email, both codes are good at one particular part of asteroid impact modeling, but bad at the other.

“ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” Moore told us. “This is a problem for asteroid deflection simulations, because as the gas expands around the asteroid, the calculation time goes up.”
Earlier asteroid simulations using ALEGRA typically modeled asteroids as spheres to reduce calculation times.
“SPARTA is more efficient at low gas densities,” Moore said. “The problem is, conversely, SPARTA gets more difficult to run at high gas densities. So the key here was using both codes.”

In Moore’s model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA tackles the more dilute regions of an irregular shape. The result is two codes handling the parts of the problem they're best suited to solve, reducing the overall computational burden.

The combined approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods, Moore said in a Sandia press release, while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection in irregularly shaped asteroids.
Moore data, more problems
The improved simulations reveal just how much asteroid shape and orientation can complicate attempts to calculate the outcome of a nuclear deflection.
“We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.”

Deflection simulations using detailed models of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu, and Itokawa – found that irradiating different sides of the same asteroid with X-rays from a nearby nuclear detonation could produce as much as a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences in deflection velocity depending on which side faced the blast.
In other words, we need to be incredibly precise about where we detonate a nuclear device near an asteroid, or we risk giving it a much smaller shove than intended.

With that in mind, the paper points out that we might know little about an incoming asteroid, and might not have enough time to get a good picture of it before attempting to deflect it and prevent life as we know it from ending in a planet-wide conflagration. We also can’t be quite sure an asteroid’s orientation will cooperate once our deflecto-bomb arrives. The team also pointed out that it’s tricky to get an accurate prediction without knowing the composition and internal structure of an asteroid.

One small step for asteroid deflection, one giant heap of new things to worry about, in other words. But hey – at least we’re no longer limited to deflection models that treat asteroids as perfect spheres, even though the real threats are likely to be considerably lumpier.
Let’s just hope we spot an asteroid threat from far enough away that we get a chance to study it first. ®

03e6647c805e886d: Google's Threat Intelligence Group says it has shut down a massive botnet called x.cpe. At its height, x.cpe ran on more than 1.3 million Android TV devices, and unusually, these were Google-certified boxes. Google says its screening process missed the malware due to "obfuscation techniques" employed by Shenzhen-based Videostrong Technology.

In a detailed blog post, the Threat Intelligence Group explains how the x.cpe botnet evolved quickly from a single-stage dropper into a modular three-stage malware platform that sold access to third parties. Manufacturers must have their devices certified if they want access to Google apps and branding, a process that is supposed to catch threats like this. However, Videostrong's compromised boxes, mostly sold under the MECOOL brand, evaded detection by using a backdoor to remotely install the malware after the devices were set up and online.

After devices appeared online, a stub application called x.cpe or com.oemservice would phone home. This package did not have any malicious capabilities of its own, but it had the system-level permissions necessary to install malware modules at the operator's behest. It also disabled Play Protect, which would have otherwise flagged the silently installed packages as malicious.

e631c23b6969916d: JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities have arrested three people for allegedly tapping President Prabowo Subianto's phone, police said Tuesday, with a minister identifying the suspects as a general and senior police officers.
Prabowo, who took office in 2024, has come under increasing pressure for his government's handling of the economy and destructive wildfires in the Southeast Asian archipelago.

Top detective Asep Safrudin identified the suspects only by their initials, LSP, ASN, and EH, and said they were under investigation for allegedly tapping "the telephone number of the President of the Republic of Indonesia" and other prominent figures.
These included government officials and politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople.
Asep told reporters in Jakarta on Tuesday that numbers including Prabowo's were "tapped without any legal basis or without any investigative or inquiry process in accordance with applicable laws."

A police officer who became aware of the alleged crime filed a report on Friday, Asep said. Since then, police have examined 10 witnesses and three expert witnesses and seized evidence in the form of 11 mobile phones, an iPad and four flash drives.
If convicted, the suspects face up to 10 years in prison.
In a separate news conference, Justice Minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra identified LSP as an "active police general", but would not name him.

Indonesian media said it was thought to be Listyo Sigit Prabowo – no relation to the president – who was appointed his chief of staff a month ago after serving as national police chief for five years.
Listyo holds the rank of general.
The two other suspects were senior police officials, said Yusril.
A fourth person was also under investigation.
The minister said there was no suspicion of treason.
"As to what material was tapped, and for what purpose the wiretapping was carried out, that is still in the investigative process, which is only at an early stage," he said.
'DELETED TRACES'

Prabowo has in recent weeks faced mounting protests against economic hardship, graft, perceived authoritarianism and his government's handling of months of devastating wildfires emitting a toxic haze that has made thousands ill.
Two years into his term, Prabowo's popularity has reached record lows.
His government has also come under fire from politicians in neighbouring countries as the wildfires have polluted the air as far as Malaysia, Singapore, East Timor and the Philippines.

Asep said the suspects are alleged "to have ordered wiretaps without an official written request from investigators." They were then carried out beginning in 2025 "without any connection to law enforcement efforts."
The suspects also "deleted traces of these actions in October 2026", Asep said.
Prabowo, a former general himself, reshuffled his cabinet for a seventh time last month, appointing Listyo Sigit Prabowo as his chief of staff.
The 57-year-old is reported to be an ally of Prabowo's predecessor and political rival Joko Widodo.

99d1b942fc554f03: TEHERAN: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday confirmed launching strikes on Iran as President Masoud Pezeshkian warned no one would benefit from a return to war.
It came as US voters prepared to cast their ballots in midterm elections that threaten Trump's grip on power.

Iran's chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Islamic republic was "ready for battle with its finger on the trigger", while deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Iran retained the right to "legitimate self-defence" after the strikes.

Trump confirmed the strikes on Iran in an interview with Fox News, after the Wall Street Journal, CNN, The New York Times and other outlets had reported strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
"They built an anti-aircraft facility... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely," Trump said on the Fox & Friends show, adding that it was a "minor attack."

The US and Israel launched their war with Iran with a massive wave of strikes in late February. The conflict has been stalemated for months.
Asked if Israel was involved in the latest reported strikes, an Israeli military spokesperson told AFP, "No."

The Qeshm attack came just hours after Trump signalled a deal with Iran "could happen", as US voters prepared to cast their ballots in midterms dominated by public dissatisfaction with the war and the inflation it has brought.
"Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible," Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
Iranian state news agency IRNA reported five explosions in rapid succession on Qeshm island, and that some residents reported seeing two aircraft flying in its skies.
Ghalibaf said Tehran had made its position clear.

"The countries of the region should know that, just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.
"The ball is now in America's court to prevent war."
'COMMITTED'
Qatar, a mediator in protracted indirect negotiations between the US and Iran, said it remained hopeful of an interim deal in the war.

"Both parties remain committed to the negotiation process; as we mentioned, we are facilitating the real-time exchange of proposals between them," foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters.
Both sides "are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented," he added.
"We remain hopeful that there is still a chance for a deal to take place," he said, adding Doha was working "towards an interim deal."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Monday confirmed indirect negotiations were taking place.
"Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive," Araghchi told state media.
REOPEN THE STRAIT
US Vice President JD Vance said both he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement.
"We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more," Vance told reporters on Monday.
A senior Iranian official said that Tehran was ready to reopen Hormuz, a key route for global oil and gas supplies, within two days but only if Washington agreed to its long-standing list of demands.

In September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the strait, with demands including ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
"The possibility of implementing this plan in two days is another indication of Iran's good-faith approach," Teheran's foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told reporters at a briefing.
In the lead-up to Tuesday's vote, Trump kept up his threats against Teheran, saying on Sunday that the United States may have to give Iran "the hammer" at some unspecified time.

On Saturday, the US leader said he still had to "take care" of one or two targets including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Teheran denies is such a facility.
Iranian officials have repeatedly warned of wide-ranging retaliation if the US resumes the war.
Authorities in Teheran installed a huge billboard in the heart of the capital, AFP journalists said on Tuesday.
Over a photo of the US president, it reads: "We will kill Trump."

7493204c9aa3fb2f: PARIS: Binance said on Tuesday hackers used a bogus job interview to compromise a computer and an internal artificial intelligence (AI) tool to gain control over the company's wallets before draining US$6.3 billion worth of crypto, in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

In a initial report into what went wrong, the world's largest crypto exchange detailed a sophisticated hacking endeavour that began with an advert for a tampered version of a coding tool in June and set in chain a series of security breaches that culminated in the theft of the crypto on Oct 29.
The FBI has blamed a North Korean hacking group, a claim North Korea has rejected.
Binance has said it is repaying all customers who have lost funds through the hack.
Binance said that the attack started when an employee from its wallet developer team in June downloaded an AI tool that had been tampered with.
The crypto exchange detected this, replaced the device and changed credentials but the employee's role and that of others on the wallet team were exposed to the hacker.

Then in September a second software engineer seeking a new job downloaded "malicious code repository" onto his computer after interviewing for what the person thought was a legitimate role, including meeting virtually with the CEO of a fictitious company.
On Oct 20, the attacker used the compromised computer plus an internal AI tool to gain control of the wallet developer's system and that of a second wallet developer on that team.
On 29 Oct, the attacker used the second wallet developer's computer, using stolen credentials from the first wallet developer, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack.
"This should not have happened, and we apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," Binance said in the report

Binance said that as a result of the hack, it was increasing investment in AI-enabled detection and is working on establishing a security research fund and targeted initiatives with leading AI companies.
7dbe5bea71707eaa: KUALA LUMPUR: Service providers have taken down more than 117,000 pieces of offensive content since 2022 following requests from the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Council.

7d0095c45f87610f: THERE are no compromises when it comes to the concept of halal for Muslims. It governs a Muslim's relationship with God, their spiritual salvation and moral existence.
The concept is encapsulated within the religion's five pillars of profession of faith, prayers, fasting, zakat and pilgrimage to Makkah.

For the pious, the concept of halal goes directly to the core of their Muslim identity. While halal usually refers to dietary requirements, it goes beyond livestock slaughter and dictates how Muslims live their lives.

Wealth, according to halal rites, must be free from mendacity, fraud, thievery or exploitation. Halal compels Muslims to constantly evaluate their careers, consumption and ethics to align with a divine purpose.
The same goes for handling livestock as animals must be treated compassionately before and during slaughter.

That is why Muslims nationwide reacted with shock at the seizure of 6.5 tonnes of raw chicken suspected of being processed without complying with halal certification standards at a Puchong slaughterhouse.

The thought that some of these birds were supplied to Muslim restaurants and eateries is sickening. The abattoir had operated for 20 years yet had evaded enforcement, raising serious questions about regulatory oversight.
Islamic law dictates an animal must be alive at the moment of slaughter, but the method used to stun the chickens — low-voltage water baths — was excessive, enough to kill them.
At a proper voltage, stunning knocks out but does not kill the chickens.
Police, religious authorities and regulatory bodies have scrambled to make this investigation a priority and have been quick to issue updates to the public, even if the investigation is ongoing.

In order to obtain clear answers, every party involved in the chicken processing chain must be identified. The need to trace distribution networks for affected suppliers and businesses is paramount, especially on detecting non-compliant chickens that entered the market.
Consumers and food operators must be given appropriate guidance while investigations continue.
If anything, these measures must be taken to reinstil confidence in Muslims wondering whether the chicken they're consuming is halal. This is a wake-up call on the enforcement of halal standards.
Halal certification, inspections and compliance must not be considered mere administrative exercises.

Effective monitoring must be carried out to identify those who compromise halal requirements, and they must be held accountable through stiff penalties. Above all, transparency is vital to prevent unnecessary panic, especially in an information vacuum.
In essence, halal integrity cannot be left in the slightest doubt and it requires the highest level of sensitivity in handling and communications.

a76e757757c181c9: Password manager mSecure has warned customers to change their passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and potentially remove their passkeys after detecting suspicious activity, but it has not explained what happened or whether anyone's secrets were exposed.

In an email sent to customers on November 3, seen by The Register, US-based developer mSeven Software said it launched an investigation after discovering something amiss with its password management application.

"mSeven Software ('mSeven') recently learned of suspicious activity associated with the mSecure password management application," the company wrote. "In response, mSeven quickly launched an investigation, took steps to mitigate the issue, and engaged external cybersecurity experts to assist."
The company has yet to answer what the suspicious activity involved, when it occurred, or whether attackers accessed customer information.
Its advice to customers, however, suggests that they should take this seriously.

"Given the potential security implications, mSeven recommends that you immediately take steps to protect all confidential information stored within the mSecure password management application," the email continued. "This may include changing passwords, resetting or re-enrolling two-factor authentication methods, or removing existing passkeys."

For anyone with hundreds of passwords stored in mSecure, that's potentially hours of work. And without knowing what happened, customers have no way of telling which credentials they actually need to replace.
The warning has understandably gone down poorly with customers, who have taken to mSecure's support forum demanding answers.

"Please provide more context to your email below advising there has been a security breach," one customer wrote. "It is not acceptable to offer the vague advice 'take steps'. Please state what remedial action is required, and what data was compromised."
Others are wondering whether they're expected to spend the next several days changing every password they've ever saved.
"I have over 800 passwords in mSecure, is the email saying I need to change all of them!" another customer asked.

A separate user, who said they had more than 500 passwords stored in the application, questioned whether the warning applied to every two-factor authentication method and passkey associated with their accounts, or just those used to access mSecure itself.
The confusion has also spilled onto Reddit, where customers have shared copies of the vague notification and questioned what might have happened.

mSeven has yet to respond to The Register's questions, leaving customers to guess whether their data has actually been compromised or the company is simply being cautious. That's not exactly reassuring from a business whose entire purpose is keeping other people's secrets safe.
The company's email concludes: "We regret any inconvenience that this may cause." For customers contemplating hundreds of password resets, "inconvenience" may be putting it mildly. ®

3964f1b6a771e4cc: In 2023, malware tracked as BlackLotus became the first publicly documented in-the-wild UEFI bootkit capable of bypassing Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11 systems. With the industry-wide chain-of-trust mechanism subverted, the malware was able to run malicious code before Windows was fully loaded and many security defenses were operational.

Microsoft had already patched the vulnerability that BlackLotus exploited in 2022. In 2023 and 2024, Microsoft issued additional updates. The first added a new certificate that no longer trusted the vulnerable boot managers. The second provided the means to revoke trust in the digital certificate used to sign older vulnerable Windows boot managers. The organizations infected by the new bootkit, which is tracked under the name BlackX, had installed all of these patches. So how did they fall victim?

Before discussing the incident further, a brief review of BlackLotus and UEFI malware is in order. Short for Unified Extensible Firmware Interface, UEFI is firmware that runs immediately after a computer is turned on. One of its main jobs is to load system configuration settings, identify and initialize hardware components, and prepare the computer to start its OS.
58ffebb1276826ab: GhostBSD, the easiest-to-install flavor of FreeBSD for the daemon-curious desktop dabbler, is back with a fresh update.

GhostBSD 26.2-R15.1p6, to give it its slightly unwieldy full version number, is based on FreeBSD 15.1. It brings a new installer, full-disk encryption support, a smaller installation image, and fixes across its desktop tools.
FreeBSD 15.1 was released back in June, and at the time of writing, it's the most recent point release of FreeBSD.

The original plan was that FreeBSD 15.1 would include the option of installing KDE Plasma directly from the setup program, so that the OS would have a graphical desktop from its very first boot. However, this feature isn't ready just yet.

That gap inspired Daemonarchy, which we covered late last month. But its Omarchy-derived, keyboard-driven tiling desktop can feel unfamiliar even to experienced Linux users accustomed to conventional desktops.

GhostBSD has different goals. It brings Linux-like desktop convenience to FreeBSD: a live graphical environment to explore before installation, a graphical installer, and tools for managing software and updates.

These conveniences are familiar to desktop Linux users, but a standard FreeBSD installation takes more work. Its text-mode installer leaves users to install and configure a graphical desktop themselves, if they want one.

This is just how the BSD family does things, and most BSD users we've talked to regard it as standard operating procedure and see nothing wrong with it. For Linux users who are curious about how things are on the other side of the FOSS Unix fence, though, those extra steps can form formidable barriers. GhostBSD is an attempt to lay down a welcome mat.

The standard edition of GhostBSD installs the MATE desktop, and the downloads page also offers a community-maintained version with Xfce instead. As the project said it would back in February, this release uses the XLibre fork of the X.org X11 server.
That's one fewer desktop than when we last tried GhostBSD in August 2025. That release also offered the Mac OS X-like Gershwin environment.

There are practical hardware fixes too. The release notes list improvements for Intel AX200 Wi-Fi cards, open networks, password alerts, and non-ASCII network names, while USB HID support is enabled by default.

Gershwin remains in active development, so we asked project lead Joe Maloney why it wasn't included. "It has been difficult to find time to package for GhostBSD. It's the only distro I have ever packaged for," Maloney said. He added that rapid contributions from AppImage creator Simon Peter, known as probono, had made packaging increasingly difficult.

He also pointed to the fact that GhostBSD project lead Eric Turgeon is developing his own environment too: the Mocka desktop. Mocka is still in its very early stages – alpha version 0.0.2 appeared early last month – but the plan is that when it's ready, it will become GhostBSD's default desktop. For now, the only available module is a dock for the MATE desktop, but the curious can follow its development on the GitHub project page.

There may be no Gershwin included, but GhostBSD 26.2 offers MATE 1.28, and there's also a community-supported version with Xfce 4.20 instead. We tried the default MATE edition, and it works as well as ever. It defaults to a dark theme and the classic two-panel GNOME 2 desktop layout. The System menu in the top panel has an Administration submenu with a few of the project's own apps that aren't from upstream FreeBSD: "BE Station" for managing system boot environments, "Software Station" for browsing and installing applications, and "Update Station" for updates.

We regularly hear from users growing tired of the Linux vendors' headlong rush into Rust, Wayland, systemd, containerized app formats, and so on. Some are curious about whether FreeBSD offers a usable alternative. GhostBSD is the easiest way to get a complete, ready-to-use graphical FreeBSD desktop. There is a price to pay for switching to FreeBSD: for a start, most proprietary Linux apps, from Chrome to Slack, are not available here. Hardware compatibility needs more checking than on mainstream Linux, especially with recent GPUs and Wi-Fi adapters. If Windows gaming is a priority, this isn't the obvious choice.
But if you can live without those proprietary apps and find suitable open source replacements, FreeBSD is a viable alternative – and GhostBSD takes much of the setup work out of trying it. ®

434383af97f0d061: Egypt convicted Mada Masr's Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations and ordered it closed
Originally published on Global Voices
Lina Attalah. Picture from Mada Masr website. Used with permission.
A crackdown on independent media in Egypt is escalating.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.

The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news. They remain in pretrial detention.

The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah. On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.

The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial. She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later. The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.

According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected. The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.

Mada Masr was founded in 2013, an independent, critical, investigative outlet. In other a decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region. It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.

Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns. The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
An attack on journalism
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism. At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday 30 October, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.” A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.

“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about. But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads. It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.” It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.
Solidarity and journalism

In an op-ed published on October 26, the Mada Masr team wrote: “in this ongoingness of normalcy and crisis, perhaps a feature of our world today, but also a mastery we have mastered in the region, in learning to live in the world with the genocide on Gaza, we will go to court on Tuesday while continuing to publish Sunday through Saturday.”

They added: “There is something psychically bordering on horror when you see your own image as a journalist, instead of your journalism, surfacing on repeat through the scrolling movement of the Internet. But, in a moment like this, there is no tomorrow without solidarity and journalism.”

And: “We are reassured, once more, that the journalism we do is not for itself. And together with the few independent voices wrestling with sense-making and truth-snatching in a world where power condescendingly tells us to give up, this is not just about a small us, Mada Masr, but a much bigger we.”

In Egypt, journalists who documented torture, political imprisonment, and security crackdowns now face courts that process them quickly and unfairly, under a licensing scheme that has left applicants without an answer for years.
For journalism to be free, that licensing scheme and its chilling effects on access to information, knowledge production, and critical voices in Egypt and beyond must be stopped.
Written by Walid El Houri

Two bomb warnings targeted flights heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from London's Heathrow airport operated by Polish airline LOT.

Tuesday's Ryanair flight landed without incident in Murcia, and the emergency plan was deactivated after checks by Spain's Civil Guard.

"The aircraft landed normally in Warsaw and the passengers have disembarked," it said.

On Sunday, a bomb threat forced an Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna to reroute to Bulgaria. No explosives were found.

53c6adc7891f9d81: Most JavaScript programmers default to their ride-or-die frameworks, but such loyalties can hinder them when they task AI agents with doing their dirty work. Human-friendly tools aren't necessarily the most effective ones for the model-powered minions.

"One of my pet peeves with the web development community is that so many of the decisions we make are vibes-based,” wrote Seattle-based Nolan Lawson, currently a developer at AI security firm Socket. That’s an understatement; the JavaScript wars have been well underway for over a decade now, with each new framework promising to cure the woes of last year’s release.

Not wanting these vibey biases to seep into the realm of AI, Lawson created a benchmark to compare how different JavaScript frameworks perform under the same agentic model. He subsequently ran the test on 12 JavaScript frameworks, publishing the results in a post that compared each framework in terms of build cost, maintainability, and end-user performance of their agent-built apps.

The results are illuminating. In general, agents tend to work more efficiently with server-centric frameworks than with client-heavy “Single-Page App” (SPA) frameworks (which should tickle for React haters).
But the biggest take-away should be less controversial: agents best utilize those frameworks that favor convention, API stability, and concision.
How to compare JavaScript frameworks

For the experiment, Lawson wrote a set of instructions for a Claude Code agent to build a basic Pokémon web application using the PokéAPI. The model used the identical setup on 12 different frameworks and JavaScript stacks: Angular, Astro, Gracile with Lit, Hono with htmx, vanilla JavaScript with Vite, Next.js, Nuxt, Qwik, React Router, TanStack Start, SolidStart, and SvelteKit.
Lawson evaluated each stack across five independent sandbox runs; the repeated iterations smoothed the variance in the model’s performance.

To verify the resulting app met the specs, Lawson deployed a custom automated test suite that queried the browser's accessibility tree to ensure interactive elements like buttons and inputs weren’t faked – a shortcut LLMs occasionally take. Lawson also used Google Lighthouse to measure transfer size and runtime performance.

If the frameworks specified official MCP servers, Claude plug-ins, and agent-skill files, Lawson provided them as resources to the agents (though they weren’t always consulted). Otherwise, he did not mandate any specific architecture for rendering the app.
Comparing 12 JavaScript frameworks
The differences between the most cost-effective builds and the most expensive ones are substantial, to say the least, with the best lapping the efforts of the stragglers.
If you want to build a Pokéworld cost-effectively, the strongest bet is on Hono paired with htmx. This tag-team of technologies had the most economical run, with a median cost of $2.67 per Pokéapp.

Perhaps this is not surprising, given that the duo runs entirely on the server, thereby eliminating a whole set of checks required to synchronize an architectural split between client and server. It also helped minimize the code, which resulted in fewer output tokens being consumed.

Nearly as effective was Astro ($2.76). Like Hono/htmx, Astro does everything server-side. Server-side data crunching also helped Astro achieve the fastest median time to build and test the app, at 8.2 minutes.

Nuxt ($2.82) was the most cost-effective option for an SPA-like approach. Nuxt renders code on the server that gets hydrated on the client. Nuxt is actually built on Vue.js, but is “opinionated,” eliminating a lot of boilerplate that the agent must write. Nuxt also handles data transfer and file routing internally, which is more code not to fuss over.

It’s also worth noting Nuxt consumed the fewest tokens of the bunch (3.85 million), though that did not make it the cheapest, given how Claude charges different rates for input and output tokens. Nuxt produced the app in 1,415 lines of code, which is second only to Hono/htmx's 1,370 lines.
Overall, these top three frameworks were within the margin of error of each other, which means any one of them could have gotten the top score depending on what kind of day the LLM was having.
Some of the more traditional frameworks lumbered way behind, however.

A SvelteKit-based app cost $4.28 to generate, with the agent repeatedly going back to the SvelteKit documentation to get a better handle on how the recently-updated Svelte works. Angular was the most expensive way for an agent to build an app, costing $4.97 while taking 17.2 minutes and chewing up 9.76 million tokens (with the agent failing to even finish a working app in two of its five attempts).
All the resulting apps aced the Lighthouse accessibility and performance tests. It’s a pretty simple app to render, Lawson acknowledged.

Astro’s app had the fastest loading time (called Largest Contentful Paint or LCP) of 810 ms, while the slowest frameworks in the cohort – Next.js (2,090 ms) and TanStack Start (2,028 ms) – took more than twice as long to deliver the goods, perhaps because of all the JavaScript they shipped to the client.
Gold stars for all
Lawson hopes this work will set the stage for applying a bit more rigor in selecting frameworks for AI jobs, now that developers won’t have to do the actual heavy lifting themselves.
But a few developers on Hacker News pointed out AI efficiency isn’t the only factor to consider. There’s the human component of maintaining the framework as well.

“After a decade of React, I'm not going to go learn htmx or any other marginally better same-shaped tool for a new project, especially when it'd degrade my ability to review and debug another actor's work product,” one wrote.

After all, the frameworks themselves might evolve with the help of AI, minimizing their differences over time. “Besides a rewrite to another framework using AI, another option is to modernize the framework with AI instead,” someone else noted. ®

NHS England awarded the FDP contract in November 2023. It says the platform brings together operational data held in separate systems to help staff work more efficiently.
NHS England's September figures list 142 trusts as live on the platform - 137 of which it claims are benefiting.

"137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently."

83dd1055a8c29bfd: <!--kg-card-end: html--> World of Warcraft: Forever, a re-imaginging of the legendary MMO, comes out Wednesday. The idea is to recapture the feeling of discovery and wonder players had when adventuring across its world for the first time back in 2004.

But 2026 is a very different time. Subreddits dedicated to the game are already overrun with AI-generated addons that rip off longtime developers’ work, and a company that helps players track their damage output tells me it is making changes to its API because of the inundation of AI slop addons.

Warcraft Logs is a long-running site made by Archon.gg that lets players track and share their logs of particular in-game fights so they can analyze them for ways to get better. This works by players downloading Archon’s software which records the data of their fights and uploads them to the site. Warcraft Logs makes its API available for free to other developers. It used to be mostly hobby developers, the CEO of Archon.gg and Warcraft Logs, who goes by Sildri Silentcrest, told me. Now, it’s increasingly commercial projects, which are supposed to ask for permission in order to head off projects that would break Warcraft Logs’ terms of service or wouldn’t be able to scale.

<!--members-only-->“There’s been [an] explosion of development,” Silentcrest said. “Now, we’re averaging a[t] least one commercial ask per day. And I’m sure there are more that are commercializing without our approval. One new World of Warcraft analysis company every day! It's hard to keep up.”

At the root of many of these is the explosion of vibe-coded sites and addons. Addons are custom pieces of software a World of Warcraft player loads into their game for a specific benefit. Maybe they want a guide on the most optimal questing path to take, so an addon shows them the way on their minimap; or they want to make big changes to the UI. Some developers make real money from these, either by running Patreons or receiving ad revenue from Curseforge, the main repository for World of Warcraft addons.

If you scrolled any of the World of Warcraft subreddits in the past few weeks, you likely came across someone posting about the new addon they ‘created’. Sometimes the poster discloses they used AI, other times they add an update later after being called out. There’s even a tool for players to use Claude or Codex while they’re in World of Warcraft, so they can keep making addons in the game.

And with the flood, Warcraft Logs is changing its own API. “We're changing our API to better align with the applications we want to enable. We like things that help our community to dive deeper into their data, like tools that give you a deep dive on why you died to a boss or how you can improve on your next attempt. We don’t like things that effectively scrape lots of the data from our site to show surface-level info on their own site. Unfortunately, the ‘scrape and show basic statistics’ type has become much more prevalent,” Silentcrest said. They said Warcraft Logs is also introducing a paid commercial key “so that developers with commercial ambitions can support the foundation for the projects.”

Addons have been a crucial and thriving part of World of Warcraft for essentially the game’s entire life. Developers have spent many, many hours crafting those over the years. Now, AI is ripping those off too.

“People are making rip-offs of my work and copying my ideas,” plusmouse, a well-known addon creator, told me. Plusmouse gave one example: a particular design for nameplates in the game, which are the bars that appear above an enemy’s head.

“Prior to that releasing I hadn’t seen any addons adopt that style of design, and now, it feels like every AI addon ends up using that idea,” they said. Plusmouse has found in some cases the code is so similar in the AI-generated versions, that they submit copyright complaints to Curseforge. “Sometimes the code is so similar the complaint results in a takedown, other times it’s just different enough to get away with it, despite feeling like my solution. Borrowing ideas is normal in addon development, but doing it on the scale that AI permits isn’t,” they said. Plusmouse said they made some of their GitHub repositories private, which they believe has stopped LLMs from using their code.
Another key part of World of Warcraft: Forever is that the game is letting players engage with it in their own, preferred way.

“If I can be hopeful, the ubiquity of services under development will allow people to pick their own experience,” Silvercrest added. “If they want to take their time and explore in a relaxed manner, then they can. If they have limited time and want to get to endgame content quickly, they can do that too. On the flip side, my worry is that there will be lots of abandonware that will frustrate users with out-of-date information, buggy software, and vulnerabilities.”

Silvercrest said staff at Warcraft Logs “feel pressure to do more,” and the site has used some AI itself for research and some code review. “We have a small team. People are using our API to vibecode features that are on our own to do list. Should we take those features off our list? Or should we bite the bullet and lean into AI tools ourselves?”

They added, “Two years ago, say we had 200 developers using our API and two or three or four were being abusive. Today, 10,000 developers are using our API and 1,000 are being abusive. The ratio has changed, and that really feels bad. It used [to] be developers respecting other developers’ hard work. I'm not sure what’s changed. Is it that Claude doesn’t read the ToS? Or is it that the new developers don’t care as much as the old? We seriously love some of the tools that this coding accessibility has enabled, but policing API use has become a struggle.”

f3846775ebd28bb7: Britain's AI infrastructure boom could soon have an unlikely new home: Drax Power Station, where the operator of the country's largest biomass power plant has unveiled plans for a £20 billion datacenter development capable of consuming more than a gigawatt of power.

Drax announced on Tuesday that it has teamed up with investment giant Brookfield and its UK-based AI infrastructure business Radiant to build the facility at its North Yorkshire site. The money would come through a joint venture between Brookfield and Qatar's Qai, although the £20 billion headline figure is more ambition than actual money on the table at this stage.

The companies plan to start relatively small, at least by the standards of the AI industry's apparently bottomless appetite for electricity. The first phase would deliver up to 100MW of capacity by early 2028, backed by a proposed £2.5 billion investment. A second phase could add another 500MW between 2028 and 2031, with further expansion taking the site beyond 1GW after that.

However, a few hurdles remain between today's announcement and a functioning AI megafactory. According to Drax's regulatory filing, the first phase still requires planning permission, regulatory and network approvals, commercial agreements, and final investment decisions.
It also needs a tenant, which is a fairly important detail when you're proposing to spend billions on somewhere to house other people's computers.

Drax reckons its existing infrastructure gives it an advantage over developers struggling to secure electricity connections. The 1,000-acre site already has access to 4GW of grid capacity, 2.6GW of active generation and cooling infrastructure, along with proximity to the UK's fiber network.

The UK government estimated last week that all of Britain's existing data centers use around 2GW of electricity. Drax's proposed development alone could eventually need more than 1GW, although how much power it actually consumes will depend on how fully it's used.

The first phase would draw electricity from the grid, but Drax wants to supply up to 500MW directly from its existing generating capacity under a long-term power purchase agreement, potentially allowing AI servers to run on electricity produced by burning imported wood pellets.

That brings another complication. Drax signed a government-backed Contract for Difference agreement last year covering biomass generation between April 2027 and March 2031. The agreement allows the company to request permission to redirect up to 500MW of capacity towards a datacenter, but ministers and the Low Carbon Contracts Company would have to agree, taking into account consumer value, energy security, and sustainability.

The announcement also arrives as enthusiasm for enormous AI server farms is proving rather less universal outside government and industry circles. Opposition to data center developments has been growing on both sides of the Atlantic, with communities raising concerns about electricity bills, water consumption, and the impact of industrial-scale facilities on their surroundings.

A recent investigation found that businesses accounted for 84 percent of the stakeholders UK ministers met to discuss datacenters between July 2024 and June 2026, while environmental groups secured precisely zero meetings.

Drax and its partners are promising a community benefits fund and say public consultation will begin this month. Whether that will reassure residents concerned about another enormous consumer of electricity is a moot point.
Drax CEO Will Gardiner said the project could "help secure the long-term future of the site and protect hundreds of jobs," while supporting Britain's ambitions to become a major player in AI.

The government, unsurprisingly, is enthusiastic. Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds welcomed the proposed investment as an opportunity to create jobs and support Britain's reindustrialization.
“Investments like this will help pave the way to a new age of British reindustrialization, creating good jobs in Yorkshire and delivering growth right across the country,” she said.
Ministers may be enthusiastic, but Drax still has to find a customer, secure planning permission, and convince regulators before anyone starts plugging in servers. ®
7ed83203a08a1d77: Virgin Media O2 (VMO2) wants to chop a third of its labor costs and is expected to lay off thousands of workers, giving staff more to think about than Christmas presents during the run up to year-end.
Shrinking the workforce is one of a number of cost reduction measures designed to save the UK's second largest telecoms provider some £800 million by 2029.
It currently employs 16,000 people and redundancies will "equate to roughly 30 percent of the company’s total people costs" over the next two years, VMO2 said on Tuesday.
The majority of the redundancies will come from "non-customer facing roles," it claimed. The Register asked the telco to be more specific on the headcount cuts and the type of roles are at risk.

A spokesperson refused to provide a number, saying those plans are being finalized and consultations are due to take place. Logically, if more senior head office positions are hit then fewer people will need to leave to meet the £300 million ($402 million) target figure.
The Reg understands thousands of roles are at risk.

Another lever management at VMO2 is pulling involves halting investment in any further fiber network upgrades beyond existing commitments. Instead, a low-cost upgrade will be deployed to its hybrid fiber-coaxial (HFC) network (i.e. cable customers) to bring 2 Gbps services to the majority of the network in 2027.
Full fiber merger pledges

VMO2 was formed in 2021 by the merger of broadband and TV biz Virgin Media and mobile operator O2. The pair pledged to spend £10 billion (c $13.4 billion) on beefing up 5G coverage and laying gigabit "full-fiber" fixed-line networks.
Both Virgin Media and O2 talked up those connectivity commitments when justifying the case to combine their businesses, saying they needed greater economies of scale to compete with their rivals.

However, business has not gone as planned, with revenue falling over several successive quarters. The latest figures for Q3 ended September 30 show total revenue down 5.7 percent year-on-year to £2.43 billion. The networks giant blamed consumer fixed market pressures, among other things.
VM02 forecasts a revenue decline of 3 to 5 percent for the whole of 2026.
In the consumer division, VMO2 talked of more clearly defining the role for each of its brands. O2 Business is planning to streamline the product portfolio.
Tom Oughton, senior analyst at Megabuyte, said the changes were expected.

"VMO2 has undergone a strategic review as it looks to address rising leverage, with today confirming a transformation program to ultimately bring c. £800 million ($1bn) in cost savings ahead of its first debt expiry in 2029. The routes to achieve this are the most obvious ones: reduce capex on full fiber and focus on HFC upgrade (lower cost, quick payback) and reduce operational costs by cutting headcount," Oughton said.

"The obvious question is how a significant transformation will impact the business. VMO2 focuses on the benefits, but the business is declining 3-5 percent organically with 16-17k staff, so reducing headcount by 25 percent or more could stretch operations, worsen customer support, and cause broader disruption."

Paolo Pescatore, founder and analyst at PP Foresight didn't mince his words either: "Virgin Media O2 is in serious trouble, with customer losses and declining service revenue and earnings exposing the scale of the challenge."

2e9cb50661edbc26: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

While game theory predicts how rational actors behave under particular rules, reverse game theory designs rules to elicit the behavior we want. Think of splitting a cake: if one person cuts it and the other gets first choice, the cutter has an incentive to make the portions equal.
Researchers believe the approach could align AI more closely with our rules and instructions. But big questions remain about whether these mechanisms will work in practice.
Here’s how reverse game theory could help make AI agents behave.
—Amit Katwala
Here’s who is falling in line for Trump’s “Super Intelligence” loyalty test
At the end of September, President Trump signed an executive order with just one directive: government agencies must rebrand artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.”
One month on, the rebrand is slowly appearing across government websites and documents, but it hasn’t caught on with everyone. Even some of the biggest names in tech still use “AI.”
But the bigger concern is the new term becoming a political loyalty test: Those who use it signal allegiance to the administration. Those who don’t become targets for attacks.
So one month in, who’s on board?

0a9b97d385f9ab31: KINGSTON, Nov 3 — British adventurer Karl Bushby enjoyed an emotional reunion with his mother and family on Monday as he arrived back home after a 28-year, 50,000-kilometre (31,000-mile) trek from South America, crossing four continents on foot.
Cheers erupted as the 57-year-old former paratrooper was greeted in the street outside his mother’s house in the northeastern UK port city of Hull.
Bushby, who set off on his odyssey from Chile in 1998, had two golden rules for his journey—avoid all forms of transport to advance and not return until he completed his challenge.
He was met in the centre of Hull by a crowd of up to 1,000 cheering people before being reunited with his mother, Angela, 36-year-old son Adam and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

Speaking after the reunion, Bushby paid tribute to the kindness of the strangers he had met, from hotel owners to the “poorest of the poor” who had given him bowls of rice and something to drink along the way.
”And that would happen throughout the world,” he said adding that the world had been his “support network”.
‘Indiana Jones’ moments

The route back to his home city has seen him walk the length of the Americas, across the frozen Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia and then through parts of Central Asia and Europe covering jungles, mountains, and deserts.
The journey had been full of logistical headaches and scary “Indiana Jones” and “I think I’m going to die moments”, he told reporters.

Bushby had already been applauded Sunday as he crossed the iconic Humber Bridge near Hull in thick mist, ahead of his final push into the city centre and then on to his mother’s home where he grew up.
”So many people have followed Karl on his epic journey. We have all felt inspired by his spirit, tenacity and dogged determination,” Hull Mayor Maria Coward said ahead of his arrival.
”It’s quite emotional. I’m proud of him and what he’s done. What an achievement,” neighbour Laura Chaplin, 47, told AFP as he returned home.
British leader Andy Burnham’s spokesman said it was “an extraordinary achievement and the prime minister welcomes him back to the UK”.
Challenges met
Bushby began his adventure when he was 29, after his marriage broke down and his wife returned to Northern Ireland with their son.
He was forced to pause the journey several times, including when Moscow refused him a visa. The 2008 financial crisis and then the Covid-19 pandemic caused other hold-ups.
At those times, he stepped away from the journey, living notably at a base in Mexico, then once the situation had been resolved, he would resume from the exact spot where he had left off.
Erin Anderson, 28, a theatre marketing officer among the crowd in Hull, said she thought Bushby was “amazing”.
”I’ve been following him for the last eight years. He’s been walking for as long as I’ve been alive. It’s brilliant”.
UK soil
Bushby swam across the Channel from France in early October to arrive back in the UK.
Legendary German filmmaker Werner Herzog and a film crew accompanied Bushby on his homecoming, making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled “Walk of Life”.
The production company behind the film has been supporting Bushby’s progress for the past 16 years, providing financial and logistical assistance.
Bushby said he would now be focusing on the documentary as well as writing a book and making the adjustment back into normal life.
”I’m still in that shocked phase,” he told AFP. “Over the last few days it’s been the last time I’ve been camping in my tent... last time spending all day on the road.
”Each one of those has been an emotional event and then walking down my childhood street into my childhood home with mother (there), that’s been quite something,” he said.
He added that he still had the drive for adventure but ruled out any more big walks.
”I think I’m hanging my boots up -- 28 years is a good run,” he said. — AFP

3ee6a34d50f4fb08: The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says AI-powered malware is "highly likely" to be a part of a future ransomware attack on Britain's critical national infrastructure between now and 2028.
The warning accompanies its annual review and a separate assessment exploring how AI could change cyber threats over the next two years.

The cyber arm of signals intelligence agency GCHQ did not provide much detail about what form this AI malware may take. However, it alluded to open source AI security tools that were initially intended to assist security researchers being repurposed for nefarious activity.

Attackers are already repurposing such tools. For example, researchers are increasingly seeing widespread abuse of ARTEX, an open source, Chinese-made AI red-teaming platform, in attacks on UK registrar 123 Reg, Microsoft 365, and others since its launch in July.

In its pessimistic scenario for 2028, the NCSC envisages "a significant increase in the frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks worldwide," with wider adoption of AI tools making attribution harder.
China "has likely played a role" in supplying those tools in this future, "enabling them to hide their activities within the noise," the report states.
It also considers a further threat: an autonomous attacker operating beyond its human operator's control.
The NCSC says it "is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyberattacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint."
Such attacks would likely complicate geopolitical relationships, owing again to attribution difficulties, making it easier for countries that order attacks on others to deny their involvement.
The UK's plans for AI defense
At a time when each Patch Tuesday seems to come loaded with record numbers of bugs, the NCSC acknowledges that AI is already changing vulnerability discovery and patching.

The body is also exploring how AI could help defenders keep pace. Project DROMOS began earlier this year with a four-week pilot analyzing government code repositories, before expanding into selected operational environments.

The Government Cyber Coordination Centre (GC3) launched the project with the AI Security Institute and other departments. The NCSC says it uncovered hundreds of potential security issues, including critical vulnerabilities.
The review also reaffirms plans for Cyber Shield, an agentic cyber defense system first teased in July.

Cyber Shield is expected to be delivered in stages over the next five years. It will involve the NCSC providing defensive agents deployed by participating organizations with data that will strengthen national resilience to ongoing cyber threats.

The NCSC will be running the scheme alongside the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), but acknowledged that this kind of automated defensive activity currently sits outside many organizations' risk tolerances, meaning it has a role to play in building trust in the system before adoption can go mainstream.
As reported last week, the government has set aside £60 million to fund the initiative, and an additional £70 million to support a new National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre.
The NERV Centre's job will be to identify and maintain an ongoing understanding of vulnerabilities across CNI organizations and the wider economy.

Per last week's budget, £40 million will fund a National Agentic Security Unit responsible for responding to uncontrolled bots and other agentic mishaps, and £24 million was assigned to strengthen public sector defenses.
An undisclosed sum will also help establish a new NCSC-managed AI Cyber Security Centre in Manchester to develop AI security expertise across government.
In the meantime, NCSC CEO Dr Richard Horne is calling for organizations to "invest with urgency" in their security and resilience.
"For decades, we have collectively got away with doing tech on the cheap," he said today, announcing the annual report.

"We can be a nation where leaders of all organizations actively choose to invest with urgency... And where all organizations make security and resilience a fundamental requirement, not an afterthought.
"The collective result would be a source of enduring national strength for us all."
Horne said organizations should treat the NCSC's Cyber Essentials certification as the starting point, but scale up resilience efforts in line with organizational size, complexity, and risk.
The government also announced a 75 percent discount on Cyber Essentials certification for micro, small, and medium-sized businesses applying for their first certificate. ®

d3f0528600d0917e: Since it’s election day, let’s discuss the polls. Specifically, why their track record has been so poor. I love this topic because it closely tracks prediction errors in market and economic forecasts.

In 2024, I discussed a major source of polling error: the pools pollsters use. Today, I want to discuss a more challenging failure: what is termed “respondent error,” but you are probably more familiar with as Human psychology.
The key respondent errors are Attitude, Intention, and Behavior. These three phenomena affect our ability to predict our own future decision-making and/or behavior.
I have made various arguments over the past twenty years; rather than reiterate these, consider three questions that confront pollsters:
1. What do people really believe?
2. How well do they know their own actual intentions?
3. How likely are they to act on those?
That is the challenging psychology of polling voters, and it has plenty of interesting wrinkles.

Note that I am not addressing whether pollsters reach a representative audience (they don’t) or whether they use unbiased polling questions (it varies). Instead, I suggest that the better pollsters understand the psychology, the more accurate their numbers will be.
Let’s discuss a few details.
1. What do people really believe?

A surprisingly challenging question. We assume people know what they believe; after all, we know our religion, partisan affiliation, favorite sports teams, hobbies, etc. But with so many complex, emotional, and conflicted issues, what people say and what they truly believe often don’t match.
We also assume they answer honestly; ask who they think will win, and you get a biased response based on who they prefer.

This tension creates problems for pollsters. People hold “non-attitudes” on many (most?) issues — ask about a policy they’ve never considered, and they’ll create a response on the spot that’s unstable.1 Answers can reflect weak opinions, conflicting values, and are impacted by the way a question is presented.

Ambivalent voters who like one candidate’s personality and the other’s policies will respond to pollster questions with a squishy answer they’ll likely revise. This is especially problematic for issue polling.2
Then there is expressive answering: some respondents use a poll to send a message rather than report voting preferences.
2. How well do they know their own actual intentions?
Humans declare their intentions to do a specific act with high confidence. After all, we wouldn’t say it if we didn’t think we’d do it (would we?).

What tends to happen is that we say what we either want to believe or what we think the listener wants to hear. This again creates a gap between stated intentions and future behavior. Expressing support costs the poll respondent nothing; their commitments to those responses may be conditional or aspirational.
Then there is the bandwagon effect: Some state their preference based on who they perceive will win. We don’t want to back a loser, and we often claim support for who we expect will win.
3. How likely are we to act on these?
This is the big one: Self-reported turnout intention overstates actual turnout by a large margin. Many people say they’ll vote, but don’t.

Pollsters try to model this from election to election with various degrees of success. But turnout shifts in ways past models can’t anticipate. The 2022 midterm “red wave” never materialized; 2024 showed the reverse. The low-propensity voters who show up only for a specific candidate (e.g., a Trump-only voter) are exactly the people a likely-voter model often excludes. The results of these model adjustments have been decidedly mixed.

People can state what they want to do, and then the world intervenes: bad weather on Election Day; breaking news that changes how we perceive one candidate or the other; geopolitics, the economy, markets, and inflation. The electorate consists of people who vote but whose composition is uncertain beforehand. Voting history and other evidence make turnout only partly predictable.

Pollsters mistakenly believe their core work is data analytics; history suggests it’s more similar to the work psychologists do when trying to predict future behavior. Failing to discern that distinction is why their track record ranges from not bad (2024) to abysmal (2016, 2020).

Endless things can happen between when a pollster gets an answer and when it’s time to vote. A respondent to a poll who says a) I like this candidate; b) I am a registered voter; and c) I intend to vote for that person — does not guarantee a ballot will be cast as stated, if at all.

We know that the earlier the polls are, the worse their predictive values are; we also know that all models are wrong, but some are useful. Models also presume the future looks like the past, and during periods of disruption, that assumption tends to be problematic.

In a nation where partisan lines are fairly well drawn, the middle 5-10% will decide many elections. Those independent undecideds are often equal to the margin of error.3 No wonder polling has had such a mixed track record.
Get out and vote!
See also: The Undecided Voters Are Not Who You Think They Are For most, the big decision is about whether to vote at all. By Ronald Brownstein The Atlantic, September 26, 2024

6c3006c5e56fd892: Apple says it sold more Macs in fiscal 2026 than in any previous year, but soaring memory prices are threatening to spoil the Cupertino-based gadget maker's record-breaking run.
The warning came during Apple's fiscal fourth-quarter earnings call on Monday, the first since John Ternus took over as CEO.
"What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus told analysts.

Apple has already raised prices across much of its hardware lineup, including Macs and iPads in June and iPhones in September. Those increases, along with existing inventories and cheaper components elsewhere, have softened the blow. Unfortunately for Apple, memory prices haven't finished climbing.
"For the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs," Ternus said, adding that Apple expects to pay more for memory beyond the end of the year.

Mac buyers haven't been deterred so far. Apple pulled in $10.8 billion from Macs in the September quarter, up 24 percent year-on-year, following $10.35 billion in the June quarter, up nearly 29 percent year-on-year. The MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro accounted for much of the latest growth.
"We have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time," Ternus said.

Whether Apple can keep enough of them on shelves is another matter. COO Sabih Khan said the company had already experienced supply constraints across iPhone, Mac, and iPad during the September quarter, largely because of limited availability of advanced chipmaking capacity. Now memory is taking over as the chief headache.
"For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and iPad, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected," Khan said.

Apple isn't sitting idle. Ternus revealed that its manufacturing purchase obligations jumped by $33 billion between June and September as it bids to secure supplies, although he offered no indication of when the memory crunch might ease.

Higher memory costs are also squeezing Apple's margins. CFO Kevan Parekh said gross margin fell by roughly one percentage point between the June and September quarters, excluding tariff effects, entirely because of memory costs. The damage would have been worse without existing inventory, cheaper non-memory components, and those price hikes.

Apple expects its gross margin to fall from 47.9 percent in the September quarter to between 45 and 46 percent in December, primarily because of higher memory costs. Costs associated with rolling out Siri AI will also weigh on the figure.
Parekh said Apple had "reluctantly" raised hardware prices, but supply constraints made it too early to assess how customers were responding.
Meanwhile, Ternus is keen to sell customers on the Mac as an AI machine, particularly for running models locally.
"Mac mini and Mac Studio in particular are pushing the boundaries of local private AI," he said, pointing to workloads that previously would have been difficult to run on desktop hardware.
Apple has also refreshed its Mac lineup with M6-powered machines and a touchscreen MacBook Pro, giving customers more reasons to upgrade, provided there's enough memory to build the things.

Not that the wider business is struggling. Apple reported September-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent year-on-year, while iPhone revenue climbed 17 percent to $57.6 billion. Services brought in $31.6 billion, up 10 percent.
Apple forecasts revenue growth of 7 to 10 percent in the December quarter despite the supply constraints. Even with memory prices running wild, it isn't expecting to go hungry. ®
4b7a95e604e09e24: DHAKA, Nov 3 —Bangladeshi garment worker Amena, who has spent seven years sewing and checking clothes for international brands, struggles at the end of the month to afford even the basics.

The 27-year-old, who like others interviewed by AFP gave only one name fearing professional repercussions, earns 12,500 taka (RM410), barely enough to cover the rent on her small home and support her elderly parents.

Her monthly wage is roughly equivalent to the retail price of a pair of yoga leggings or blue jeans in Europe or North America — garments like those made at the factory where she works in the Dhaka suburb of Gazipur.
“I earn 12,500 taka. The highest salary I ever drew was 26,000 taka, and that was years ago,” she said, adding her salary dropped when she was transferred to sampling from stitching.
Bangladesh, a nation of 170 million people, is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for major international brands.
The sector employs millions and generates the bulk of Bangladesh’s export earnings.
But workers say rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs, compounded by inflation of around eight percent and soaring energy prices, have steadily eroded their purchasing power.
With strikes and protests since Saturday, they are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka — a 140 percent increase on the current minimum.
Protests have continued for days, with workers defying calls from the government and factory owners to return to work.
‘Kind of bonded labour’
Amena pays 4,500 taka a month in rent and sends another 5,000 to her parents, leaving just 3,000 for food, medicine or emergencies.
“Now I have no savings left to fall back on,” she said. “My bones are deteriorating, so I need to take medication. I can’t afford to buy fish or meat regularly.”
She usually buys some just after receiving her salary, in the first week of the month, and perhaps again two weeks later.

“It’s impossible to live like this, but we have no other options,” she said. “It’s a kind of bonded labour, although nobody is forcing us to continue working. We need jobs, and garment factories are the only option available to us.”
“The government and factory owners should concede to our demands because they are legitimate,” Amena said. “How are we supposed to survive when the prices of all commodities keep rising?”
Sabbir, 18, works at a small factory, earning a monthly salary of 12,000 taka.
After paying rent on a small room near her factory, “I keep 1,500 taka as pocket money and give the rest to my mother,” Sabbir told AFP.
“The price of gas has soared” since the Middle East war erupted in late February, she said. “We are always afraid that the gas might run out.”
Begum, another garment worker in Gazipur, said employees had little faith in promises from factory owners.
“Whenever we ask for a salary increase, the owners start complaining that business isn’t going well,” she said.
“If that’s true, how come the same owners keep opening factories one after another?” — AFP
