8e3227d7d7a9c199: PARIS, Nov 3 — Fifa will allow members of its ruling Council to view “key documents” related to the aborted project to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, a source close to world football’s governing body told AFP today.

“Fifa has informed the members of its Council, including all the vice-presidents, that they will have access to key documents in relation to Fifa Forward Enterprise,” the source told AFP, referring to Fifa president Gianni Infantino’s FFE proposal.

Members of the Council — a total of 37 people including Infantino and eight Fifa vice-presidents — were informed yesterday in a letter sent by Fifa Secretary General Mattias Grafstrom that they must come forward “in the next two weeks” if they want to see the documents “in person and in specific conditions”.
The documents can be consulted at the headquarters of world football’s governing body in Zurich, Switzerland, the source added.
The move came as a November 2 deadline set by European governing body UEFA to answer a series of questions related to the FFE proposal passed on Monday.
UEFA has led the opposition to the project, which was revealed in late July and would have seen Fifa open up its premium competitions such as the World Cup to private investors.

Infantino quickly abandoned the proposal in the face of an uproar, but UEFA has gone to a court in Florida in an attempt to gather evidence for a potential complaint of “criminal mismanagement” against the Fifa president in Switzerland.
Following a Fifa Council meeting on October 15, UEFA general secretary Theodore Theodoridis sent a letter to Grafstrom with a list of over 40 questions and requests for information related to FFE.

It also raised other issues such as the decision to award a Fifa Peace Prize to Trump and the decision to suspend a red card shown to United States player Folarin Balogun at the World Cup following an intervention by the US President.
Fifa did not respond to UEFA before the deadline, arguing that this was “impractical”.
Infantino is standing for re-election as Fifa president next March.
The deadline for rival candidates to declare themselves is November 18, but UEFA has so far not been able to find a credible challenger to put forward.
Infantino was handed a major boost when the Asian Football Confederation announced on October 23 that it was backing him for re-election.

CONCACAF chief Victor Montagliani was mooted as a candidate, but the Canadian has announced his desire to stand for a new term as the head of the North American confederation, meaning he is unlikely to challenge Infantino.
Ramon Vega, the former Tottenham Hotspur, Celtic and Switzerland defender, has stated a willingness to stand but it remains to be seen if he will get the necessary support. — AFP

12e69ea3424ee535: WASHINGTON, Nov 3 — Americans voted today in pivotal midterm elections with Democrats hoping to seize control of Congress and impose the first significant checks on Donald Trump’s chaotic second term in the White House.

Republicans losing the House would give Democrats the power to stall Trump’s legislative agenda and launch sweeping investigations of his administration. A Senate defeat would also threaten his ability to appoint Supreme Court justices and senior officials.
The election amounts to a nationwide judgment on Trump, with the mood turning sharply against Republicans amid anger over soaring living costs and the war against Iran.

All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are at stake, along with governorships in 36 states. Democrats need only three House gains and a net four seats in the Senate to wrest both chambers from Republican hands.
Trump returned to office last year promising to bring down prices, but inflation, tariffs and fuel costs inflated by the Middle East conflict have squeezed Americans.
The 80-year-old’s approval rating has hovered near the low 30s.
In the suburbs of Atlanta, Georgia, retired teacher Jane Callum, 77, was among Democrats canvassing for Senator Jon Ossoff who framed the race as a watershed moment for the country’s future.

“I really feel an obligation to do everything that I possibly can to change the direction that our country is going in now, and put it more on the path to democracy and away from autocracy,” she told AFP.
Economic discontent
Republicans insist that Trump’s tax cuts and immigration crackdown will benefit Americans, and they are portraying Democratic candidates as left-wing radicals.

But in his final public campaign appearance on Monday, Trump barely touched on the economy and spent most of the time in a rambling talk about his problem-plagued renovation of Washington’s Reflecting Pool.
“This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said, 26 minutes into the speech, before quickly returning to talking about renovations.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer branded it a “pathetic closing message.”
Some Republican supporters remain confident.
“We’re going to win. As a matter of fact, we’ve probably already won,” Texas military veteran Yvonne Clouser told AFP.
But while Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, the political battlefield is extending into conservative states like Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Ohio and Alaska.

Democrats must also defend competitive seats, including in Michigan, where a bitter internal dispute saw congresswoman Haley Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers rather than the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
Decision Desk HQ’s final forecast projected 241 House seats for Democrats against 194 for Republicans, and a narrower 52-48 Democratic Senate majority.
Disputed results?
Polls can underestimate one party’s support, and Republicans hope their voters turn out in force on Election Day.
More than 57 million Americans had already voted early before Tuesday, indicating the high energy.
The campaign has attracted more than $11 billion in political advertising, while mega-rich Trump ally Elon Musk has poured hundreds of millions of dollars into Republican political efforts.
As soon as polls close, concerns will mount over whether results will be accepted by the Republicans.
Trump, who tried to overturn his 2020 election defeat, has repeatedly alleged widespread voter fraud and accused Democrats — with no evidence — of cheating.

The Justice Department, run by a close Trump ally, has already sued to potentially block certification of Alaska’s Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses, although a court ruled against the effort on the eve of the election.
And the Supreme Court rejected on Monday an emergency bid to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people on the grounds they may not be American citizens.
Trump, who will watch the midterms results at the White House on Tuesday night, signaled that if he does lose control of Congress he could simply defy Democrats.
“I veto everything,” he told a podcast on Monday, although he said he might strike deals with Democrats eventually. — AFP
14cc31d58dd5150c: PARIS, Nov 3 — Students blockaded dozens of high schools across France today to maintain pressure on the government over education reforms as trade unions prepared for a nationwide strike later this week.

After returning from a two-week autumn break yesterday, some students resumed their protest campaign, calling on authorities to renovate dilapidated schools, reduce class sizes and create more university places.

Authorities said 48 out of France’s 3,700 high schools were blocked, including in cities such as Paris, Rennes, Toulouse and Lyon. The Union syndicale lyceenne (USL) contested those figures, saying 500 establishments were blocked.
The student union denounced what it called heavy-handed tactics, with “young people pinned against walls and riot police units deployed” outside schools.
“Our impression is that the objective is to suppress the movement and prevent Thursday’s mobilisation,” a union representative told AFP.
On Thursday students plan to stage a new day of blockades as trade unions called for a nationwide strike.
In the northwestern city of Rennes, around 30 students blocked access to the Brequigny High School, one of the country’s largest secondary schools.
Tensions quickly flared between students and a member of the school administration.
“You are not the majority,” the staff member protested.
“If we’re doing this, it’s because everything we’ve tried before hasn’t worked,” a student replied.

The school protests have fuelled a nationwide movement against soaring prices and inadequate public services, which has drawn hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets over the past three weekends and led to some of the worst unrest seen in France in years on October 17.
The school movement has also inspired students in other European countries, including Belgium, Italy and Spain, where the French word “blocus” (blockade) has become a popular hashtag.

Last week, the French government unveiled measures aimed at addressing some of the students’ demands, including reforms to the university admissions process, which has been criticised for a lack of transparency. Student leaders, however, say the proposals do not go far enough.
Yesterday, authorities said 42 high schools, or around 1 percent of the national total, were blocked. Student unions put the figure at 169.
About 15 per cent of higher education institutions were affected on Monday, authorities said. — AFP

1b4d140f5d072e95: PASIR GUDANG, Nov 3 — The Johor government will focus on 337 flood hotspots statewide as the northeast monsoon is expected to affect the state from this month until January next year.

State Public Works, Transport, Infrastructure and Communications Committee chairman Mohamad Fazli Mohamad Salleh said priority would be given to areas with high population density and a history of major flooding, including the districts of Kota Tinggi, Batu Pahat and Segamat.
“Based on updates from the Department of Irrigation and Drainage (DID), 35 flood hotspots, including new additions, have been identified.

“The Public Works Department (JKR) has also identified 30 high-risk road locations that comprise 21 sites on federal roads and nine on state roads,” he told reporters after a working visit to the Sungai Rinting flood wall project here today.
Also present were Permas assemblyman Baharudin Mohamed Taib and senior government agency officials.

Mohamad Fazli said the measures outlined included hotspot mapping, drain maintenance, cleaning and dredging drainage systems, ensuring machinery was ready, public outreach and the use of the eBencana (electronic disaster) reporting system.

He said the relevant projects included Phase 1 of the Sungai Johor Flood Mitigation Plan, the Sungai Pemandi Flood Mitigation Plan and a flood alleviation project in Kampung Sungai Kapal Lama in Pengerang.

In Batu Pahat, Mohamad Fazli said the DID had identified 41 flood hotspots, while the JKR had detected 21 high-risk locations along federal and state roads, covering a total distance of 6.5 kilometres.

He added that preparations would include road pavement maintenance works worth RM11.79 million, non-pavement works worth RM3.20 million and an allocation of RM1.92 million under the Malaysian Road Records Information System (MARRIS) for drainage-related works.
“Alternative route plans via the FT024 federal road and the PLUS Highway have also been planned.

“Mobile pumps at the Parit Botak sluice gate, flood mitigation projects – such as the Bandar Batu Pahat and Sungai Batu Pahat flood mitigation schemes – as well as coastal embankment upgrading works, are also being given due attention,” he said.
In Segamat, Mohamad Fazli said the DID had identified 29 flood hotspots, while the JKR had identified 16 high-risk locations, comprising eight federal roads and eight state roads.
“Efforts are also focused on monitoring river levels and roadways, as well as coordinating with the Batu Pahat district, which is located downstream,” he said.
In Muar, he said 65 flood hotspots had been identified, the highest number among the districts listed by the DID.

In Tangkak, 26 hotspots had been identified, with priority measures including inspecting culverts and drainage systems, monitoring roadways and coordinating maintenance efforts among the relevant agencies.
Mohamad Fazli said there were also 44 flood hotspots in Johor Bahru, 29 in Kluang, 19 in Pontian, 27 in Kulai and 22 in Mersing.

In a related development, he said the state government was preparing an application for an emergency allocation of between RM20 million and RM30 million to carry out maintenance works and flood preparedness measures in high-risk areas throughout November and December.

“Priority will be given to tasks that can be executed immediately, specifically maintenance work, whereas large-scale projects, such as the construction of embankments and flood-retaining walls, will require a longer timeframe,” he added.

6821263fbe7a052d: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — The ringgit eased against the US dollar today amid a pullback in global artificial intelligence (AI)-related trading and investments.
At 6pm, the local note slipped to 4.0735/0775 against the greenback from Monday’s close of 4.0695/0735.
SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said the ringgit’s weakness was largely driven by broader risk aversion, particularly as investors unwound AI-related investments.
He said Malaysia has been a major beneficiary of the global AI investment boom, particularly through its semiconductor industry and technology-related investment flows.
“The trouble is that this relationship cuts both ways. When investors start pulling back from the AI trade, the ringgit can come under pressure even when the broader US dollar is weakening.

“On the AI investment bubble, there seem to be mixed signals among Wall Street firms at a conference in Hong Kong today.

“Some argued that AI infrastructure may have gone overboard, but others pointed to the potential benefits to the economy. Reversing risk appetite in the AI space could mean missing an opportunity to record further gains in investment returns,” he said.

Mohd Afzanizam also noted that Brent crude oil prices rose 1.94 per cent to US$106.80 per barrel, as concerns over a possible renewed US attack on Iran following the US midterm elections remained a source of market uncertainty.

Amran said this could potentially result in millions of ringgit in revenue losses to the government.

Jeyenderan said the key concern was traceability, particularly how the authorities and relevant parties could establish what happened to the cargo after it entered storage tanks containing existing inventory, including any subsequent movement, mixing or blending.

He said the relevant records should show the quantity discharged into each tank, the existing inventory, subsequent product movements, laboratory specifications and the quantities eventually removed or transferred, to ensure an unbroken documentary trail.
He stressed that Maritime Network had acted only as the vessel or shipping agent for the cargo movements, and was not the cargo owner, terminal operator, laboratory or Customs authority.
As such, he said, the roles and responsibilities of all parties involved must be clearly established.
Jeyenderan wants MACC to clarify whether the Customs disclosure warrants further investigation, particularly regarding the accuracy of cargo declarations and the applicable regulatory treatment.
He said the main concern was whether the cargo declarations, supporting documents and actual physical movement of the petroleum products were consistent with the relevant Customs requirements.

He also called on the authorities to clarify whether there were any regulatory or revenue implications arising from the handling of petroleum cargoes, particularly where shared storage tanks and blending arrangements were involved.

f8b8e4febc05a3b4: Euro cloud trade association CISPE can keep the identities of members backing its VMware merger challenge confidential from Broadcom following a ruling by the EU General Court.
Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe filed an action last year seeking to annul the European Commission's approval of Broadcom's acquisition of the cloud and virtualization giant.

CISPE believes the Commission erred in allowing the purchase to go ahead without imposing any conditions on Broadcom to protect the many European cloud providers and their customers who depend on VMware's software.

Broadcom sought access to redacted information identifying members supporting the action, arguing that it needed the information to challenge the action's admissibility. CISPE says the ruling allows the case to proceed without disclosing those identities to Broadcom.

"It is a procedural ruling on confidentiality rather than a decision on the substance of the case, but it removes the immediate obstacle to the action moving forward," a CISPE spokesperson told The Register.

CISPE argued that identifying the members, which are or have been VMware customers, would expose them to a significant risk of retaliation because of Broadcom's market power. Those members had supplied information about their commercial relationships with VMware.

As far as the case itself goes, CISPE says it warned the Commission that Broadcom would use VMware's pre-eminent position in the private cloud market to rewrite licensing terms and reshape the market in its favor.

Just a month after Broadcom's acquisition concluded in November 2023, partners were informed that VMware's channel program was to end in early 2024, and that Broadcom was also ditching the majority of VMware's Cloud Services Providers, keeping only a select few that had the largest turnover.

Despite Broadcom CEO Hock Tan publicly stating that inflating prices was not his strategy, that is what happened. AT&T says that Broadcom proposed a 1,050 percent price increase, for example. Meanwhile, nine out of ten respondents to a recent survey of VMware customers said they were considering moving to alternatives.

CISPE, which represents 48 cloud infrastructure service providers across the EU, says fewer than 20 European providers remain authorized to offer VMware-based services, down from more than a thousand.
Commenting on the latest ruling, CISPE Secretary General Francisco Mingorance declared it a good day for the organization and for the rule of law in Europe.

"The case matters even more today than when we filed it. In the three years since the European Commission waved this deal through without conditions, Broadcom has dismantled the European VMware channel," he said.

"Those excluded have until 31 March, 2027, to sell their infrastructure or their customers to a competitor chosen by Broadcom, or to close. This is the foreclosure the European Commission was warned about."
We asked CISPE what outcome it hoped to achieve, nearly three years after the acquisition closed.

"The immediate objective is to have the Commission's unconditional clearance annulled, on the basis that it failed to properly assess the effect of the acquisition on European cloud providers and the VMware channel," CISPE's spokesperson told The Register.
The Commission did impose conditions concerning interoperability with rival hardware, but CISPE argues these did not address the risks to cloud providers.

"We appreciate that it's a long shot (although there is precedent)," the spokesperson continued. "We have (along with others) also filed a competition complaint with the Directorate-General for Competition against Broadcom for its actions post-merger."

The precedent referred to is the EC approval given to the merger of Sony and BMG's music divisions in 2004, which was ruled to be not of "the requisite legal standard" two years later. The deal was subsequently reassessed and re-cleared.

"Ultimately, we want to do whatever we can to bring Broadcom to the table to negotiate and ideally end some of its most egregious practices so that European cloud providers can once again support cloud customers in a commercially fair and viable manner," the spokesperson added.
The Register asked Broadcom to comment The European Commission declined to comment on procedural matters . ®
9b2a53b52d19c1cb: MELAKA, Nov 3 — The new Bill to replace the now-repealed Universities and University Colleges Act 1971 (AUKU) will not affect students’ freedom of expression, Deputy Prime Minister Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said.

He said the Cabinet agreed that the proposed legislation would be limited to matters concerning university administration, including academic affairs, governance and the appointment of senate members,
Ahmad Zahid also said that the new law would also cover the selection of university management personnel, including vice-chancellors and deputy vice-chancellors.

“The new legislation, which will carry a different name, will no longer include the seven provisions concerning students, including those on freedom, under AUKU, which restricted their freedom to engage in activities,” he said.

He was asked about the latest developments in the proposal for a new law to replace AUKU after attending the Apa Khabar Mahasiswa: Patriotisme Diperkasa programme at Universiti Teknologi Mara’s (UiTM) Alor Gajah Campus in Melaka today.
Also present at the event was Higher Education Minister Datuk Seri Zambry Abd Kadir.

Ahmad Zahid, also the Rural and Regional Development Minister, said universities should not penalise students for expressing their opinions unless their remarks involved sensitive issues relating to race, religion and the royal institution (3R).
“Under AUKU, universities did take action against students. Now that the Act has been repealed, students remain subject to existing laws, including criminal legislation.

“...if students are simply expressing differing opinions, political beliefs or the views of young people, I believe universities should welcome this rather than take legal action against them, unless their actions breach the law,” he said.
In a separate development, Ahmad Zahid said enrolment for the Department of Quantum Technology at UiTM was expected to begin next semester under a training-for-trainers concept.

“Initially, the academic staff will be sent for master’s or PhD studies, or short courses, to equip those with backgrounds in information technology and digital technology to lead the department before it is upgraded to the Faculty of Quantum Technology,” he said.
Ahmad Zahid announced earlier in October that RM500,000 would be allocated as initial funding to establish UiTM’s Department of Quantum Technology. — Bernama
a312adbc2b5e0af7: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules.

As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all.

Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution—a sort of moral code.
The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions, and mislead their evaluators.

Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage.

An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay.

In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.

A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).

Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.

The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.

A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?”

Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.

During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.

There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.

Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.

Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.”

One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.

It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.

“Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior.

Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)

Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?

“It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.
549299fe86cd0f66: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 3 — The Madani government has approved more than RM250 million to strengthen the East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) development in Kelantan, according to the Ministry of Finance (MOF).

3d20c786289bbf95: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — The Sessions Court hearing the case involving Fashion Valet Sdn Bhd (Fashion Valet) founders Datin Vivy Sofinas Yusof and her husband, Datuk Fadzarudin Shah Anuar, was told today that investment funds could not be used to pay dividends to any party, including the company’s shareholders.

Corporate lawyer Anne Wong Wai Yee, 49, who was involved in drafting the shareholders’ agreement between the couple and seven other companies, including Fashion Valet, on March 5, 2018, said the agreement did not contain any provision allowing investment funds to be used for such payments.
The other six companies were Proven Holding Sdn Bhd, MY E.G. Capital Sdn Bhd, Transasia E-Commerce Inc., Start Today Co. Ltd., Reussi Sdn Bhd and Pulau Tiga Ventures Sdn Bhd.

“The declaration of dividends requires the approval of a majority of the directors, including those appointed by Start Today Co. Ltd. and Pulau Tiga Ventures Sdn Bhd,” she testified during the trial of the couple, who are facing charges of criminal breach of trust involving RM8 million in investment funds from Khazanah Nasional Berhad (Khazanah) and Permodalan Nasional Berhad (PNB).

The sixth prosecution witness said the agreement also specified the permitted uses of the investment funds, namely expenditure on technology development, stores and warehouses, as well as products and brands.

“The permitted allocation of the investment funds was as follows: 30 per cent for consumer acquisition, 30 per cent for technology development, 20 per cent for store and warehouse expansion, and 20 per cent for product and brand acquisition, based on the total investment value.
“Typically, such expenditures require approval from a majority of the board of directors,” Wong said.
She said Fashion Valet was required to submit summaries of the utilisation of the investment funds to the board of directors on a quarterly and annual basis until the entire amount had been utilised.

“However, I have no knowledge of the distribution of dividends or the transfer of investment funds received by Fashion Valet, as my scope of work was limited to drafting and coordinating the contractual agreements.
“The subsequent execution of these agreements by the parties involved falls outside the scope of my professional duties,” said Wong, a partner at Karen Kaur & Anne Wong Partnership.

She further testified that Fashion Valet was prohibited from extending loans or credit to its directors, shareholders, related companies or any other parties without the approval of a majority of the board of directors.

“Furthermore, Fashion Valet is restricted from entering into any agreement or understanding with parties related to the company, its directors or shareholders, involving RM50,000 or more annually, without the approval of a majority of the directors, including those appointed by Start Today Co. Ltd. and Pulau Tiga Ventures Sdn Bhd,” she added.

Referring to a Subscription Agreement dated June 4, 2018, Wong said the document constituted a binding agreement between the relevant parties, namely Fashion Valet, Proven Holdings and PNB, concerning PNB’s investment in the company.

“Essentially, this agreement sets out the terms and conditions of PNB’s investment in Fashion Valet, whereby, in exchange for the investment, Fashion Valet would issue Redeemable Convertible Preference Shares (RCPS) to PNB,” she testified.

Vivy, 38, and Fadzarudin, 37, are charged with criminal breach of trust, allegedly committed with common intention in their capacity as directors of Fashion Valet, involving RM8 million in investment funds from Khazanah and PNB.

The charge alleges that they had authorised payments totalling RM8 million from Fashion Valet’s corporate bank account to a company known as 30 Maple without the approval of the company’s board of directors.
The alleged offence took place at the Public Bank Berhad branch in Bukit Damansara, at 36-40 Medan Setia 2, Plaza Damansara, Bukit Damansara, on Aug 21, 2018.
The charge, under Section 409 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34 of the same Code, provides for imprisonment of between two and 20 years, whipping and a fine upon conviction.

The couple also pleaded not guilty to an alternative charge of dishonestly misappropriating, with common intention, property belonging to Fashion Valet, namely RM8 million in investment funds from Khazanah and PNB, at the same location and on the same date.
The alternative charge, under Section 403 of the Penal Code, carries a penalty of imprisonment of between six months and five years, whipping and a fine upon conviction.
The trial, before Judge Rosli Ahmad, continues on Nov 20. — Bernama
be09bd6f6a87bcd6: WASHINGTON: The US plans to deepen engagement with Myanmar’s military-backed government to counter China’s influence and gain access to the war-torn nation’s vast rare-earth deposits.

According to a state department strategy document published last month, the US aims to become a “major trading partner and supplier” in Myanmar and see the Southeast Asian nation triple imports of American goods and agriculture products by 2030.
It also plans to take an active role in nationwide peace discussions over the same period “to increase US influence and create an environment for US investment over other regional actors”.
Washington and its Western allies heavily sanctioned the regime following its 2021 coup.

That isolation allowed Beijing to cement a strategic foothold by funding infrastructure projects and dominating critical mineral supply chains, often leveraging relationships with factions controlling resource-rich territories.

Myanmar is among the most commodity-rich nations on the planet, with significant resources including natural gas, copper, coal, teak, gemstones, tin, gold and rare earths, of which the country is the world’s fourth-largest supplier.

Since being installed as president in April, former coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign to bring Myanmar back into the international fold, making high-profile state visits to China, India and Malaysia.

The US strategy also aims to advance “fiscal federalism and territorial demarcation” that will create opportunities to access the country’s “bountiful rare earth resources and combat scam centres,” the document states.
It adds that expanding diplomatic efforts “will advance Administration priorities to counter China’s influence and promote a free and open Indo-Pacific”.
2f3c228d081fe139: KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit eased against the US dollar today amid a pullback in global artificial intelligence (AI)-related trades and investments.
SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said the ringgit's weakness was largely driven by broader risk aversion, particularly as investors unwound AI-related investments.
He said Malaysia has been a major beneficiary of the global AI investment boom, particularly through its semiconductor industry and technology-related investment flows.
“The trouble is that this relationship cuts both ways. When investors start pulling back from the AI trade, the ringgit can come under pressure even when the broader US dollar is weakening.
“Therefore, the ringgit is getting caught up in the broader unwinding of the AI trade, and that may remain the bigger influence in the near term,” he told Bernama.

Similarly, Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the ringgit traded within a narrow range against the greenback as traders and investors weighed concerns over a potential AI investment bubble, the upcoming US midterm elections and Friday’s US jobs data.
“On the AI investment bubble, there seem to be mixed signals among Wall Street firms at a conference in Hong Kong today.

“Some argued that AI infrastructure may have gone overboard, but others pointed to the potential benefits to the economy. Reversing risk appetite in the AI space could mean missing an opportunity to record further gains in investment returns,” he said.

Afzanizam also noted that Brent crude oil prices rose 1.94% to US$106.80 (RM435.42) per barrel, as concerns over a possible renewed US attack on Iran following the US midterm elections remained a source of market uncertainty.
“Hence, overall, market sentiments are effectively guarded as there are a lot of moving parts that could easily tilt the balance of risk,” he added.
At 6pm, the local note slipped to 4.0735/4.0775 against the greenback from yesterday’s close of 4.0695/4.0735.
Against major currencies, the ringgit traded mostly firmer.

The ringgit was marginally higher against the Japanese yen to 2.5762/2.5789 from 2.5766/2.5793 at yesterday’s close, inched up versus the euro to 4.5587/4.5631 from 4.5652/4.5697, but edged down vis-a-vis the British pound to 5.4658/5.4712 from 5.4621/5.4675, previously.
The ringgit was mostly lower against its Asean peers.

It slipped versus the Thai baht to 12.0696/12.0858 from 12.0496/12.0661 yesterday, inched down against the Indonesian rupiah to 224.3/224.6 from 224.1/224.4, and fell vis-a-vis the Philippine peso to 6.42/6.43 from 6.39/6.41 previously.
However, it rose against the Singapore dollar to 3.1807/3.1841 from the previous close of 3.1825/3.1862.

Held at Car Park C of the TM National Stadium in Bukit Jalil, today’s merchandise pre-sale drew crowds of eager fans, personal shoppers, and supportive parents, all braving the sweltering afternoon heat.
Fortunately for fans, organiser Livenation Malaysia has prepared several water stations around the area as well as a medic team on standby to accommodate queuing fans.
And not just that, several fans also came prepared with umbrellas, snacks, handheld fans and some even brought along foldable chairs to get through the day.

Personal shopper Ammarcs is one of the earliest in line for the merchandise. — Picture by Arif Zikri

“I was afraid the line would be massive by the time I got here, but luckily the crowd wasn’t too big yet.
“If I came late, my main concern was missing out on the exact sizes my customers asked for,” Ammarcs told Malay Mail.
Ammarcs who is also a student, said that he has been a personal shopper for around two years now and for today’s session, he decided to open up 20 slots where he would charge RM10 per item.

ebc8a0d6a96192e3: Public bodies in the UK expect higher operating costs and energy charges as a result of climate changes and the transition to lower carbon energy, but few have a good picture of the risks, according to government auditors.

A new report from the National Audit Office (NAO) says some public bodies expect financial impact from the risks they identified, although bodies were often not able to cost these – even approximately.

"Bodies anticipate costs to arise from damage to assets and infrastructure, driven by physical damage from extreme weather, as well as from chronic shifts to higher temperatures and more precipitation. Bodies also expect higher maintenance and repair costs, potential asset upgrades, and transition costs. Many bodies expect increased operating costs, including energy charges. Bodies controlling significant property or infrastructure are particularly concerned with decarbonization and adaptation costs," the report stated.

His Majesty’s Treasury (HMT) has set out rules for climate-related financial disclosure in larger central government bodies' annual reports, which produced their first set of reports for the 2025-26 financial year. Other rules for disclosure have been in place since 2022.

However, the NAO found [PDF] that understanding of the risks in the impact of climate change – increasing temperatures, higher risk of flooding, higher winds and longer droughts – was poor, as was insight into costs of moving to a low-carbon economy.

"Bodies did not articulate transition risks as well as physical risks in the strategy disclosures. In the disclosures we reviewed, while several transition risks were listed, few specifics were given, unlike physical risks, which were explained in greater detail," the report from the watchdog stated.

"The transition risks most frequently identified included the financial cost of transition, and supply chain disruption. Anticipated transition costs included the costs of: switching to lower-carbon energy sources, including investments in new technology; complying with new regulations; and of fluctuations in the price and availability of materials, water, energy and specialist skills," it added.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "UK public services will need to adapt to the impacts of climate change. Parliament needs clear information on the resilience of infrastructure, service provision and finances to climate change, and on how these risks are being managed."

"Although public bodies are still learning how best to report their most pressing climate risks, the requirement on all large central government bodies to make such disclosures from 2025-26 is an important first step. We expect this reporting to become more useful over time."

e62e866427a74a6c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 3 — Traders who impose hidden charges or disclose additional fees only at the final stage of a transaction may face legal action, including fines of up to RM100,000, said Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Minister Datuk Armizan Mohd Ali.
He said the practice misled consumers and undermined their right to know the actual price before making a purchase.

“This means consumers should have clear information on the amount they need to pay, rather than discovering certain charges at the final stage of a transaction,” he said in a written reply in the Dewan Rakyat today.

He was responding to a question from Muhammad Islahuddin Abas (PN-Mersing) on measures taken by the ministry to curb the practice of imposing additional or hidden charges disclosed only at the final stage of a transaction, resulting in the actual price exceeding the displayed or advertised price, particularly in the services, food and beverage, and online transaction sectors.

Armizan said Section 10B(1) of the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act 2011 [Act 723] allows action against businesses that fail to include all taxes, duties, and other charges in the prices of goods or services they display, advertise, publish, or quote.

The same Act stipulates under Section 57 that corporate bodies found in breach of the provision may be fined up to RM100,000, while individuals face penalties of up to RM50,000 in fines, two years’ imprisonment, or both.

He said the Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry (KPDN) also had enforcement powers under the Consumer Protection Act 1999 [Act 599], particularly Section 12(1)(a), which makes misleading representations about the price of goods or services an offence.

Section 12(3)(c) of the Act further stipulates that a price display is considered misleading if it gives the impression that the stated price covers everything, when additional charges are in fact imposed separately.

“Sections 9 and 10 of the Act also prohibit false or misleading claims about the nature and characteristics of goods or services. The provisions cover both transactions at physical business premises and online transactions.

“Those found in breach of the relevant provisions may be penalised under Section 145 of Act 599. The penalty for corporate bodies is a fine of up to RM100,000, while individuals may be fined up to RM50,000, jailed for up to three years, or both,” he said.

Armizan said KPDN had introduced guidelines on the All-Inclusive Pricing Policy to promote price transparency, particularly in the food and beverage, e-commerce and delivery sectors, requiring consumers to be informed of the total price, including the base price, service charges and delivery fees, before confirming an order.

He said the ministry also enforced the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering (Price Marking of Goods and Charges for Services) Order 2020, which requires service providers and business premises to display clearly and prominently a list of services offered and the charges imposed.
“The ministry will continue to step up monitoring and enforcement to ensure traders comply with price disclosure requirements, and urges consumers to check the final price before making payment.
“Consumers should also report to KPDN any instances of hidden fees or discrepancies between advertised prices and the actual amounts charged,” he added. — Bernama

ac9cca840060979a: AMSTERDAM: Dutch electronics and medical device manufacturer Philips said Tuesday it had reached a deal "in principle" with US authorities to settle a long-running case over faulty sleep machines.
The company has for years been weighed down by a series of crises over the recall of its DreamStation machines for sleep apnoea, a disorder in which breathing stops and starts during sleep.
Millions of devices were recalled over concerns that users were at risk of inhaling pieces of noise-cancelling foam and fears it could potentially cause cancer.

Presenting its third-quarter (Q3) results, the Dutch firm said it had "reached an agreement in principle with the US justice department to resolve the previously disclosed criminal and civil investigations related to the... recall".
The company set aside €288 million (US$322 million) in Q3 of this year to settle the case, with payment expected in the first quarter of 2027.
"The settlement is subject to finalisation of the relevant documentation," said Philips.
The provision pushed down the company's Q3 profits to €28 million, compared to €187 million in the same period of last year.
Chief executive officer Roy Jakobs told reporters the deal was clinched "in the last few days", but declined to give further details while the paperwork was being finalised.
"It's for sure an important milestone for us as it marks a step forward in resolving the sleep and respiratory care related proceedings," he said.
Market traders appeared to agree, pushing up the stock around six percent at the opening bell.
'AI-enabled innovations'
Once famous for making lightbulbs and televisions among other products, Amsterdam-based Philips in recent years has sold off subsidiaries to focus on medical care technology.
The firm recorded quarterly turnover of €4.4 billion, compared to €4.3 billion in Q3 of 2025.
Philips maintained its forecast of sales growth over the full year of between 3% and 4.5%.
"We delivered a strong Q3," said Jakobs.
"We see our customers responding well to our latest AI-enabled innovations," added the CEO.
In February, Philips posted its first annual profit after three straight years of losses, turning in a better-than-expected gain of €897 million.
In the second quarter of this year, the firm reported net profits of €386 million, helped by a refund from US tariffs later struck down by the US Supreme Court.
Jakobs painted a bright outlook for the firm.
"Our year-to-date results, together with our strong order book, give us confidence in delivering our full-year outlook and achieving our medium-term ambitions," said the executive.
601cfd26de0279b1: Raspberry Pi has announced yet another round of price hikes, this time adding $80 to the cost of its 16GB Pi 5, which now sells for more than three times its original launch price.

The latest bump, announced by Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton, takes the 16GB Pi 5 to a whopping $385. The 16GB Compute Module 5 variants are also getting $40 more expensive, although the Raspberry Pi 500+, which packs the same amount of RAM, has escaped this particular round.
Upton blamed a familiar culprit: soaring memory costs, worsened by a lack of alternative suppliers for 16GB DRAM and ongoing shortages of other components.

"Unfortunately, a lack of alternative supply for 16GB DRAM, compounded by other ongoing component shortages, means we now need to make further price increases on some of our highest-density products," Upton wrote.

It's becoming an expensive habit for Raspberry Pi customers. The 16GB Pi 5 cost $120 when it launched in January 2025, which seems almost reasonable now. Raspberry Pi added $25 in December, another $60 in February, and a further $100 in April. With today's $80 increase, buyers are being asked to cough up $265 more than they were less than two years ago, a price hike of 221 percent.
And it's barely been a month since Raspberry Pi raised prices on its 2GB Pi 4 and Pi 5 models by $12.50 apiece, taking them to $67.50 and $77.50 respectively.

The repeated markups come despite Raspberry Pi reporting record first-half results in September. Revenue jumped 90 percent to $256.9 million, while gross profit rose 79 percent to $59.4 million. Gross profit per board climbed 53 percent to $12.20, helped partly by memory purchased before prices went through the roof. That stockpile advantage has since largely disappeared.
For customers unwilling to pay nearly $400 for a single-board computer, Upton advises buying something with less RAM, using an older Pi, or optimizing applications to make do with less memory.
He also warned that some sellers are exploiting the shortages by charging inflated prices or offering products that aren't what they appear to be, urging customers to stick to approved resellers.

“We’re aware that a few bad actors have been taking advantage of the current memory supply circumstances to sell Raspberry Pi products at inflated prices or shift products that aren’t what they seem,” he said.

There is, apparently, some good news, as Raspberry Pi continues to insist the increases are temporary. "As we've said from the beginning, the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again," Upton wrote.
That could be a long wait. Micron has previously warned that memory shortages could drag on into 2028 or beyond, so anyone hoping to see a $120 Pi 5 again probably shouldn't hold their breath. ®
d933ea1c8ca3a2ee: TEHRAN, Nov 3 — Iran unveiled a massive billboard and banners pledging to kill US President Donald Trump across Tehran on Tuesday, bringing to a new level the official rhetoric displayed in the capital.
“We will kill Trump”, read the billboard towering over the busy Enghelab Square in Tehran, which depicted the US president behind bars with his head bowed.

New designs of billboards and displays mocking and vowing revenge against Trump have frequently been set up around Tehran since the war began on February 28 when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

In recent days, renewed diplomatic efforts have been underway to bring Tehran and Washington to negotiate to prevent a resumption in fighting which has spread across the region and driven prices up globally.
Trump, who on Tuesday faces crucial US midterm elections amid voter discontent driven in part by the Iran war, has said that a deal “could happen”.

In the busy Tajrish Square in northern Tehran, an open-air exhibition featured paintings of Trump, including one showing him with his face lying bloodied on the ground as a foot presses down on his head.
Another depicted a bomb obscuring his face, in an apparent reference to Belgian surrealist René Magritte’s 1964 painting The Son of Man.

Nearby, a life-sized replica of a jail cell has remained on display, with an actor impersonating Trump spending the day inside. An adjacent screen showed images of the damage caused by US strikes on Iran.
Tehran accuses Trump of deliberately targeting civilian sites during the war, including a school and a wedding ceremony, killing dozens of people including women and children.

State-sponsored billboards and murals have been a fixture of Iran’s public spaces since the 1979 Islamic revolution, used to honour allies, celebrate military figures and send political messages to adversaries, particularly the United States and Israel. — AFP
1329ba9be395653b: KOTA KINABALU, Nov 3 — The ongoing construction of a high-altitude training centre on Mount Kinabalu has come under scrutiny, with indigenous groups and tourism stakeholders questioning its environmental impact, approvals and whether communities with customary ties to the mountain were adequately consulted.

The controversy surfaced around October 30 after photographs showing structures and apparent drilling activities near Sayat-Sayat circulated on social media, prompting calls for authorities to clarify the nature and purpose of the work.

The photographs prompted criticism over a lack of transparency, including from Kundasang Tourism and Culture Association chairman Datuk Japiril Suhaimin, who called for an investigation into the project's location, scope and approvals, as well as its potential effects on water sources, soil stability and biodiversity.

Bundu Tuhan Village Heritage and Culture head Adrian Soros also questioned whether communities with customary ties to the mountain had been consulted, saying many villagers were unaware of the construction.
He raised concerns about drilling into the mountain, which he said went against customary beliefs, as well as the protection of local water sources and the management of human waste at high altitude.

Tourism, Culture and Environment Minister Datuk Jafry Ariffin subsequently issued a statement saying the project was not new and had originally been proposed under the Kinabalu Park Development Plan in 2015.
He said the project had obtained approval from the Sabah Parks Board of Trustees and endorsement from the Mount Kinabalu Native Customary Advisory Council.
“The HATC was originally proposed under the Kinabalu Park Development Plan in 2015, but its implementation was deferred following the earthquake that struck Mount Kinabalu that year.

“The initiative was subsequently revived and officially launched in 2025 as part of Sabah’s efforts to diversify its tourism offerings and strengthen its position as an internationally recognised mountaineering destination,” he said.
The new development would provide basic accommodation and specialised facilities to support high-altitude training and mountaineering activities.

Jafry said the centre was intended to cater to mountaineers preparing for expeditions to higher-altitude destinations, including Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua and Mount Everest, by providing facilities for altitude acclimatisation, technical training and familiarisation with specialised climbing equipment.

He said construction involved lightweight, prefabricated and modular building materials to minimise environmental disturbance, with the structures designed to withstand strong winds and challenging weather conditions at higher elevations.
The construction method also avoided the use of heavy machinery in view of the mountain’s sensitive natural environment.

Jafry said the project’s approval and implementation must respect Mount Kinabalu’s cultural and spiritual significance to indigenous communities, as reflected in the involvement of the Native Customary Advisory Council.
The minister nevertheless emphasised that the approval did not exempt the project from complying with stipulated conditions, technical specifications and environmental regulations.

“We take the concerns raised by the public seriously. The ministry will consider a comprehensive investigation to ascertain whether all approved specifications, environmental safeguards and regulatory conditions have been fully observed.
“Should any non-compliance be established, the ministry will not hesitate to pursue the necessary enforcement measures in accordance with the law,” he said.

However, despite his statement, the Dayak International Organisation (DIO) today called for all construction, drilling and installation work at the site to stop, alleging that the development violated indigenous customary law protected under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP).

Its United Nations representative, Datuk Petinggi Andrew Ambrose Atama Katama, questioned the use of the Mount Kinabalu Native Customary Advisory Council to endorse the project, saying this did not replace the need for consent from communities, particularly the Kadazandusun and Momogun.
Andrew described Aki Nabalu as a sacred living entity and ancestral repository rather than a commercial asset for generating state revenue.

DIO also called for an independent environmental audit, including an assessment of wastewater impact on local water catchments, and said it would raise the matter at the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues and the Unesco Global Geoparks Network.
Mount Kinabalu, also known as Aki Nabalu, is Sabah's highest peak at 4,095 metres and holds deep cultural and spiritual significance for indigenous communities, particularly the Kadazandusun.
Every year, locals hold sacred rituals to honour the mountain spirits, seek permission and protection, and ensure the safety and well-being of climbers.
Kinabalu Park was inscribed as a Unesco World Heritage Site in 2000 for its exceptional biodiversity, including thousands of plant species and a wide range of habitats.

9b404c2ab078ecdc: SINGAPORE, Nov 3 — Reformative training and jail time should be the default sentencing options for scammers and those who facilitate scams, according to a Bill proposed in Parliament on Tuesday (November 3).

The Sentencing (Scams) Bill, introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), reaffirms Parliament's intention that scam and scam-enabling offences should be met with strong deterrent sentences because of the serious harm they cause to victims.
However, on September 10, the High Court published its judgment regarding the case of Mohamed Erzan Taib Zohri, one among six young offenders who allegedly committed scam-enabling offences.
The court allowed four of the six appeals and replaced the offenders' reformative training sentences with probation.

The High Court also held that reformative training or imprisonment should not be the default sentence for young offenders who commit scam-enabling offences. According to MHA, this is inconsistent with Parliament's intention that such offences should generally attract deterrent sentences.

Under the proposed Bill, the High Court's decision will not be binding on and need not be considered by any court when considering any sentence imposed on scam offenders or scam-enabling offences, or when hearing appeals relating to such sentences.

In addition, courts, except the Youth Court, should consider reformative training or imprisonment as the primary and default sentencing options for offenders aged 21 and below, unless there are exceptional circumstances, the Bill states.
Youth offences relating to scams on the rise
Scams remain the most prevalent crime type in Singapore, with an average of 90 scam reports amounting to S$2 million (RM6.4 million) in losses each day in the first half of 2026, MHA said.

Over 1,000 youths were investigated in connection with scam reports in 2025, while the number of youths who committed cheating and related offences rose 37 per cent, from 814 in 2024 to 1,114 in 2025.
These youths were largely involved in scam cases as mules, according to MHA.
“We need to do more to deter young offenders from being enticed by the prospect of quick financial gains to commit such offences,” the ministry stated.
MHA added: “If a deterrent approach is not taken, Singapore's scam and youth offending situation could deteriorate.”
MHA emphasised that scams can cause serious harm to victims and must be met with a strong deterrent message, which the Bill seeks to reinforce. — AsiaOne

54f490c3507bf531: The Register and LucidLink are hosting a dinner for senior technology, infrastructure and data leaders at the Covent Garden Hotel on Tuesday 24 November. Joe Fay of The Register is in the chair. The subject is one most of them will know from their own shop, where the same file lives in several places at once and nobody is quite sure which copy is current.
Most organisations have a folder that proves it. There's a file called final, another called final2, and then the one people are actually using, which somebody emailed to a contractor last Thursday.

It's mildly funny until two people spend a week editing different copies and one of them loses the argument. Meanwhile the storage bill picks up another copy of everything, and each team that builds its own way round the problem gives IT another place it can't see into.

Alan Marshall, Strategic Director, EMEA at LucidLink, joins a small group of peers at the table, and nobody is there to give a presentation. Because the evening is held under the Chatham House Rule, people tend to say what really happened, like the team that quietly built its own sync service because the approved one was too slow, or the leaver who could still open a file share months after going.

From there the conversation widens out to unstructured data that won't stop growing, the duplicate storage piling up, the security risk of access scattered across all those copies, and how to modernise without binning the storage and governance the business has already paid for.
Drinks start at 6.30pm, then it's dinner around one table until 9pm. Places are limited.
Request your place at the November 24 dinner
Places go by invitation and each one is confirmed personally.
a1bb83c79c172522: HONG KONG, Nov 3 — Asian stock markets struggled Tuesday following another AI-fuelled tech selloff on Wall Street that overshadowed a possible breakthrough in talks to end the Middle East war.
However, oil prices clawed back some of Monday’s plunge in oil prices following a report that US forces had struck an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Investor fears about the vast sums being invested in the artificial intelligence complex have cast a pall over trading floors in the second half of the year, with many questioning firms’ profitability.

Earnings reports from titans including Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft have shown they will keep pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into data centres and chips even as investors grow impatient for returns.
Monday saw Apple post forecast-topping sales and profits but warned that its gross margin — the per centage of sales left after output costs — would drop in October-December.

The investment pledges come amid a surge in borrowing costs, which have raised concerns about some companies’ financial positions owing to their huge debts, adding downward pressure to stock prices.
After a tough run last week, the selling continued at the start of this week with losses in Asian giants followed by their US counterparts on Wall Street where the Nasdaq ended 1.1 per cent off.
And there was not much improvement Tuesday — Seoul-listed SK hynix and Samsung tanked five per cent and 4.2 per cent respectively, dragging the Kospi down more than three per cent.

Even a more than seven per cent plunge in oil prices Monday was unable to provide support.

“Cheaper energy takes heat out of inflation, eases the rates pressure and normally gives long-duration tech a meaningful updraft.
“Instead, the Nasdaq handed back the entire opening bounce and broke Friday’s lows, a fairly ugly sign that the selling is now being driven by something deeper than oil, yields or the dollar.”
US President Donald Trump on Monday signalled progress in talks as Tehran said “intensive” exchanges were underway while offering to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions.
“But here’s the thing: we’re dealing from total strength. We can end it at any time. If I can make a deal, I’d rather do it, save a lot of lives.”

Vice President JD Vance separately said he and Trump were optimistic about securing an agreement, while Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian announced his government had been granted more authority by the supreme leader to pursue peace talks.
The country’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, added that “the ball is now in America’s court to prevent war”.

And National Australia Bank’s Rodrigo Catril offered a word of caution over the chances of peace.

“Iran wants US restraint and economic relief (i.e. an end to hostilities, the lifting of the US naval blockade, relief from oil sanctions and the unfreezing of at least $12 billion in assets) before delivering the concessions Washington seeks, including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.

d8cc90e87c6d98db: FRANKFURT: German auto parts supplier Schaeffler said Tuesday that it planned to cut almost 3,500 jobs and close five sites in Europe as the crisis gripping the region's car industry deepens.

Like other German carmakers and suppliers, the group has struggled with competition for its key products, which include ball bearings and electric vehicle parts, especially from Chinese manufacturers.
Three-fourths of the 3,460 job cuts and four of the five site closures will be in Germany, the company said in a statement, pointing to "above-average" costs for workers in Europe's top economy.

The cuts, to be completed by 2028, are around 3% of the group's global workforce of almost 110,000. They should result in annual savings of around 300 million euros (US$336 million) from 2030, it said.
Schaeffler, in a statement, said it was "responding to the persistently challenging environment in the automotive industry."

There was "an overall downturn in the market and intensifying competition... characterised by weakened demand for internal combustion engine vehicles and a delayed ramp-up of electric mobility," it added.
The cuts would be mainly focused on production and research and development.
Sites would be closed in Berlin, Dortmund, and two other towns in western Germany. A small site in Belgium will also be shuttered.
There will also be job cuts at sites in France and Slovakia.
Schaeffler said some of the job losses would be offset by the creation of positions in "future-oriented fields", such as humanoid robotics and defence.

While not as well known as the car titans they work with, such as Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes, Germany's suppliers are a crucial part of the auto ecosystem, providing everything from braking systems to in-car electronics.
But as their customers have fallen into crisis, battling Chinese competition, high production costs at home and weakening demand, suppliers have been hit hard.
Volkswagen is planning to cut around 120,000 jobs across its brands by 2030.
German industrial titan Bosch, the world's biggest supplier of car equipment, announced last year 13,000 job cuts, mostly in its auto division.
88eb9953ac71af8f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A vibe-coded site that scraped Archive of Our Own (AO3) fanfiction works, reuploaded them and charged for audiobook versions is down now after the creator said they received over 2,000 takedown requests from authors in the single day it was up.

ao3.life, a website that sprung up following last week’s announced weeks-long outage of fanfiction repository AO3, scraped the internet for works to populate the site using “a swarm of AI Agents controlling 40 virtual machines were scraping the internet for all drives, scrapes, and sources,” the site’s creator, named Ganesh, wrote on a page apologizing for the entire project. AO3.life went down on Monday evening following widespread backlash from readers and authors on social media.
Before it went down, the ao3.life homepage said, “AO3, saved before it slips away. Search every fandom, ship and trope. Read it here, keep the EPUB, or let it read to you when your eyes get tired.”

AO3 went down on Thursday following a security incident, according to the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW) which owns the repository. The site is expected to be down for as long as four weeks. OTW says no data has been lost. Readers and authors are generally distraught, unable to access the site at all for potentially a month. AO3 hosts nearly 18.5 million works.

ao3.life offered works as EPUBs for reading on e-readers, and as AI-generated audiobooks that Ganesh charged for after the first three minutes. They claimed on a page titled “Authors get paid here” that authors would get 91% of the profits, with AO3.life getting 9% to cover “narration and processing” costs. “Your earnings wait for you. You don't need an account here to earn. We hold your share indefinitely until you collect it, however long that takes,” the site said.

On AO3, authors can “archive lock” their works, making them visible only to logged-in users, which keeps AI bots like this one from scraping them and also gives better control over how far a work spreads or whether it breaks the containment of the repository’s intended audience. Of course, authors couldn’t access AO3 while it was down to lock their works if they were publicly available before the outage.

But some authors reported the archive lock not mattering. “I had everything archive locked on ao3 and it's still all here and I as the author have 0 control over any of my fics on there,” one AO3 author posted on Bluesky.

ao3.life said at the bottom of the homepage that authors could request their works be removed from the site: ”Every work belongs to its author; if one is yours and you want it gone, email legal@ao3.life and it goes.” Proving that you’re the author of the work to ao3.life required authors “leave a note on your AO3 profile so we can confirm it's you,” the site said. But how authors could do that while AO3 was — and still is — completely down is a mystery.

A lot of authors clearly used the legal complaints email. “In the time this site has been up, I’ve facilitated over 2,000 takedown requests. It was never my intention to hurt so many authors - and I’m truly sorry to you all. There’s no way to show my sorry [sic] better than taking this site down,” Ganesh wrote. “Why did I charge for AI Slop audiobooks? I doubt anyone knows how expensive it is to run a server like this, especially with the amount of usage this site got. It had 126,592 unique users within 24 hours of going up, and had terabytes of bandwidth in usage. In an attempt to keep the site up, I thought audiobooks were a good option. I sold like 11 audiobooks, if it’s any consolation.”

Fanfiction has become a target of AI scraping, repackaging and reselling in recent years. In 2024, I reported on how Etsy sellers turn free fanfiction into printed and bound physical books, then list them for sale for as much as $100 a book.

With AO3 down and fans scrambling to find ways to keep consuming the works they miss, some people have started sharing links to Google Drives on Reddit and Discord of works they’d downloaded from the site previously, even if they aren’t the original authors of those works. This has alarmed and angered a lot of writers; whether authors have the right to profit from their works depends on the content and their use of existing intellectual property. Fanfic is typically considered fair use — I can write a VeggieTales Bob and Larry fic without getting sued by Universal Pictures if it’s sufficiently transformative, for example — but selling it could draw the ire of their lawyers, and a potential lawsuit even if I happened to ultimately win it. Authors on AO3 are prohibited by the platform from monetizing their works or linking to payment platforms.

“It was never and is not my intention to hurt authors, and I hope every subequent [sic] action I’ve taken is representative of that,” Ganesh said. “From an attempt at revenue sharing, to responding to takedown requests as fast as I could, to taking down the site as a whole.” They signed the note: “Yours truly, a 17 year old from India that thought they were doing something good.”
09d414a2d3db0b6a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 3 — US chipmaking giant Nvidia is ordering its data centre partners to scale back work with Chinese customers, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
Nvidia’s cloud computing clients must now sell at least 51 per cent of their services to non-Chinese companies, the FT reported, citing five people with knowledge of the matter.
The new rules only affect future contracts and not existing agreements, the report said.

Nvidia neither confirmed nor denied the report to AFP, but said in a statement that “datacentres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide.”
“Longstanding US policy encourages every cloud to build on American infrastructure and to win business everywhere they can,” the statement said.
“America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well.”
Asked about the report, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she was not aware of it.

“As a matter of principle, we consistently hope that all parties can provide a fair, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for companies from all countries, including Chinese companies,” she said.
China and the United States are locked in a race for dominance in the fast-moving artificial intelligence sector.
In recent months, the two countries have traded accusations of stealing AI technologies and jeopardising security.
Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company thanks to the global drive to build data centres packed with specialist computer chips and other hardware that runs AI systems. — AFP
8272e20d7aaa9a41: FRANKFURT, Nov 3 — German airline giant Lufthansa said Tuesday it expects its 2026 fuel costs to be €2 billion (RM9.12 billion) higher than last year as the Iran war keeps global energy prices elevated.
Releasing third quarter results, the group predicted its fuel bill across the full year will come in at €9.3 billion.
That is 600 million higher than it had anticipated just a few months ago, as the US war against Iran drags on.
The group, which also operates carriers including Swiss, Brussels and Eurowings, also slightly downgraded its forecast for core profit to a range of between €1.7 and €2.0 billion for 2026.
Previously it predicted a range of between €1.7 and €2.2 billion.
Despite the slightly bleaker outlook, the group reported a 30-per cent jump in profits for the July-September period, beating forecasts.
Net profit came in at €1.26 billion, with the company saying there had been strong demand for premium tickets to Asia and North America.
Revenues increased nine percent from a year earlier to €12.2 billion.
Fuel costs however were more than €500 million higher in the quarter compared to a year earlier.

“We improved our result compared with the previous year, despite higher fuel costs weighing on the quarterly result by more than half a billion euros — we are satisfied with that,” chief financial officer Till Streichert said.
“This was supported by robust demand in passenger traffic.” — AFP
