226d6d5c25cb9ac1: People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs?  MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory, to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky, Assistant Professor Chara Podimata, and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots.  The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country.  MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots. Q: What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory? Podimata: People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves. One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public. Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation.   Q: Professor Podimata, you studied how LLMs shaped political discourse and information during the 2024 election. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project? Podimata: The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024 presidential election, which found evidence of meaningful variation in AI models’ responses over time and across prompt framings, as well as differences in how models characterized candidates and implicitly anticipated the election outcome.  The 2026 midterms give us an opportunity to expand that work substantially. Midterm elections are particularly interesting because there are many state and local contests unfolding simultaneously, alongside broader national political narratives. Our new audit survey therefore asks both contest-specific questions about the U.S. House and Senate candidates, but also broader questions about voting information and other aspects of the election information environment. Q: Why do you think it’s so important to be studying how chatbots are responding to political queries across different groups of users? Podimata: We all build our own “microcosms” through our interactions with chatbots. And yet, we lack systematic ways of understanding how these individualized information environments are shaped by who we are or how they evolve over time as we and the information environment changes.  For example, people may not realize that what their favorite chatbot tells them about a political issue may be quite different from what their friend’s favorite chatbot tells them about the exact same issue. And importantly, these differences matter even when the information being provided is factually correct. Chatbots may frame the same facts differently, emphasize different aspects of an issue, express different levels of uncertainty, or draw on entirely different sources, even when responding to identical queries between different users. As a result, two users may walk away with very different perceptions of the same underlying facts, without ever realizing that their experiences differed.  In some ways, this brings back many of the concerns we (as researchers and society) have grappled with in the context of social media. On social media, users and researchers could, at least to some extent, observe the information circulating across different Facebook groups, Instagram accounts, or TikTok communities. With chatbots, these information environments are largely invisible to anyone outside the individual conversation. We cannot easily observe what different users are being told, let alone systematically compare those responses or track how they change over time. This is precisely why projects like the LLM Election Observatory are so important: By systematically collecting and publicly sharing chatbot responses, we can begin to make these otherwise invisible differences observable and open to scrutiny. Q: What sorts of questions and AI responses are you tracking through the dashboard? Podimata: There are several questions we ultimately want this dataset to help us study. For example: Do different models provide systematically different information for the same questions? Do their responses change over the course of the campaign? Does the answer a particular model gives change depending on how a user frames the question or describes themselves (e.g., does it change if the model gets informed that the user is a Democrat or a Republican)? And, finally, what are the sources that the models pull information from when answering election-related questions?  Our public dashboard is an important part of the project. We want people both from and outside of academia to be able to see the data we are collecting as the election unfolds rather than only seeing the results months later in an academic paper. The dashboard therefore presents the underlying data and some preliminary descriptive analyses, and we plan to make the dataset available for other researchers to study as well. We expect the dashboard to evolve as the data and our methods evolve. Through this dashboard, we wanted to build on the scientific methodology we developed in 2024 but also to make the research much more accessible and useful to the public while the election is actually unfolding. Not only that, but the addition of MIT political science experts in the team cannot be overstated; Adam and Charles have really helped expand the questions that we are asking in our audit. Q: What do you wish voters across the country knew about AI chatbots when it comes to searching for election information? Berinsky: People should be sure to remember that just because a chatbot sounds confident doesn’t mean it is accurate. AI systems are designed to answer the questions that people ask them in an authoritative voice even when they are wrong, incomplete, or leaning on a weak source. These answers are a reasonable place to start, but voters shouldn’t stop there. Q: What are your findings thus far? Podimata: We have not yet done the full, longitudinal analysis, so we are only going to talk about broad strokes here, but a few broad patterns seem to be visible in the 2026 data. Across the different user identities we present, we see differences in how the answers are presented, in which sources a model cites, and in tone — sometimes even when the underlying facts are the same. What we cannot yet say is how stable those differences are, how they move over the course of the election, or how a real person would read and react to them. Our future analyses will take this up. It also underscores why the continuous record of responses we are collecting matters more than any single snapshot that you might see in the days around the election. Q: Professor Berinsky, your research has also shown that in some cases AI chatbots can be harnessed to help refute misinformation. Can you talk a bit about this? Berinsky: In my undergraduate course on information and social media I have been talking for a while about how AI can cut both ways. On one hand, these tools can generate misleading claims in text, pictures, and video at a scale we have never seen. Basically, AI can help bad actors “flood the zone” with misinformation. On the other hand, some of the most promising recent work demonstrates that evidence-based dialogues with a chatbot can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other beliefs that are not supported by the balance of publicly available evidence.  AI has the potential to do such debunking at scale — something we have long struggled to do. The lesson from decades of misinformation research is that any technology (be it print, radio, or television in earlier eras) is not inherently good or bad for promoting truth. The devil is in the details in how it is built and deployed. Independent auditing like this project can help us assess the ultimate impact of such technologies. Q: Can you talk a bit about your overall goal with this research?  Podimata: AI is a transformative technology, and people understandably have very different expectations (and feelings) about what it will mean for society at large. All of us have people in our lives that are overly enthusiastic about AI, others that are deeply concerned, and many more that are somewhere in between trying to understand what this technology can and cannot do. Our goal here is not to begin from the assumption that AI is either good or bad for elections. Instead, we hope to shed some light onto one part of this transformation: what information major AI systems are actually giving people about an election as it unfolds.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> In the wake of fanfiction repository Archive of Our Own (AO3) announcing a weeks-long security incident outage, readers and writers are reflecting on why the site is important to the fanfiction community, and how they’re coping with the downtime.

On Thursday, the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted that the site was down for maintenance, eventually updating to say the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month. OTW confirmed in an updated status report Friday morning that this outage is due to a security incident.

Some have speculated that the outage is a result of the PHP scramble this week that led to several sites going down to update their security, but AO3 doesn’t use PHP. An OTW representative told CNET: “I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”
Massive Fanfic Site Archive of Our Own Says It’s Going Down for 'Up to 4 Weeks'
Oh my god?

A lot of people are grieving the loss of Kinktober, AO3’s annual group writing exercise where writers upload a chapter or fic every day throughout October based on a prompt of the day. (The prompts are horny, if that’s not clear.) Several of the writers and readers who reached out to me following the outage brought up the poor timing around Kinktober.

One writer I spoke to who posts her writing and reads others’ writing on AO3, told me that she was in the middle of racing to finish a work that was deliberately timed to Kinktober and Halloween when the outage happened. She was hitting “next chapter” while reading a fic on Wednesday night when she got the message that the site was down for maintenance, “which I initially took as a sign from the universe to go to bed,” she said.
“The outage hasn’t derailed my desire to write. If anything, I want to have more chapters ready to go so my readers can eat good once it’s over,” she said.

Do you know anything else about what happened to Ao3? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

Some writers are considering posting elsewhere while they wait for AO3 to return, but it’s not an ideal workaround. AO3 author who goes by Selkie Myth told me they’re moving to Space Battles, another fanfiction site, during the outage. “I'm shrugging and just posting on SB [Space Battles] while the site's down. Hopefully I'll remember to post the chapters over on AO3 once it's back up — the story is projected to end during the outage. I anticipate the same is true for a lot of other authors,” they said.

Some people have said they’ll try fanfiction.net in the meantime, but it’s a much more bare-bones website. Fanfiction site Sufficient Velocity added a banner to its homepage welcoming AO3 refugees: “We’ve had a big influx of guests due to the AO3 outage. If you've been affected by the outage we're sorry to hear that and hope that they're able to get that fixed soon.” Wattpad, which many fanfiction writers and readers really, really hate for reasons I won’t get into here, posted on X: “we're here to support you during this difficult time.” Overwhelmingly, the replies are from people telling Wattpad to go away.

Another AO3 writer who goes by Ren told me she has two long works in progress right now with nowhere to post them. Posting elsewhere poses continuity and discovery problems, as some of these fanfiction works span chapters and hundreds of thousands of words of character and worldbuilding. “I could technically keep posting updates on sites like tumblr through the downtime, but both of these fics are quite long and I haven't been posting them anywhere other than AO3 — if I drop a new chapter for my 130k Pokemon Black and White fanfic on Tumblr completely out of context, people just now finding my work aren't going to be able to read the rest for a while :(“ she told me in an email. “I have seen other authors posting their gdocs and Ellipsus reader links in the meantime, but my draft files aren't exactly presentable... I will keep marinating but what will probably happen is my wips [works in progress] will just be on hiatus for a bit. My readers are used to hiatuses at least.”

Another writer said she’s not considering posting elsewhere. “Wattpad can piss off,” she said. “But I may go back to fanfiction.net to save and physically print some of my favorite fics from way back in the day (the ancient/sacred texts, if you will) to ensure I have copies of those somewhere. This outage is a good reminder that things can vanish in the blink of an eye, whether a website crashes or is hacked or an author decides to suddenly delete their fic. If you love something, smash the kudos button, comment on it, bookmark it, subscribe, and consider downloading it. You never know.”

A reader who emailed me following the outage said they’ve been enjoying getting into AO3 as a new fan. “I was a big fanfic skeptic, but that’s changed lately. I’ve found some truly excellent writers, and real creativity. The free nature of it in this increasingly horrifying stage of capitalism is refreshing,” they said.

AO3 has said in status updates and to journalists that they don’t expect any data loss. Losing works would be devastating for writers and readers, but AO3 is more than just a repository for writing; it’s a community of people commenting and reacting to those stories. Selkie mentioned the rigorous tagging habits of AO3 members, where stories are tagged with sometimes dozens of fanfiction tropes, character names, content hints and warnings, and can constitute a language specific to the platform and its readers; “Crack Treated Seriously,” for example, means writing a silly premise with a straight face, while “Idiots in Love” is self explanatory.

“To me, the more devastating thing would be to lose the comments and kudos on my fic. Technically I have them saved elsewhere because I get AO3 email alerts, but seeing them threaded in one place at the end of a chapter hits different,” a writer said. “Comments can turn an author’s entire day around and restore their will to live. I often reread them if I have writer’s block or a bad bout of imposter syndrome. They also turn the otherwise solitary act of writing into something communal. Seeing someone experience your story chapter by chapter is incredibly motivating and makes the writing process feel less isolating.”

OTW is entirely volunteer-run, and people on social media and in speaking to them directly have said they hope AO3 users go easy on staff during this time. “So many people rely on AO3 as an outlet for creativity and escapism as the real world burns, myself included. It’s also important to remember that the site is run by volunteers,” that writer said. “The work they do to protect writers, fight censorship and safeguard freedom of expression is extremely important and necessary, especially right now. They deserve all the respect and patience in the world as they work to get the archive back up and running. Be kind.”
Ren, echoing those sentiments, sent me a meme:

“An additional sentiment I've seen is ‘ok so when AO3 comes back we're all going to tell our favorite authors how much we missed their work, right?’ which I hope catches on — I'm writing for niche fandoms and had to disable guest comments due to bot spam, so comments are few and far between as it is,” Ren said. “I do kind of hope that the extended outage serves as a sort of wake-up call to anyone who's been taking ao3 for granted lately. It certainly was for me.”

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Researchers have amassed a trove of more than 25,000 calls to a support hotline for people during and after psychedelic trips, making it “the largest dataset of psychedelic support interactions ever assembled—exceeding the combined sample sizes of all published psychedelic clinical trials by an order of magnitude,” according to a study published on Friday in Science Advances.

Despite the popularity of psychedelics as recreational drugs, and increasing interest in them as medically-prescribed therapeutic treatments, there is very little research about the effects of these substances outside of clinical settings with carefully-selected patients. That, scientists say, is limiting what we can learn about the effects of these drugs, because the vast majority of psychedelics are consumed by all kinds of people in homes, festivals, ceremonial gatherings, or other uncontrolled environments.

The Fireside Project, a nonprofit founded in 2020, has filled this knowledge gap with its Psychedelic Support Line, which connects callers who are on bad trips, or who are seeking more information about psychedelics, with trained volunteers who offer confidential peer support.

The team has now published a compendium of 25,419 anonymized interactions with 220 hotline volunteers that took place between April 2021 and February 2026. The database opens an unprecedented window into the experiences of people on psilocybin, ketamine, MDMA, LSD, ayahuasca, and even cannabis, which is not generally considered a psychedelic but can trigger similar effects, such as mild hallucinations.

It’s a “treasure trove,” said Félix Schoeller, a senior research scientist at the Institute for Advanced Consciousness Studies, a California-based nonprofit, who led the study, in a call with 404 Media. “In general, we're really lacking any evidence and data beyond what exists in the underground world, if you will, for psychedelic therapy.”

“There's different types of knowledge,” continued Schoeller, who is CEO of ReWire Neurotechnologies, a startup focused on novel experiential treatments for depression. “Some cultures and communities have been doing that for thousands of years. But there's a question about how to do this in a way that follows the principles of biomedical science.”

The interactions included phone calls and text exchanges with hotline volunteers who provided support by talking through the experience or connecting callers with emergency services in the most urgent cases. About 40.2 percent of callers (10,208 interactions) were actively tripping, while 32.1 percent of callers reached out after they had tripped, a period known as “integration.”

The rest of the calls fell into smaller categories, such as informational inquiries about certain substances, requests to prepare or buy drugs, or calls from “trip-sitters” assisting a person on psychedelics.

Psilocybin was the most commonly reported substance (9,348 callers), followed by LSD (2,247callers), cannabis (2,004 callers), and ketamine (1,194 callers), and MDMA (682 callers), with ayahuasca and other drugs logging much smaller numbers.

Surprisingly, callers who had used cannabis reported the highest distress rate—47.2 percent had bad experiences with the drug. Though cannabis has a reputation as a low-stakes substance, the study confirms that it can induce real distress in some cases that warrant consideration for harm reduction. The distress rates for the rest of the commonly used psychedelics were only slightly lower than cannabis, ranging between 40 to 42 percent.

The study also revealed 43 rare but disturbing instances of “facilitator abuse,” including at remote retreats or ceremonial gatherings involving ayahuasca. In these cases, callers reported abuse from the people providing psychedelics, such as reports they had deliberately been given extra doses without consent.

Those reports “provide the first quantitative documentation of this phenomenon in a community help-seeking sample,” according to the study. “The pattern of these reports—clustering in ceremonial settings involving plant medicines, presenting primarily as trauma-processing calls, and involving callers with elevated rates of prior PTSD diagnoses—suggests that even modest surveillance through existing peer support infrastructure can detect harm occurring in unregulated psychedelic settings.”
Some calls also came from people who said they suffered from schizophrenia, or had taken multiple psychedelics, offering a rare glimpse of situations that could not be observed in clinical settings.

“This kind of data can inform us on these topics in the context of legalizing these drugs and making them accessible,” said Schoeller. “I'm glad that there's this data that exists that people can look into to support or contradict the claims that they make as to how these things should be done.”

The study also outlines several limitations, including its sample bias of people who are inclined to call a hotline in the first place—which is not representative of psychedelic consumers at large—as well as self-reported accounts of doses, among other factors that are impossible to verify.

Despite the noisiness of the data, however, it contains helpful clues about avenues for future research. In Schoeller’s view, one of the most important revelations was that the success of a call was strongly linked to the perception that the hotline volunteer showed genuine care and empathy toward the caller. Using 2,777 postinteraction satisfaction surveys, the team found that the few negative experiences with the hotline tended to stem from feelings that the volunteer was dismissive, or didn’t seem to care about the caller.

“My takeaway is that the number one thing that predicts whether a support call will not work” is “the volunteer being perceived as genuine,” Schoeller said. “That's something that, in many ways, poses a problem to the biomedical system of centralized hospitals. I'm not trying to be ideological in any way, but when you create a centralized institution where you throw everybody to a single place to get care” then “clinicians become burned out.”

For this reason, Schoeller and his colleagues plan to follow up on the role of perceived care and empathy in treatment, and to emphasize this factor in guidance for community-based peer support for people in crisis due to psychedelics. It also reinforces the value of the Fireside Project’s hotline, which provides a safe and confidential service for people who might be reluctant to contact emergency services because of the criminalization of these substances or fear of incurring medical debt.

“For many people, they have experiences with psychedelics, and they may not be required to go to the ER, but they still need someone to help them navigate the difficult experience,” Schoeller concluded. “The hotline can truly be a lifeline for them.”

db28dde45a2fbb76: For the first time in the country, a candidate managed to turn the results in the run-off
Originally published on Global Voices
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves Brazil’s flag surrounded by a crowd of supporters in São Paulo, during the 2026 election campaign. Photo by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr (CC BY-SA 4.0).

On April 7, 2018, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had been president of Brazil twice, waited in the building of the Metalworkers’ Union, in São Bernardo do Campo, São Paulo state, where his political life started in the 1970s, to be arrested by the Federal Police following convictions for corruption and money laundering.

Gilberto Carvalho, one of his oldest allies, later recalled that they hoped for a crowd of 50,000, but only 10,000 people waited outside. Lula looked through the window, grabbed his arm, and said, “Gilbertinho, we go to war with the soldiers we have.”
Eight years and six months after that day, on October 25, 2026, Lula was elected president of Brazil for the fourth time, supported by millions of people in the streets and an army of his own online.
The convictions against him were later annulled by the Federal Supreme Court (STF), which ruled that the lower federal court lacked jurisdiction and was biased. Lula spent 580 days in prison.

His latest victory was also the first time a candidate was elected after losing the first round in Brazil. In 20 days, Lula, a member of the Workers‘ Party, managed to turn Flavio Bolsonaro’s advantage of 2.2 million votes into a win by a 4.4 million-vote difference.

As the BBC explained, both candidates increased their votes in the second round, in an election with the lowest abstention rate since 2006. The leftist’s victory came from five million new voters, with a drop in absences, blank and nulled votes, says UOL news portal. Also, it left the world in awe, wondering just how he did it.
On the streets and an online army

Lula gathered the support of massive crowds in the streets and an online army led by federal deputy André Janones, who poses with him during a livestream. Photos by Ricardo Stuckert/Lula Oficial on Flickr. Collage by Global Voices on Canva Pro.

Lula reset his campaign in the second round, bringing new people into his team and riding on the so-called R-factor — ruas e redes, Portuguese for “streets and networks” — which started organically and was embraced by his team. On October 5, while many were dispirited by the first-round results, students from UFF (Fluminense Federal University) took to the streets in the city of Niterói, Rio de Janeiro state, in a pro-Lula act that spread nationally in the following weeks.

Lula’s official events also left the stage used in the first round and instead moved to the streets for massive marches, during which he led the crowds from a truck and talked to supporters about his proposals, his own history, and the threats presented by his opponent, all while waving Brazil’s flag.

On October 7, federal deputy André Janones posted about an initiative that would hack social media and contribute to turning the election around. On X, Janones wrote that he had recruited 1.5 million people for a WhatsApp channel, inviting more to join and saying: “This is the ONLY way of bursting the bubble, since Meta only organically delivers right-leaning content.” After threats of being taken down by the electoral court, by voting day, the public channel had 11 million people.

Janones’ guide for social media, nicknamed “cultural Janonismo,” included ignoring opponents’ posts and setting coordinated actions, like the viral trend of Lula’s supporters wearing the national team's yellow jersey, a symbol hijacked by the right for over 10 years. Every command delivered to the soldiers of “Lula's Army” — new hashtags, a post to engage, a live feed to watch — Janones would follow up in capital letters with an order: “EXPLODE.” The methodology is already inspiring people in Spain and France.
ATTENTION! People are mistranslating what I said!
I NEVER said people should block far-right accounts. I said they should IGNORE THEIR POSTS!
Blocking actually works against this strategy because the algorithm will understand that you didn’t see the content simply because you blocked the account.

However, when a post appears in your feed and you ignore it, you don’t read it, don’t like it, don’t comment on it, or engage with it in any way, the algorithm will interpret that content as irrelevant because it was shown to you and you chose not to engage with it!
THERE IS A HUGE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN BLOCKING CONTENT AND IGNORING IT!
— André Janones (@AndreJanonesMG) October 28, 2026

During the campaign, users accused Meta of affecting their engagement when posting pro-Lula content. On October 16, Folha de S. Paulo reported that Meta employees admitted that Lula’s accounts “were hindered by ‌restrictions.” The tech company denied any political bias after the electoral court ordered it to give equal treatment to both candidates.

The campaign was also boosted by a change of rhetoric, says anthropologist Rosana Pinheiro-Machado. “This was not mobilisation in a vacuum. Lula focused less on sovereignty and more on people’s concrete concerns.”
On voting day, the pro-Lula mobilization also resulted in Brazilians over 70, who are not required to vote, showing up, some brought by relatives, in the call for democracy.
The Bolsonaros’ risk

On the other side, bolsonaristas began the second round by celebrating their candidates’ major wins in seats for state governments, the federal senate, lower chamber, and state parliaments from north to south. Two of Jair Bolsonaro’s sons, his wife, and one of his brothers were elected.

But in the 20 days that followed, scenes from bolsonarista events led many Brazilians to question what country they wanted. In an act by Flavio’s campaign, at Paulista Avenue, in São Paulo, a traditional point for political protests, his supporters carried an inflatable missile with the message “Trump nuke Brazil,” which many saw as a treasonous statement. In another event in Rio, a white man was seen holding a Black man in plastic chains, with Lula’s name on his back. The man told the police that the idea was to represent the leftist leader as Satan. There was also an escalation of political violence, including threats, beatings, and killings.

Add to those the weight of the Bolsonaros’ own history, along with a growing anti-Bolsonarista sentiment. Jair, the father, is under house arrest for a coup attempt that included a plan to assassinate Lula, his VP Geraldo Alckmin, and a Supreme Court justice. Flávio himself vowed to change the 1988 Constitution, created after the military dictatorship, once elected.

Forty-five-year-old Flávio was always considered less radical than his younger siblings, despite selling himself as anti-establishment, even as an elected politician since 2002. This always guaranteed him a privileged forum and protection when investigations drew closer. In 2020, former judge Sergio Moro, who convicted Lula, resigned as Jair Bolsonaro’s justice minister after the president tried to intervene in the Federal Police to protect Flávio, then a suspect in “an embezzlement and money-laundering” scheme within his state deputy office.

During the 2026 campaign, Flávio’s links to other scandals were exposed by the Brazilian press. Among them, the money he received from a disgraced banker for his father’s movie biopic (Dark Horse), without ever proving the final destination of the funds.

Flávio is currently under investigation in three different inquiries at the Supreme Court. After he lost the election, he fled to the US after the Federal Police asked to seize his passports (he also has Italian citizenship), considering him a flight risk.
Lula’s last dance
Brazilians waiting in line to vote, in Brasília, the country's capital, on October 25. Photo by Fabio Rodrigues-Pozzebom/Agência Brasil. Used with permission.

On voting day, both campaigns asked the electoral court (TSE) to extend the voting period. Lula’s campaign requested the extension following reports that Bolsonaro-allied mayors reduced public transportation in some capitals, while Flávio’s claimed storms in states where he had stronger support affected voter turnout. After the TSE failed to rule on the requests, they were referred to the Supreme Court, where Justice Cristiano Zanin, Lula’s former defense lawyer, appointed by him to the court, ruled that polls should remain open for two more hours. Zanin was randomly selected for the case.

Despite having his own request answered by the ruling, Flávio has been using this as a motive to contest the results, even though they were recognized by the electoral court's president Kassio Nunes Marques, a Supreme Court justice appointed by Jair Bolsonaro, following Flávio’s suggestion. His own party — PL, Liberal Party — also published a note acknowledging Lula’s election win. Around 34,000 votes were registered during the extended period, which had little impact on the final numbers.

The 2026 candidacy was Lula’s seventh time running for president and his fourth election. Even though he is known as a popular leader, back in August, 43 percent of Brazilians disapproved of his government. The campaign underestimated frustration with the government’s fiscal performance, public debt, inflation rates, and how people still link corruption scandals to the left, even when right-linked figures are at the center.

Flávio’s counter-medicine at the beginning of the campaign was the promise of a super-scissor cut to all public spending, modelling Javier Milei’s steps in Argentina. One of the people appointed to his economic team talked openly about privatization. This brought many investors and the upper classes to his side. On the second turn, however, eyeing the election, he toned down and started promising to keep all social programs from Lula’s governments, without explaining the math of his actual government plan.
With the majority of bolsonaristas and right-leaning politicians in both the Senate and the Lower Chamber, Lula will start the most challenging of his four terms next year.

Besides dealing with the 11 trillion BRL of federal debt (around USD 2 trillion), he promised in his victory speech: “This will be the term in which I'll listen to the Brazilian people the most about what they want me to do in this country. We'll work to make our digital communication stronger. And I even got a cell phone now. Get ready.”
Written by Global Voices Brazil
01e3da261c2e8c21: A court-ordered reassessment will set new values for every property in Allegheny County. Robert D. Strovers/Moments Collection via Getty ImagesAllegheny County will undergo a countywide reassessment of every property it taxes for the first time since 2012. A county judge ordered the reassessment in August 2026, requiring the work to begin by July 1, 2027, and finish within five years. The goal is to bring property values in line with today’s market. That could shift the tax burden among property owners across the county. State anti-windfall rules may require local governments to lower their tax rates after a reassessment to ensure they balance and equalize the tax reassessments. Individual bills may go up or down. For many homeowners, property taxes are confusing. Terms such as assessment, millage rate and school district tax come up often, but taxpayers may not know what they mean or how each one affects their annual tax bill. In Pittsburgh, property taxes pay for schools, parks, libraries, public safety and other local services. I research and teach government finance at Penn State Harrisburg, including a course on state and local taxation. Here’s a plain-language guide to how Pittsburgh’s property taxes work. What your home is worth – on paper The first concept is the property assessment. Allegheny County’s Office of Property Assessments gives every property an assessed value. That value is the basis for calculating property taxes. The Allegheny County Courthouse is also home to the county treasurer’s office, which collects county property taxes. tupungato/iStock Collection via Getty Images Plus An assessed value isn’t necessarily what a home would sell for today. Some places, such as Philadelphia, assess property at full market value. Other jurisdictions assess property at a set percentage of market value. In Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago, homes are assessed at 10% of their market value. That doesn’t mean Chicago-area homeowners pay less. When assessments are a smaller share of market value, tax rates are set higher to raise the same amount of money. Allegheny County assesses at full value, but it uses what properties were worth in 2012. The court-ordered reassessment is meant to close the gap between those 2012 values and today’s market. Allegheny County’s 14-year gap would be unusual almost anywhere else. Pennsylvania is the only state that doesn’t require counties to reassess on a regular schedule, while most states do so at least every six years. Within Pennsylvania, though, Allegheny is far from the worst: Butler County hasn’t reassessed since 1969. Homeowners can look up their assessment on the county’s real estate portal. What a mill means Once a property has an assessed value, each local government applies a millage rate to figure out the tax owed. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. A home assessed at $100,000 has 100 units of $1,000 in value. Pittsburgh property owners pay property taxes to three government entities: Allegheny County, the City of Pittsburgh and Pittsburgh Public Schools. Each one sets its own millage rate. For 2026, the city’s general rate is 9.67 mills. The city also charges 0.5 mill for parks and 0.25 mill for libraries. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, and Allegheny County charges 6.43 mills. Together, those rates add up to 27.307 mills. For a city home assessed at $100,000, that comes to about $2,731 a year before any exemptions or discounts. The county’s property tax worksheet and the county treasurer’s millage rate page list current rates. These rates are set each year, and all of them will be cut when reassessed values take effect, since the law requires rates to drop as total values rise. The biggest slice: Schools School taxes are often the largest share of a homeowner’s property tax bill. In Pennsylvania, property taxes are a major source of revenue for public schools. They help fund salaries for teachers, updates and maintainance for buildings, transportation, and technology and educational programs. School tax rates vary widely across Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Public Schools charges 10.457 mills, well below the suburban districts around it. North Allegheny, one of the lowest-taxing suburban districts, charges about 20.4 mills for the 2026-27 school year. Two of the highest are Mt. Lebanon at about 32 mills and Penn Hills at about 32.6 mills. The county treasurer publishes a full list of school district rates. Help for homeowners and seniors Some homeowners qualify for programs that lower their tax bills. The Allegheny County Homestead exemption, known as Act 50, cuts $18,000 from the assessed value of a qualified, owner-occupied, primary residence property’s county taxes. There’s no income limit: Any homeowner who lives in the property as their primary residence qualifies. A home assessed at $100,000 is taxed on just $82,000, which saves about $116 a year. Enrolling in Act 50 also automatically applies Pittsburgh’s $15,000 exemption, which covers the parks and library levies, and a larger Pittsburgh Public Schools exemption that is set each year. Applications for this exemption are due March 1 and need to be filed only once. The senior citizen tax relief program, known as Act 77, takes another 30% off county taxes for homeowners who are at least 60, have household incomes of $30,000 or less and have owned and lived in their home for at least 10 years. For a qualifying senior with that $100,000 home, the county bill would drop from about $527 to about $369. If you think your assessment’s too high Homeowners who believe their assessment is too high can appeal their assessment to the county’s Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review. Filing is free; appeals can be submitted online, by email or in person. Appeals are filed the year before the tax year they affect. The appeal window for 2027 bills closed Sept. 1, 2026. The next window, for 2028 bills, is expected to run from July 1 to Sept. 1, 2027, around the time the reassessment is set to begin. At an appeal hearing, homeowners can argue their property’s value using either 2012 prices or today’s market. Recent sales of similar homes nearby can help show whether an assessment is out of line. The board can lower the assessment, leave it as is or raise it. What reassessment means for you Pittsburgh property taxes come down to two elements: the property’s assessed value and the millage rates set by the county, the city and the school district. Understanding how these elements work together can help homeowners read and comprehend their tax bills and better plan for one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a home, next to the mortgage payment. That understanding will matter more as the reassessment gets underway. When new values take effect, some homeowners will see their share of the tax burden rise and others will see it fall. The direction depends on how their property’s value has changed compared with changes of other similar properties since 2012. Read more of our stories about Pittsburgh and Pennsylvania. 62c5ca7a60baabf4: Economic pessimism among Americans in both political parties is deepening ahead of the November midterm elections, amid factors such as high energy prices and cost-of-living pressures. AP Photo/Jeff ChiuPolling is looking grim for Republicans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, 2026, due in large part to deep pessimism among the public about the economy. At first glance, this might seem surprising. With the exception of inflation, many economic measures remain strong, including gross domestic product growth. But consumer sentiment continues to languish. This has prompted a debate over whether mere “vibes” are in play, or whether these long-used metrics are no longer capturing something fundamental to Americans’ economic well-being. This debate matters politically because voters are placing an overwhelming priority on the economy as an issue in the midterms. A Pew Research survey in early October 2026 found that 84% of registered voters said the economy was very important to their vote, and the concern is bipartisan. Among the issues in that Pew survey, for example, “the economy” was the least polarizing, with 82% of Republicans and 88% of Democrats ranking it as very important. Meanwhile, the overall drop in voters’ economic outlook has largely been driven by growing pessimism among Republicans. While Democrats remain much gloomier about the economy than Republicans, the gap is narrowing. These trends help explain why Democrats are expected to make significant gains in Congress: This election will likely be seen as an indictment of how well the economy is working for ordinary Americans under President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress, despite strong macroeconomic measures. So what is going on? As a scholar of financial markets and global inequality, I believe the relationship between how people see their own finances and their view of the broader economy is also changing on a more fundamental level. And this shift will affect how they judge the next class of lawmakers in power. Reality versus ‘vibes’ When scholars try to understand how people judge the economy – and how they separate their own personal circumstances from the broader economy – one of their key reference points is the University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index. It asks respondents about their personal finances, their short-term and long-term economic outlook, and whether they think it’s a good time to make major purchases. This gauge has historically tracked key economic measures of consumer spending and inflation: The state of the broader economy usually shapes the way people think about their own financial well-being. But in recent years, these have diverged. By many measures, the economy is doing well, but people feel they’re falling behind. And this has only become more pronounced ahead of the midterms. Despite strong consumer spending, robust business investment and low unemployment, consumer sentiment keeps slipping and is now 10% below where it was a year ago, according to the Michigan index. Some commentators point to ongoing inflation as the reason for gloom. It has remained stubbornly above the Federal Reserve’s annual 2% target rate due to drivers like tariffs, energy price hikes stemming from Middle East turmoil, and massive amounts of investment in the artificial intelligence build-out. But what’s really happening is that consumer sentiment data and inflation data have become untethered. Inflation has actually dropped sharply from its 21st-century peak of 9.1% in June 2022 after the pandemic to 3.7% in September 2026, but consumer sentiment is lower now than it was even then. What about wages? Here, too, the data also doesn’t fully explain this disconnect. While inflation makes consumer goods pricier, it also lifts pay. Inflation-adjusted wages actually increased between 2022 and the first half of 2026, all while consumer sentiment remained weak. What has changed in recent months is that inflation-adjusted wages are now falling – which could help explain the darkening outlook among voters. Inequality versus growth One possibility is that deeply entrenched inequality explains this divergence. Compared with other eras of moderate-to-high inflation, the U.S. economy today is much more unequal. Income inequality has increased over the past 20 years, narrowing only during the 2008 and 2020 crises before quickly widening to prior levels. This trend is important for understanding which consumers are shelling out cash. The Fed has consistently cited strong consumer spending in its economic assessments, but the richest 10% of Americans account for half of that spending today. Meanwhile, spending by the bottom 80% of earners has fallen behind inflation. In other words, the strong total consumer spending figures reported as official data are being driven by very wealthy Americans and fail to reflect the experience of typical consumers who are the bulk of the electorate. This trend of increasing inequality has been particularly acute in terms of wealth: The top 0.1% of American households together own five times as much wealth as the bottom 50%. Much of this reflects the uneven gains of the stock market boom and how wealth is taxed. In short, Americans’ economic malaise might be driven by concerns over income and wealth that conventional measures don’t fully capture. A surging stock market in 2026 helped boost Americans’ retirement accounts, but it hasn’t translated into greater consumer confidence. AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura It’s not just about me When it comes to consumer surveys like the University of Michigan index, economists generally assume that the answers reflect the personal experience of respondents. But I agree with other scholars who argue that sometimes these answers may be based less on people’s own circumstances and more on how they view the economy as a whole. This assessment could reflect, for example, concerns like equity, equality of opportunity and economic justice. When responses are driven by a concern for collective well-being rather than just personal material self-interest, social scientists refer to such perceptions as “sociotropic.” This last point isn’t just theoretical. Research suggests voters tend to weight their perceptions of the economy more heavily than their personal financial circumstances when deciding whether to vote for the incumbent party. Trade is one good example. Americans’ preferences for trade policy are driven less by how a particular measure, like tariffs, would impact them personally and more by how they think it would affect the country as a whole. If consumer sentiment follows a similar path, that could explain the divergence between generally strong economic trends and weak consumer sentiment. People are thinking not just about their own conditions but those of the U.S. as a whole, and it’s possible that their understanding of “the economy” includes its relationship to inequality. Understanding the disconnect between the economic data traditionally used to assess the economy’s health and Americans’ perceptions of that economy is important not just to the scholars trying to make sense of it – it could also help set an agenda for the incoming Congress. If economic insecurity punishes the governing party at the polls, the next Congress will be expected to do something about it once sworn in. Voters generally back the incumbent party when the economy is doing well and the out-party when it’s not. But how they judge the health of the economy is not straightforward, and the past six years suggest that improving headline measures of economic health – without regard to Americans’ lived experience and their concerns about what kind of economy is being built – may not be enough to assuage voters’ concerns. e60a65d0c75b0995: Recent elections in Brazil and Israel have yielded different political outcomes. In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow and ultimately surprise victory in a presidential runoff vote has kept him in office. In Israel, meanwhile, an inconclusive election result has left uncertainty over the formation of the next government. These outcomes are likely to have an effect on the stability of the financial systems in both countries. Historically, financial experts believed elections primarily caused brief, nervous jitters in national stock markets. As prior evidence shows, the impact of political uncertainty is often concentrated around the election period, with short-lived spikes in market volatility. But our 2026 study of 147 national elections across 22 OECD economies between 2000 and 2023 reveals a much deeper, longer-lasting reality. To understand this, we must first demystify a common banking term: systemic risk. This is the financial equivalent of a domino effect. It is the danger that a shock to one institution or sector could trigger a widespread collapse across the entire financial system. We saw this in action on a large scale during the 2008 global financial crisis. At that time, the distress of a few highly interconnected institutions threatened to bring down the entire global financial system. Massive government intervention was required to stop the dominoes from falling. Our findings show that systemic risk follows a broadly hump-shaped trajectory. It dips before scheduled elections, then rises during and after the vote. The risk remains elevated for up to 12 months, particularly when the incumbent government loses office. Pre-election spending that supports economic activity, alongside possible government suppression of adverse information about economic and financial conditions, offers an explanation for the temporary calm observed before elections. How elections affect systemic risk Systemic risk dips before elections, then rises during and after the vote, remaining elevated for up to 12 months. Kladakis and Skouralis (2026) / Journal of Banking and Finance, CC BY-NC-ND Our study suggests that political continuity can be a financial asset for national banking systems. But Brazil’s recent experience nevertheless shows that continuity does not automatically reassure investors. Lula reversed a first-round election deficit of more than 2 million votes to secure his reelection. This was the first time since Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy that a president has managed to overturn a first-round defeat. So the result surprised markets that had positioned for Lula’s challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, to take office. On October 26, the day after the runoff vote, Brazil’s benchmark stock index fell 13.9%, while its currency lost 8.1% against the US dollar. There was a modest recovery the following day, with stocks gaining around 1%. The immediate market reaction does not suggest a banking crisis is underway in Brazil. Whether it develops into broader financial instability depends on how financial institutions and borrowers absorb the shock. Our study also found that elections that yield no clear winner raise systemic risk, as they leave policy uncertainty over budgets and regulation unresolved. Israel has long struggled to establish durable governing coalitions, and its October 27 election left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority. While the US president, Donald Trump, had openly endorsed Israel’s incumbent prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, some investors had been positioning for a change of government. The inconclusive result has unsettled markets that had anticipated a clearer political outcome. During trading on October 28, the day after the election, Israeli stocks fell around 3%. Israel’s currency, the shekel, also weakened by approximately 2% against the US dollar. And the ten-year government bond yield rose nearly five basis points to 4.13%, signalling higher borrowing costs. Finally, our data shows that snap elections are associated with larger increases in systemic risk. Here, again, Israel is an instructive example. Israel experienced ten elections between 2000 and 2023, seven of which were snap elections. This included five snap elections during its 2018-22 political crisis. Cushioning the blow Strong economic growth and high public trust in government cushion the financial blow of elections, as they naturally insulate the banking system. Macroprudential policies, the regulatory guardrails designed to protect the entire banking system, also play a crucial role. By strengthening financial safeguards such as capital buffers for banks, regulators can help the system absorb political shocks. Unfortunately, evidence suggests that political incentives to stimulate lending before an election can encourage the loosening of these safeguards. This leaves national financial systems more exposed to subsequent shocks. In Turkey and India, for example, governments have historically used state-owned banks to expand consumer and mortgage credit aggressively before tightly contested elections. This creates a short-term boost in economic activity and voter goodwill, but often leaves the financial system vulnerable to a hangover of non-performing loans and instability once the votes are counted. As well as being political events, elections are macroeconomic shockwaves. While the stock market might experience a brief spike in volatility on election night, the true test lies in the systemic risk that lingers in the banking sector for months afterwards. In Brazil, Lula eventually secured backing from voters for a fourth presidential term. Strengthening financial stability there after this surprise result will require rebuilding market confidence with a credible fiscal plan that explains how campaign promises will be funded and puts public debt on a sustainable path. In Israel, prospects for a viable government remain uncertain. And even if one emerges, it may offer markets only limited reassurance while the war in the Middle East continues to pose risks to financial stability in Israel and worldwide. 298d4aed9fdf5e94: My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle. Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament. Studying the anatomy of the skeletons of living and fossil gavials has given us a better understanding of the group’s evolution in recent years. CT scans have enabled us to look inside their skulls, giving us a window into their brains and sensory systems. This has revealed new anatomical information that helps differentiate species, and has allowed us to infer aspects of the biology and ecology of some of the extinct species. For example, in an extinct group of crocodile relatives known to have lived entirely in the ocean, other researchers found thickening of the outer wall of their inner ear to cope with the higher pressures seen at ocean depths. My colleagues and I have found similar evidence for a marine lifestyle in some fossil gavials. This ability to live in the ocean was lost in living species, which are restricted to rivers and lakes. Several of the gavial fossils we have been studying from Africa and Europe were first reported in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and they were often described as species of Tomistoma, i.e. closely related to Tomistoma schlegelii, one of the two living species of gavials. Our previous work and that of others has shown that some of these extinct species are not closely related to Tomistoma, with new names given for some of them. However, many of these historically described species remain neglected. Led by my former PhD student, Paul Burke, now a researcher at the Swedish Museum of Natural History in Stockholm, along with colleagues from Egypt and Germany, we re-examined one of these species in a new study. In the 1920s, several fossils were collected from northeastern Egypt. These were found in a limestone rock, known as the Mokattam Formation, that had formed 45 million years ago in a shallow marine environment when sea levels were higher. This region was submerged at this time. These fossils, including a nearly complete skull, were described in 1927 as belonging to Tomistoma, because of their superficial resemblance to the living species, Tomistoma schlegelii. However, aided by the use of CT scanning, our team was able to identify several anatomical differences, including the presence of raised rims around the eye sockets, which are absent in Tomistoma. The Great Sphinx of Giza. Fernanda-Belen/Shutterstock The Mokattam Formation already has a legacy: 4,500 years ago, these rocks were used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza. The gavial skull shares more than this origin story though. Just as the Sphinx is famously missing the tip of its nose, the fossil is also missing the tip of its snout. This coincidence led us to name the new crocodile Herugavialis cairensis after the Egyptian falcon-headed god Heru (also known as Horus), who is often thought to be the inspiration for the iconic Sphinx. Both northern Africa and southern Europe hosted a high diversity of gavials (and other crocodiles) during much of the last 80 million years, with these species thriving in the shallow, marine environments that covered much of the Mediterranean region at the time. Unlike living gavials, it is likely that some of these species could cross oceans. This diversity appears to have persisted through the devastating mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, and probably fluctuated during alternating warmer and cooler intervals over the next 60 million years, tied to higher and lower sea levels, respectively. However, crocodiles disappeared from the Mediterranean region approximately 6 million years ago and never returned. Their demise coincides with an event known as the Messinian salinity crisis, when the Mediterranean essentially dried up as a result of being sealed off from the Atlantic Ocean. As the seawater became increasingly salty with the heightened evaporation of water, it would have become ever more intolerable to the animals inhabiting it, even those usually able to live in saltwater, leading to the loss of crocodiles and many other species. The signature of this event can still be observed today, with the Mediterranean Sea still much saltier than the oceans, and crocodiles entirely absent from this region. The remaining living gavials live far away from the Mediterranean, but the loss of the adaptations that would allow them to live in saltwater means that they would not be able to survive there regardless. Rapid and extreme changes in temperature, sea level, and aridification are critical components of the current climate emergency, and events such as the Messinian salinity crisis show that they can have a lasting impact on biodiversity, spanning millions of years. 5254ea631641939f: When the Booker prize was first launched in 1969, its aim was to get more people reading and to stimulate discussion about contemporary literature. Now, we all know reading is at an all time low but there really has never been a better time to reignite your love of fiction and to discover (or rediscover) your love of reading. And, this year’s shortlist is really a testament to the breadth of stories available out there. There’s poetic historic fiction with May we Feed the King about a reluctant medieval king from Rebecca Perry. For lovers of science fiction, M. John Harrison has written a tale about aliens and social collapse set on the Kentish coast. And, there’s laughter to be found in Black Bag by Luke Kennard about an out-of-work actor who lands a gig in a psychological experiment. There are also new works by previous winners and nominees. Marlon James is back with a startling portrait of the lives of gay men in Jamaica. Douglas Stuart gives us his chilly Hebridean family drama, John of John. And, finally there’s the gentle political commentary of Elizabeth Strout’s The Things We Never Say about what happens when good people stay quiet. Ahead of the prize being announced on November 9, we’ve asked six experts to guide you through the nominations for 2026. Black Bag by Luke Kennard Black Bag was inspired by a 1967 experiment at Oregon State University in which an individual cloaked in black sat mutely in a seminar for a semester. Where the study focused on the reactions of the witnesses, Black Bag is the story and meditations of the man who becomes increasingly attached to his role and, amusingly, his bag. Kennard’s protagonist is a flat-broke actor relying on cash-in-hand corporate murder mysteries and the kindness of his friend Claudio in an otherwise dismal world. Wearing the bag outside of the classroom not only removes the problem of how to be but even attracts the attention of a female professor who wants “to fuck nothing” – he is both strikingly visible and anonymous. The novel is laugh-out-loud funny but melancholy and provocative too. Some of Bag’s strongest relationships are those he imagines, like ongoing conversations with his parents’ dog and narrated village life with a fictional Swedish wife. By Tory Young, associate professor in English literature The End of Everything by M. John Harrison The backdrop of The End of Everything is alien invasion, but treated with a ludic contempt for genre conventions. An ineffectual war is being waged against the sardonically named iGhetti – amorphous entities who have leaked into the world “from the astral plane”. Phillip Tennent, a beachcomber somewhere on the Kent coast, finds an iGhetti artefact washed up by the tide, a thing that slowly begins to ape humanity, an event which throws Tennent’s life and the life of his ageing, forgetful aunt, Marnie, into brutality and random violence. In his 2023 “anti-memoir”, Wish I Was Here, M. John Harrison writes of his world-building: “I’d rather pile up real facts to reveal something evidently unreal than pile up invented facts to make something unreal seem real.” The real facts pile up here – cheek by jowl with dense allusion and the surreal – into a work of slippery unreality, which is nevertheless congested with raw feeling and startling poetry. Tim Jarvis, senior lecturer in creative writing The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout Elizabeth Strout’s slight book is a series of snapshot insights into the thoughts and memories of protagonist, Massachusetts Bay high school History teacher Artie Dam. With Artie at the centre, it captures the problems, relationships, and futures of a community: extended family, students, colleagues, whose lives connect unexpectedly, or are influenced by brief interactions – statements of support or honesty. Sometimes, Artie worries he lies through kindness; he isn’t to know that his positivity manifests unexpected joys. Nominated for the prize three times before, Pulitzer-winner Strout’s elegant text is both melancholic and evocative. Measured, thoughtful, and good, Artie Dam is caught up in political, socioeconomic, personal, and philosophical questions threatening to derail his life. These also bring him closer to people he loves, including his son Rob and his extravagant, reckless friend, Flossie. Artie clings on to the possibility of free will while the reader hopes that everything will work out well for Artie. Jenni Ramone, associate professor of postcolonial and global literature The Disappearers by Marlon James The Disappearers pulls the reader into a seemingly knowable time and place – the Jamaica of 1988 to 2005. Yet what James seeks to make known and felt is not to be found in any record or archive. The action begins as eight men gather to rehearse John Herbert’s provocative and unsettling 1967 US prison play Fortune and Men’s Eyes about homosexuality and sexual power play. A homophobic mob storms a rehearsal and by the end of the evening, one man is murdered and another blinded. Shortly afterwards, two disappear. Six years later, the search for the disappeared continues and the novel makes it clear that gay men in Jamaica disappear way before anyone notices they’ve gone. In Marlon’s writing of their differences in class, ethnicity, social privilege, sexual preference, desire for attachment, emotional intelligence, eloquence, and identity constructions, the novel writes away the enforced flatness of slurs and stereotypes of gay men to humanise at scale. It’s an everyday act of narrative restitution that has revolutionary significance given the continuing sexual politics of Jamaica. Read more: The Disappearers: Marlon James’s new novel gives voice to the gay men Jamaica erased Alison Donnell, professor of modern literature John of John by Douglas Stuart An omniscient narrator presides over John of John as we follow John-Calum Macleod – Cal – a recent Edinburgh art school grad, who has been studying fashion and textiles. Learning that his maternal grandmother Ella is ill, Cal is persuaded to return home by his lay-preacher father, John, during one of their weekly phone calls. Once home, we’re witness to the claustrophobic dysfunction of the Macleods’ home, a small croft where John rears sheep, weaves tweed, and has strong connections to the “Wee Free” church. John struggles to show anything other than contempt towards his son, who has come home with growing debt and orange hair. As a young gay man hailing from a strict and repressive Free Presbyterian background, Cal remains still in the closet as far as his island is concerned. The torment and guilt of his sexuality weigh heavily on Cal throughout the novel. The drama and (sometimes verging on implausible) twists of this book make it feel like a soap opera, in the traditional sense of the term: small, interconnected characters and high melodrama, with domestic spaces as scenes of desire, revelation and unpredictability. But this is not a criticism. Stuart’s lyrical prose and atmospheric narrative elevate the genre – reimagining the domestic and familial tropes by focusing on the unrequited affections of the men in the story. Read more: John of John: weaving an island tale of secrets that lie beneath repression and shame Stevie Marsden, lecturer in publishing May We Feed The King by Rebecca Perry This is a poet’s novel, without the seductive immersion more usual for those on the Booker shortlist. In three parts, the first and last are narrated by a person – their sex is never given – whose job is creating food scenes in historical sites. Following a never specified tragedy, they are commissioned to create a tableaux in a former palace. In the archive they come across a page detailing the failings of a medieval king. The middle part of the novel is that king’s story. While the narrator’s work is about bringing the past close, the novel itself is an exercise in distance. We are told very little about the tableaux maker; the characters in the middle section are known only by their roles. This distance enacts the novel’s central questions about history and storytelling, but it is not a cold distance. The novel is full of passages of beauty and delight. The narrator’s description of a website that sells replica food made me laugh and took my breath away. edf030352b667085: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders.

What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue.

Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says.

Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others.

It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson.

Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps.

That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost).

The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai.

Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people.

It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says.
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here?

Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says.

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content. But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result.

When researchers at the University of Melbourne investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders. They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising. Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month. Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders.

The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders. Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020.

Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023. But anecdotally, things seem to be getting even worse. “There are more eating disorders, more severe eating disorders… and we’re seeing earlier ages of onset,” says Levinson. “We’re seeing eight- and nine-year-olds with eating disorders.”
“From what I’m hearing and seeing, I am not going to be surprised if that number isn’t at least doubling again,” she adds.

Levinson particularly worries about the impact of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, which have exploded in popularity in recent years. A Gallup survey conducted earlier this year suggested that 15% of Americans had used one of these drugs for weight loss. And they’re becoming more accessible—drug companies are working on new formulations that are both easier to take and more effective, and many people can buy versions of these drugs from compound pharmacies or dubious online sources.

In a small study published earlier this year, Levinson and her colleagues found that 30% of people with eating disorders had used GLP-1 drugs. The drugs might benefit some of those people. But 10% appeared to have misused the drugs. And Levinson thinks that figure is also an underestimate.

Levinson says she and her colleagues have seen children develop eating disorders after being prescribed GLP-1s for medical reasons. They’ve seen others—even children as young as 11—buy versions of these drugs over TikTok.

“We’re very concerned that GLPs will lead to even faster and more extreme weight loss in people with anorexia nervosa, and that patients will come to us in even more advanced stages of illness that become difficult to reverse,” says Bulik.

Both Bulik and Levinson are continuing to study the impacts of these drugs in eating disorders. In the meantime, both urge medical professionals to consider the risks GLP-1s might pose to people with those disorders. Bulik contributed to a set of research and clinical guidelines, published earlier this month, that recommends doctors screen for eating disorders before prescribing the drugs, for example. The guidelines also recommend more patient education and more robust monitoring of people who take GLP-1s.
If you think you or someone you know might have an eating disorder, you can find information and support at the National Eating Disorders Association.
